sent.prompt: When one collection is loaded into several resource groups, GetShardLeaders tags every leader with a resource group instead of taking a resource group in the request. Why was it done that way, and why can't the proxy just work out each leader's group from which nodes are in which resource group? While you're at it, how is one resource group's load progress reported?

output.text:
I answered this from the design note on per-resource-group load and shard-leader readiness. I didn't open the code it points to, and the note's design-doc file shows as missing on disk.

## Why leaders are tagged and the request has no resource group

A request-side `resource_group` filter was built first and then replaced. These are the reasons the note gives for the change:

- **Proxy cache:** A request filter would add a resource-group dimension to the proxy's shard-leader cache. That means one fetch and one entry per group per collection, and `InvalidateShardLeaderCache` would need new semantics. With a tag, the cache keeps one copy per collection and filters by group in memory.
- **Coverage:** A request filter returns one group per call. The tag returns every group in one call, so a caller can compare them.
- **Rolling upgrades:** An old coordinator ignores a request field and returns an unfiltered answer that looks like a normal one. With a response tag, an old coordinator leaves `ShardLeadersList.resource_groups` empty, and the proxy reads that as "unknown group". Routing a scoped request against unknown tags gets a retriable refusal, not a node from the wrong group.
- **Response shape:** The new field is `resource_groups` on `ShardLeadersList`, parallel to `node_ids`. It is appended in the same `info != nil` branch as the other arrays, so a dropped leader can't misalign the tags.

## Why the proxy can't derive the group from node membership

- **Borrowed nodes:** A replica's group is not the same as the group of the nodes it sits on. Replicas can borrow nodes from another group (`num_outgoing_node` / `num_incoming_node`). Intersecting a leader's node with a group's node set therefore isn't replica membership. The two diverge during rebalances, which is when this question matters most.
- **Lost mapping:** The `GetShardLeaders` response flattens all replicas into one list per channel and drops replica identity. Once the answer leaves QueryCoord, the mapping from leader to replica to group exists nowhere else, so only the coordinator can supply it.
- **Absent groups:** The tag also can't tell you whether a group has no replica or is still coming up. Replicas that aren't query-visible yet are dropped before the list is built, so their group is simply absent. The readiness surface (`ShardLeaderReadinessByResourceGroup`) is what separates those two cases.

## How one resource group's load progress is reported

- **Computation:** `LoadPercentageByResourceGroup` in `internal/querycoordv2/utils/resource_group_load_percentage.go` selects the replicas in that group. It computes each replica's coverage of the target (measured against `NextTargetFirst`) and reports the minimum, so the group counts as ready only when its slowest replica is.
- **Wire access:** You reach it through `ShowLoadCollectionsRequest.resource_group`. When set, `inMemory_percentages` is that group's progress. When empty, you get the old collection-wide figure, so `GetLoadingProgress` and existing callers are unchanged.
- **Return values:**
  - `-1` with no error means the group has no replica of the collection.
  - `0` means a replica exists but carries no targets yet.
  - `-1` with `ErrServiceNotReady` is retriable. It means the coordinator's stores aren't wired up yet.
  - `-1` with `ErrCollectionNotLoaded` is terminal. It means the load failed, and the failure reason is in the message.
  - `-1` with `ErrResourceGroupNotFound` means the group name doesn't exist.
- **Not a servability check:** The figure includes query-invisible replicas, so it can read 100 while readiness says `Ready=false`. It can also drop back below 100 when new segments land. Use it to answer "how far along is this group". To decide whether to route traffic to the group, use readiness.

sent.prompt: When one collection is loaded into several resource groups, GetShardLeaders tags every leader with a resource group instead of taking a resource group in the request. Why was it done that way, and why can't the proxy just work out each leader's group from which nodes are in which resource group? output.text:
I answered this from the design doc (`docs/design-docs/design_docs/20260824-per-resource-group-load-and-shard-leader-readiness.md`, PR #52716). I did not re-read the Go code or the proto to check it, so the CLAUDE.md doc-versus-code cross-check is still outstanding.

## Why each leader is tagged instead of the request taking a resource group

The doc says a request-side `resource_group` filter was built first and then replaced by the response tag. The new field is `ShardLeadersList.resource_groups`. It is a repeated string, parallel to `node_ids`, and holds the resource group of the replica each leader leads. The doc gives these reasons:

- **Proxy cache:** a request filter would turn the proxy's shard-leader cache from `map[collID]` into `map[collID]map[rg]`. That means N fetches and N entries per collection, and `InvalidateShardLeaderCache` would need new semantics. With a tag, the cache keeps one copy per collection and the group is filtered in memory, the same way the existing `serviceable` flag is.
- **Information:** one call returns every group, so a caller can compare them. A request filter returns one group per call.
- **Rolling upgrades:** an old coordinator would ignore a request field and return an unfiltered answer that looks like a filtered one. An old coordinator also leaves `resource_groups` empty, and the proxy reads that as "unknown". A scoped request then gets a retriable refusal instead of a node from the wrong group.
- **Readiness is separate:** the strict per-group refusal codes the filter design offered are covered by `ShardLeaderReadinessByResourceGroup`, which returns a structured verdict. Keeping both would have meant two contracts for one question.

## Why the proxy can't derive each leader's group from node membership

- **Borrowed nodes:** a replica can borrow nodes from another resource group (`num_outgoing_node` / `num_incoming_node`). A node being in a group's node set therefore doesn't mean the replica on it belongs to that group. The two diverge during rebalances, which is when the question matters.
- **Lost mapping:** before this change the builder flattened every replica's leaders into one list per channel. The replica, and so the resource group, was discarded inside QueryCoord, so only the coordinator can put it back.
- **Dropped leaders:** the `append` for the tag sits in the same `info != nil` branch as the other three arrays. A leader dropped at the NodeManager check therefore can't shift the tags that follow it.

Two limits on the tag:

- **Absence isn't "no replica":** query-invisible replicas are dropped before the list is built, so a group still coming up simply doesn't appear. Ask readiness to tell "still coming up" from "nobody loaded into it".
- **Nothing sets the scope yet:** nothing on the proxy's request path sets `ChannelWorkload.ResourceGroup`, so deployed routing is unchanged. The filter (`FilterByResourceGroup`) and its error contract ship ahead of the first consumer.

## How one resource group's load progress is reported

`LoadPercentageByResourceGroup` in `internal/querycoordv2/utils/resource_group_load_percentage.go` selects the replicas whose own resource group is `rgName`. It computes each replica's target coverage and reports the minimum, so the group counts as ready only when its slowest replica is. Coverage is measured against `NextTargetFirst`. The outcomes are:

| Result | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `-1`, no error | The group holds no replica of the collection. This is terminal once the load is registered. A poll that lands between the replica commit and the collection registration can also read `-1`, so confirm it across two polls. |
| `0`, no error | A replica exists but carries no targets yet, or the target set is empty. Wait. Any real progress reads at least `1`. |
| `-1`, `ErrServiceNotReady` | The coordinator isn't wired up yet. Retry. |
| `-1`, `ErrCollectionNotLoaded` (101) | The load failed terminally, and the cause is in the message. |
| `-1`, `ErrResourceGroupNotFound` (300) | `rgName` doesn't exist. This is checked first, so a typo isn't mistaken for an empty group. |

Things to know before using the figure:

- **Not a servability check:** a group whose replicas are all still query-invisible can read 100 while readiness says `Ready=false`. Use `ShardLeaderReadinessByResourceGroup` to decide whether to route to a group.
- **Don't AND the two:** the percentage re-arms below 100 when flushes or compactions add segments to the next target, so gating on `== 100` as well as `Ready` can spin forever.
- **Differs from `ShowLoadCollections`:** the per-group figure counts each target once, while the collection-wide figure averages partitions. It can also fall back below 100, because it is recomputed live instead of persisted.

sent.prompt: I'm about to start on the distributed query view work. Explain to a newcomer, as briefly as you can, what it changes about who does what between Proxy, QueryCoord, StreamingNode and QueryNode and why, what a DataView version and a QueryView version are, how a query view moves through its states, how much of it serves production traffic today, and where each part is written down.

output.text:
**Short version:** the design is real, but none of it is serving production queries yet. Proxy doesn't call the new client, and the new Coordinator runtime isn't activated.

## Who does what

Today the delegator logic would have to sit on StreamingNode (SN). SN would then forward every segment load/release, apply every delete, run every shard-level reduce and relay every QueryNode result. That makes it a single bottleneck that is hard to scale or replicate. The design changes four things:

- **QueryCoord** loads and releases all sealed segments itself, and builds the complete per-shard view of who holds what. SN only accepts view updates from it.
- **Proxy** runs a two-phase query and does all distributed reduce itself.
  - Phase 1: Proxy asks SN for a query plan (MVCC, optimization, view version).
  - Phase 2: Proxy sends the plan to SN and the QueryNodes, then reduces the results.
- **StreamingNode** serves the growing data, which is the only part it sees first. It generates plans, and it no longer forwards queries or applies deletes.
- **QueryNode (QN)** serves sealed segments. After a load, it subscribes to deletes from SN and applies them itself.

## The two version numbers

- **DataView / DataVersion** is a collection-wide, immutable snapshot of which sealed segments are loadable, plus each segment's manifest version.
  - It is versioned as `(streaming_version, compact_version)`, ordered lexicographically.
  - `streaming_version` goes up only on a flush (the growing-to-sealed handoff).
  - `compact_version` goes up on every other membership change: compaction, import, truncate, partition drop, or an L0 manifest advance.
  - It is rebuilt from SegmentMeta, not derived from compaction history.
- **QueryView version** is `((S,C), Q)`, scoped to one shard on one replica.
  - Whenever the DataVersion rises, Q resets to 1.
  - Q rises alone when the same data is redistributed, for example by a balance or a node crash.

## State machine

Normal path: `Preparing → Ready → Up → Down → Dropping → Dropped`. The error path is `Preparing → Unrecoverable → Dropping → Dropped`. Coord leads, and the nodes report back through the one `SyncQueryView` RPC.

- **Preparing:** Coord persists the view, pushes it to SN and the QNs, and waits for them to report Ready.
- **Ready:** Coord pushes Up to SN only.
- **Up:** SN confirms, and the view serves queries.
- **Down:** a higher view reaches Up. SN delays its own Down until the serving lease expires and no queries still hold the view.
- **Dropping / Dropped:** every node releases its resources and confirms, then Coord deletes the view from etcd.
- **QN:** it serves as soon as it is Ready and never sees Up or Down.
- **UpRecovering:** an SN-only state used while SN catches up on the WAL after a crash.

## How much is live

- **Built and tested:** the DataView manager, the SN plan and execution path, an injectable query client, and the QN resource and execution subsystem.
- **Not wired:**
  - Proxy doesn't use the new client. I grepped `internal/` and only `internal/views/queryclient` itself imports it.
  - Coordinator runtime activation, generation of QueryViews from the legacy load APIs, and WAL-secondary routing are all pending.
  - The remote delete stream to QN is only planned.
  - DDL query visibility (truncate, partition drop) is a TODO.
  - `transform_start_after_timetick` is on the wire but not populated.
- I read the docs and spot-checked the code (the proto enum, the SN files, and the Proxy import check), and they agree.

## Where it's written down

All of it is under `docs/design-docs/design_docs/qviews/`:

- `README.md` is the overview and index. It covers the architecture, DataView and QueryView versions, the lifecycle, and the consistency level.
- `data_view.md` covers the DataView contract, persistence, GC and recompute. `data_view_schema.md` covers its schema certification.
- `query_view_state_machine.md` is the per-state analysis for Coord, SN and QN.
- `query_view_lease.md` covers the SN serving lease. `syncer.md` covers the Coord-side `SyncQueryView` transport.
- `query/query_client.md`, `query/query_plan.md` and `query/query_execution.md` cover Proxy-side planning and execution.
- `querynode_extraction.md` and `qnview/querynode_queryview_resource_preparation.md` cover the QN side.
- `../wal/streamingnode_vchannel_wal_view.md` covers SN-side preparation.
- The wire types are in `pkg/proto/view.proto`.

Several of the other files in `qviews/` and `../wal/` look relevant too, for example `balancer_scanning.md`, `ddl_visibility.md` and `transform_start_after_timetick.md`. I didn't read those. CLAUDE.md says a design task needs every sub-document read. When you start, you'll need to read all of them.

sent.prompt: What does Import V3 change about how bulk import works compared with Import V2, and why was it needed? Is it what runs by default now?

output.text:
**No. Import V2 is still the default.** The gate `dataCoord.import.enableImportV3` defaults to `false`. You can see that in `configs/milvus.yaml:1049` and in `pkg/util/paramtable/component_param.go:8004`.

## Why V3 was needed

The design doc is `docs/design-docs/design_docs/20260921-import-v3-reshard-design.md`. It names these problems with V2:
- **Every source file is read twice.** V2 `PreImportTask` parses a whole file and keeps only statistics. `ImportTaskV2` then reads it again, hashes the rows and writes them into pre-allocated segments.
- **Many small segments.** Every file-group task splits the same `(vchannel, partition)` bucket, so a bucket ends up in many small segments.
- **Oversized metadata.** The `hashed_stats` table grows with vchannels × partitions. It can exceed etcd's default 1.5 MiB request size, so for example a 1024-partition table can't import natively.
- **Mid-import schema changes.** If the collection is altered during a V2 import, the job can hang in `IndexBuilding`.
- **A needless sort step.** V2 output goes through a post-import `Sorting` compaction.

## What V3 changes

- **One read of the source.** A count-only preimport gets exact per-file row counts. Ordinary imports use those counts to allocate PK/RowID ranges. Backup imports only size their object list. A `ReshardTask` then parses each source once, routes rows to `(vchannel, partition)` buckets, sorts them and writes immutable Parquet "fragments" plus a manifest.
- **Planning decides segment shape.** A planner packs fragments into per-segment, bucket-local plans across all source tasks. File-group boundaries no longer decide it.
- **One merge per segment.** Each `ImportTaskV3` does a k-way merge of one plan's fragments and writes one sorted segment through the existing Storage V2/V3 writers. A merge with too many inputs falls back to node-local intermediates, so the object store sees each fragment once.
- **Different job states.** V3 goes `PreImporting → AssigningIDRange → Resharding → Planning → Importing → IndexBuilding`. It has no `Sorting` stage, so it skips the post-import sort compaction.
- **A loud schema-change failure.** V3 compares an import-relevant schema projection at planning, at each result acceptance and before `IndexBuilding`. A mismatch fails the job with `ErrImportSysFailed` (2101).
- **Memory control and cleanup.** Memory is bounded by a slot budget, and overflow spills to local disk. Terminal jobs get their `import_v3/{job}/` prefix garbage-collected.
- **Progress weights.** `GetJobProgress` weights the stages differently from V2.

## When V3 actually runs

The version is resolved in `internal/datacoord/services.go:2085-2091`. A request with no explicit version becomes V3 only if both of these hold:
- `enableImportV3=true`.
- The import is not an L0 import and not a snapshot-source import.

The doc only mentions the L0 exclusion. The snapshot-source exclusion is in the code but not in the doc.

The gate is described as one-way:
- The version is persisted in the WAL and the job, so a V3 job always finishes as V3.
- You should enable it only after all DataNodes and all possibly-active DataCoords support V3.
- Rolling back to a binary without V3 is forbidden while any V3 job, task or temporary prefix exists.

I read the design doc, the config and the version-resolution code. I did not read the rest of the V3 implementation or run anything. This is a "how does it work" question, not a change, so I didn't go through the full cross-check procedure from CLAUDE.md.

sent.prompt: Why is the proxy's MetaCache keyed by collection ID, with collection names and aliases kept only as hints? And how are cache fills kept from racing the invalidations that DDL broadcasts send, so that a describe started before a DDL can't put stale metadata back?

output.text:
The code matches the design doc (`docs/design-docs/design_docs/20260716-proxy-metacache-id-inverted-index.md`). I read that doc and grepped `fillMu` in `internal/proxy/metacache/meta_cache.go`. I did not read the fill and invalidation paths line by line.

## Why the cache is keyed by collection ID

- **IDs are stable and cluster-unique.** Names and aliases are not. A name can be renamed, dropped and recreated, or re-pointed by an alias DDL.
- **Invalidations arrive by id, alias or db.** The old primary store was keyed by `(db, name)`, so every eviction had to scan. Each Load, Release, Drop, Rename or Alter broadcast cost O(all cached collections), plus partition and alias sweeps, under the global write lock. At around 1M cached collections, that stalled every query on the proxy.
- **The primary store is now `collections[id]`.** Name, alias and partition entries are hints that resolve to an id.
  - `nameIdx` maps db and name to an id.
  - `aliasInfo` maps an alias to its target name.
  - The partition cache is keyed by id.
- **Every read validates its hint against the primary store.** The id must still be live, and the entry's name and db must still match. A failed check is a cache miss and costs one extra describe. It is never a stale read. A stale hint, such as an old name after a rename or an old id after drop and recreate, simply stops validating.
- **Hints are written only together with their entry.** Evicting an entry removes exactly the hints it owns (name, declared aliases, partition list) through one routine, `evictCollectionEntryLocked`. So nothing dangles, there is no background GC, and invalidation by id is O(1).

## How fills are kept from racing invalidations

The old design used per-collection timestamp floors. They had gaps: alias write-backs were unversioned, there was a `RequestTime == 0` bypass, and `RemoveDatabase` never raised the floor. The new design replaces them with a lock, `fillMu sync.RWMutex` (`meta_cache.go:420`).

- **Fills take the read side.** A fill holds `fillMu.RLock` across the whole describe RPC and the write-back (e.g. `:698`, `:1051`). Fills don't block each other, and cache hits never touch `fillMu`.
- **Invalidations take the write side.** `fillMu.Lock` (e.g. `:866`, `:888`, `:1271`) waits for in-flight fills to finish before evicting.
- **A describe started before a DDL therefore can't re-insert stale data.**
  - Its pre-DDL snapshot is written back before the eviction runs, and the eviction then removes it.
  - A fill that starts after the eviction reads post-DDL state. RootCoord commits the DDL before it broadcasts.
- **Lock order is `fillMu` then `m.mu`.** `m.mu` guards map consistency, is held briefly, and is never held across an RPC.
- **No deadlock with RootCoord.** DDL ack callbacks release the meta lock before the expiration fan-out, so a fill's describe is never blocked by the DDL whose invalidation is waiting on that fill. Proxy-side, `RemovePartition` does its ensure-describe before taking the write side.

## Trade-offs the doc accepts

- An invalidation, and so the broadcast ack, waits for the slowest in-flight fill. A fill with no deadline that is wedged below the transport can pin `fillMu`. The doc leaves deadline policy to the API and coordinator-client layer.
- Duplicate or late broadcasts over-invalidate and cost one extra describe. They are not filtered by version.
- An id-only describe whose response omits the db (older RootCoord during a rolling upgrade) is served uncached. Without the db, no database DDL could find and invalidate that entry.
- DropDatabase is the one invalidation that is not O(1). It walks the db's cached entries in batches, after only briefly holding the write lock.
- AlterDatabase invalidates only the `dbInfo` entry, because collection metadata doesn't contain database properties.

**Recommendation: don't go back to 5 seconds. Keep 20s.**

**Why 5s isn't safe.** The claim that releasing pins "normally finishes in well under a second" holds on a local or single-zone etcd. It doesn't hold everywhere. The comment on the constant (`snapshot_manager.go:88-96`) and commit 86ddf70 record a real deployment where this broke. That deployment has etcd spread over three availability zones about 40 ms apart. Releasing the pins of a large snapshot took 6–9 seconds there. At 5s the cleanup was cancelled partway, and the pins stayed until the next restart. Pinned segments are ones GC should have freed, so the failure is silent storage leakage, not a visible error.

**Why "fail quickly" is the wrong goal here.** Every use of this timeout is a cleanup that has nothing to fall back on:
- `snapshot_export_manager.go:192`, `:635`, `:784`, `:797`: these use `context.WithoutCancel` or the manager context, so nothing else cancels them. Only this timeout does.
- If a call times out, the error is logged as a warning, and the pins are left behind.
- A stuck etcd is already visible through other signals. A short timeout adds no real detection. It only turns slow-but-working into leaked pins.

**What decides the value.** It has to cover the worst-case time for the whole cleanup, not the typical time:
1. The number of etcd round-trips, which grows with snapshot size and the number of pins.
2. The etcd round-trip time. Cross-AZ or cross-region deployments multiply it.
3. A safety margin above the observed worst case. The observed worst case is 9s, so 20s gives about 2×.

A median under one second is the wrong thing to size it by. The slowest supported deployment decides it.

**A caveat.** The timeout also covers the export-job metadata updates, the staging cleanup and `DropJob`, because the constant is shared. That is why 20s applies to all of them. It also means one timeout is a rough fit for several operations. A stuck etcd now holds those paths for up to 20s each. In `cleanupTerminalJob` the unpin and the job update run back to back, so the worst case there is 40s. That is acceptable because they run in background loops.

**If the real concern is fast failure on a stuck etcd,** these are better options than lowering the constant:
- Make it a `paramtable` config with 20s as the default, so operators on fast etcd can tighten it.
- Retry the release with a short per-attempt timeout, so it survives slowness and also gives up on a dead etcd.
- Alert on pin-release failures, using the existing warn log and the active-pins gauge.

I haven't traced `UnpinSnapshot` to count its etcd operations. The 6–9s figure comes from the commit and comment, not from a measurement I made. If you want to change the value, count the round-trips first.

sent.prompt: A full (non-partial) upsert into a collection whose primary key has autoID=true now looks the primary keys up before it writes anything. Why? What happens to a row whose key exists, to one whose key is not found, and to one that has no key at all, and why isn't a row that is not found simply inserted under the key the caller sent?

output.text:
A full AutoID upsert looks the keys up first because the old behavior could lose a row. I read the code and the design doc, and they agree. The doc is `docs/design-docs/design_docs/20260803-autoid-upsert-primary-key-preservation.md`.

I haven't run any tests.

## Why it looks up first

Before this change, a full upsert threw away the caller's key for every row. For an existing key `P`, the proxy wrote `Delete(P)` and then `Insert(G)`, where `G` was a freshly generated ID. `P` and `G` usually hash to different vchannels, so the two messages can commit in different WAL transactions. A snapshot taken between them contains the delete but not the insert, so restoring it loses the entity. Existing rows also silently changed their ID on every upsert.

The proxy now needs to know whether each key exists before it decides what to write (`prepareUpsert` and `queryPreExecute` in `internal/proxy/dml/task_upsert.go:306` and `:367`). It sends one primary-key-only Strong query through the normal query path.

## What happens to each row

- **Key exists.** The proxy emits `Delete(P)` followed by `Insert(P)` and returns `P`. Both messages route on the same key, so they land in the same vchannel transaction. A snapshot can't fall between them, and the entity keeps its ID.
- **Key not found.** The proxy allocates a new ID `G` and emits only `Insert(G)`, with no delete. `G` is returned in `MutationResult.IDs`. This is the old insert-on-not-found behavior, kept so existing callers don't break. `allocateMissingAutoIDs` does the allocation at `task_upsert.go:989`.
- **No key at all.** The request is rejected as malformed input before any query or allocation. `checkUpsertPrimaryFieldData` runs first (`task_upsert.go:339`), and `queryPreExecute` also errors with "must assign pk when upsert". The test `TestPrepareUpsertFullAutoIDRejectsInvalidPrimaryDataBeforeQuery` covers the missing-key case and asserts zero reads and zero allocations. The doc says to use Insert if you want to create an entity without a lookup key.

## Why a not-found row isn't inserted under the caller's key

With `autoID=true`, the allocator owns the key space. A key the caller sent that isn't found is only a lookup value. It does not mean the caller owns that ID. If the proxy inserted it as the primary key, a later ordinary Insert or another upsert could be handed the same ID by the allocator. That would make two entities collide on one primary key.

Using `G` from the same global allocator that Insert uses means no other writer can get that ID. The test `TestPrepareUpsertFullAutoIDAcceptsAllocatorValueEqualToLookupKey` covers the case where the allocator happens to return the same number as the lookup key. That's fine, because the allocation reserved it.

## Costs and limits

- **Load requirement:** the collection must be loaded. Before, a full AutoID upsert was a blind write and worked on an unloaded collection. Now it returns a load-state error with no WAL append.
- **Retries:** retrying a not-found row isn't idempotent. A lost response can produce a second generated ID, and the lookup key is not an idempotency key.
- **Atomicity:** a request that spans vchannels can still partially commit. The guarantee is per entity, not per request.
- **Partial upsert:** it takes a different path with its own read, merge, and compare-and-swap logic. It is unchanged.

sent.prompt: I'm about to start on the distributed query view work. Explain to a newcomer, as briefly as you can, what it changes about who does what between Proxy, QueryCoord, StreamingNode and QueryNode and why, what a DataView version and a QueryView version are, how a query view moves through its states, how much of it serves production traffic today, and where each part is written down.

output.text:
**What it changes**

Today the delegator logic sits in the query path. The design moves it out so StreamingNode doesn't become a bottleneck. Routing every load, release, delete and query through StreamingNode would make it a compute and IO hotspot that is hard to scale or replicate.

- **QueryCoord** (Coord) generates the full distributed query view for each shard. It directly owns all sealed-segment load and release on QueryNodes, and it drives the view state machine.
- **StreamingNode** no longer loads sealed segments and no longer forwards search or query. It takes view updates from Coord and prepares the growing-side resources. It also produces the query plan, which includes MVCC and optimization. For the incremental data, it serves queries on its own growing segments.
- **QueryNode** loads and releases the sealed segments named in each view, and executes queries on them. It subscribes to deletes itself and applies them, instead of StreamingNode pushing them.
- **Proxy** queries in two phases.
  - Phase 1 gets a plan from StreamingNode, using the highest Up view.
  - Phase 2 sends that plan to StreamingNode and QueryNodes.
  - Proxy does the reduce itself, so the single delegator goes away.
  - If a view is invalidated mid-query, the query is cancelled and retried.

**Versions**

- **DataView** is an immutable Collection-level snapshot of loadable sealed segments, each with a manifest version. Its version is `(streaming_version, compact_version)`.
  - `streaming_version` goes up only on the flush transaction that hands growing data over to sealed.
  - `compact_version` goes up on every other membership change: compaction, import, L0 manifest advance, partition drop, truncate.
  - Versions are ordered lexicographically.
- **QueryView** is per shard per replica. Its version is `((S,C),Q)`, where `(S,C)` is the DataView version it was built from. When the DataView advances, Q resets to 1. Q goes up on pure redistribution of the same data, such as a balance or a node-crash recovery. An Up view's version can only increase.

**State machine**

Coord leads, and StreamingNode and QueryNodes follow through the single `SyncQueryView` RPC.

- Normal path: `Preparing → Ready → Up → Down → Dropping → Dropped`.
- Failure path: `Preparing → Unrecoverable → Dropping → Dropped`.
- Coord persists Preparing, Up, Down and Unrecoverable to etcd before acting on them. Ready is not persisted.
- Coord moves Preparing to Ready once all nodes report Ready. It then pushes Up to StreamingNode and persists Up once StreamingNode confirms.
- A higher view confirming Up moves the old view to Down.
- A node's response always carries its latest state, so Coord can rebuild its picture after a restart.

**How much serves production traffic today**

Essentially none of it. The docs say the new components don't switch production Proxy routing or activate the new Coordinator runtime.

- **Built:**
  - The StreamingNode query plan and execution path (`GetQueryPlan`, `SearchOnView`, `QueryOnView`).
  - An injectable query client.
  - The QueryNode extraction, with `ViewSyncService` and `ViewQueryService` registered.
  - DataView, with its manager in `internal/dataview`.
- **Not built:**
  - Production Proxy wiring.
  - QueryView generation by the Coordinator.
  - Publishing LoadInfo from the legacy load APIs.
  - The QueryNode pure-delete subscription.
  - DDL visibility, so truncate and partition drop still use the legacy QueryCoord target handoff.
  - WAL-secondary routing.
- `querynode_extraction.md` says the component tests don't prove cluster-wide routing or full production recovery.

**Where it's written down**

All paths are under `docs/design-docs/design_docs/`.
- `qviews/README.md` is the main design. Start here. Section 2 covers the role split, 3 the two-phase query, 5 DataView, 6 QueryView versions, 7 lifecycle, and 11 the Coord and node interactions.
- `qviews/query_view_state_machine.md` has the per-node, per-state detail.
- `qviews/data_view.md` and `qviews/data_view_schema.md` cover DataView.
- `qviews/query_view_lease.md` covers the serving lease on StreamingNode.
- `qviews/syncer.md` covers the Coord-side transport.
- `qviews/querynode_extraction.md` and `qviews/qnview/querynode_queryview_resource_preparation.md` cover QueryNode.
- `qviews/query/` covers the plan, execution, client, pruning and replica discovery.
- `qviews/ddl_visibility.md` covers DDL visibility.
- `wal/streamingnode_vchannel_wal_view.md` and `wal/transform_log.md` cover the StreamingNode side.
- The wire types are in `pkg/proto/view.proto`.

Explain to a newcomer, as briefly as you can, what it changes about who does what between Proxy, QueryCoord, StreamingNode and QueryNode and why, what a DataView version and a QueryView version are, how a query view moves through its states, how much of it serves production traffic today, and where each part is written down.

output.text:
**What changes, and why**

Today the delegator logic would have to sit on StreamingNode (SN). That would make SN a bottleneck, because every Load/Release, every delete, every query and every QueryNode result would pass through it. The design splits the work like this:

- **QueryCoord** generates the globally complete distributed query view and advances its state machine. It also owns all sealed-segment Load/Release. It no longer manages resource-preparation workflows.
- **StreamingNode** only accepts view updates from QueryCoord. It prepares the resources for the incremental/growing side and reports their status. It no longer forwards Search/Query and no longer applies deletes.
- **QueryNode** prepares and serves the sealed segments. After LoadSegment it subscribes to the matching delete stream itself and applies those deletes on its own.
- **Proxy** runs queries in two phases:
  1. It gets a shard-level query plan from SN. The plan carries the MVCC timestamp, the optimizations and the view version.
  2. It sends the plan to SN and the QNs, then does all the distributed reduce itself.
  
  If a node fails or the view is invalidated, the query is canceled and retried.

Reduce and RPC load now scale with Proxy. The single global delegator goes away, and SN and QN recover independently of each other.

**Versions**

- **DataView version** is `DataVersion = (streaming_version, compact_version)`. It identifies an immutable collection-level snapshot of loadable sealed segments.
  - `streaming_version` goes up only on the flush atomic txn.
  - `compact_version` goes up on every other membership change: compaction, import, L0 manifest advance, truncate and so on.
- **QueryView version** is `((streaming_version, compact_version), Q)`. It is per shard and per replica.
  - When D rises, Q resets to 1 and a new view is generated.
  - When Q rises, the data is the same but the placement changed (balance or recovery).
  - Versions of Up views may only move forward, and a shard keeps about 2–3 views.

**State machine**

The normal flow is `Preparing → Ready → Up → Down → Dropping → Dropped`. The error flow is `Preparing → Unrecoverable → Dropping → Dropped`.

- Coord leads, and each node has at most one view in Preparing.
- Losing a QN makes a Preparing view Unrecoverable. During Dropping it counts that QN's cleanup as complete.
- SN failure is handled by channel assignment, not by the per-view state machine.
- An SN serving lease delays Up → Down while queries are using the view.

**How much is in production**

None of it serves production traffic yet.
- The SN side exists: `GetQueryPlan`, `SearchOnView` and `QueryOnView`, plus an injectable query client.
- Production Proxy routing is not switched over, and the new Coordinator runtime is not activated. The balancer note says QueryCoord activation is "separate integration work".
- QN execution and resource preparation, and scoped WAL barrier production, are separate dependencies that this work doesn't deliver.
- `transform_start_after_timetick` is on the wire but not meaningfully advanced.
- Remote TransformLog publication to QN is marked planned in the design doc, but the TransformLog note marks remote subscriptions as implemented. The two conflict, so check before relying on either.

**Where it's written down**

The notes point to these files. The Read tool wasn't used, so I haven't opened any of them, and the notes flag several as "missing" from the tree.

- **Main design:** `docs/design-docs/design_docs/qviews/README.md`. It covers the sections above, plus consistency levels, the pure delete stream and DDL visibility.
- **Per-topic docs** (same folder):
  - `data_view.md` and `data_view_schema.md`
  - `query_view_state_machine.md`
  - `query_view_lease.md`
  - `balancer_scanning.md`
  - `syncer.md`
  - `ddl_visibility.md`
  - `querynode_extraction.md`
  - `qnview/querynode_queryview_resource_preparation.md`
  - `query/` (`query_plan.md`, `query_client.md`, `segment_pruning.md`, `replica_discovery.md`, `query_execution.md`)
- **WAL-side docs:** `wal/transform_log.md` and `wal/streamingnode_vchannel_wal_view.md`.
- **Wire types:** `pkg/proto/view.proto`. It defines the `DataViewOf*` and `QueryViewOf*` messages and `QueryViewState`.
- **Code:**
  - `internal/views/` holds the coord balancer and the viewquery server.
  - `internal/dataview/manager.go` is the DataView manager.
  - On the SN side: `internal/streamingnode/server/queryplan/server.go`, `.../wal/adaptor/query_plan.go` and `.../wal/snview/query_task_provider.go`.

sent.prompt: I'm adding a small holder object that is created once per read on a hot path in the managed ledger, and I was going to pool it with Netty's Recycler the way OpReadEntry is pooled. Should I? What is the project's position on Recycler in new code, and what is the reasoning behind it?

output.text:
**No, don't pool it.** The project's position is that new code shouldn't use Netty's `Recycler`. This is set out in `CODING.md:243-247` and in [PIP-443](pip/pip-443.md), "Stop using Netty Recycler in new code".

`CODING.md` says that `Recycler` "is **no longer recommended for new code** — under ZGC the `Recycler` often *costs* more CPU than it saves. Don't add new `Recycler` usage." It also says not to hand-optimize allocation away, because Pulsar runs on ZGC and short-lived allocations are cheap.

PIP-443 gives three reasons:

1. **It's slower than a plain allocation.** In the PIP's JMH numbers, a heap-allocated record ran at about 468M ops/s. `Recycler` ran at about 36M ops/s, roughly 13x slower. The best case, where the object is recycled on the same `FastThreadLocalThread` that got it, was still about 7x slower. Most of the time, `Recycler` hands out a no-op handle (7 of 8 times by default), and a recycle from a different thread goes through a `MessagePassingQueue`.
2. **It's error-prone.**
   - Every use needs a manual `recycle()`, which gets skipped when an exception is thrown (#13233).
   - If an object is shared across threads, a double recycle throws (#24697).
   - Worse, a reader can see a reset object, or one already reused by another task. That corrupts state silently.
3. **The benefit is doubtful.** Nobody has shown a measured gain, and a small code change can erase it. The PIP uses the managed-ledger read path as its example. `OpReadEntry` is pooled, but a read also allocates a wrapped callback in `RangeEntryCacheImpl`, a `ReadEntriesCallbackWithContext` and an `ArrayList` in `PendingReadsManager`. The pooling saves one allocation out of several, which makes no real difference.

The PIP says holder objects like yours are the typical `Recycler` use in Pulsar. They exist mainly to avoid long parameter lists, not because pooling was measured to help.

**What to do instead:**
- Allocate it normally. An immutable class or a `record` is the idiomatic choice, and `CODING.md` prefers immutable objects.
- If profiling shows you need reuse, the PIP suggests a `FastThreadLocal` that caches a single object or a small queue. That is the "good case" of `Recycler` without the overhead. It only works if the object is used and released on the same thread, so it doesn't suit an object handed across threads.
- Existing pooled classes like `OpReadEntry` can stay, because the PIP doesn't ask for them to be removed. Don't copy the pattern into new code.

output.text:
Topic-list responses are bounded by one shared pair of limits, a heap limit and a direct-memory limit. The broker and the proxy each have their own instance of it. I read the wiring and the config fields; I did not read the limiter classes' internals or run anything. The design is described in `pip/pip-442.md`.

## The limiter classes (shared)
- `pulsar-common/src/main/java/org/apache/pulsar/common/semaphore/AsyncDualMemoryLimiter.java` is the interface. Its `LimitType` is `HEAP_MEMORY` or `DIRECT_MEMORY`, and it provides `withAcquiredPermits` and `withUpdatedPermits`.
- `pulsar-common/src/main/java/org/apache/pulsar/common/semaphore/AsyncDualMemoryLimiterImpl.java` is the implementation. It holds two bounded async semaphores, each with a wait queue and an acquire timeout.
- `pulsar-common/src/main/java/org/apache/pulsar/common/semaphore/AsyncDualMemoryLimiterUtil.java` has `acquireDirectMemoryPermitsAndWriteAndFlush`. It takes direct-memory permits for a serialized response and holds them until the write completes.
- `pulsar-broker-common/src/main/java/org/apache/pulsar/broker/topiclistlimit/TopicListMemoryLimiter.java` is the topic-list subclass. It has `estimateTopicListSize`, which estimates a list's size from its topic names.

## Broker
- **Where the limiter is built:** `pulsar-broker/src/main/java/org/apache/pulsar/broker/service/BrokerService.java:463` creates `maxTopicListInFlightLimiter` from the config values. It is exposed through `getMaxTopicListInFlightLimiter()`.
- **Sizing the first request:** `getTopicListSizeResultCache()` (class `TopicListSizeResultCache`) remembers the last observed size per namespace. That remembered size is the initial heap reservation.
- **GetTopicsOfNamespace:**
  - `pulsar-broker/src/main/java/org/apache/pulsar/broker/service/ServerCnx.java` around lines 3755–3762 acquires heap permits with `withAcquiredPermits` before listing topics.
  - After listing, it calls `withUpdatedPermits` with the actual size.
  - Sending the response goes through `PulsarCommandSenderImpl.java` (`pulsar-broker/src/main/java/org/apache/pulsar/broker/service/PulsarCommandSenderImpl.java:140`). That takes direct-memory permits until the write is flushed.
- **Topic-list watches:**
  - `pulsar-broker/src/main/java/org/apache/pulsar/broker/service/TopicListService.java:714-748` (`getTopics`) does the same heap-permit acquire, list, and update-permits steps. The lines I read are the part that runs on the initial watch listing.
  - The watch success and watch update responses use the direct-memory limiter in `PulsarCommandSenderImpl.java` (around lines 454 and 470).
- **Admin REST API:** `pulsar-broker/src/main/java/org/apache/pulsar/broker/admin/impl/TopicListResponseMemoryLimiter.java` uses the same broker limiter. `NamespacesBase.java` around line 181 refers to it.

## Proxy
- `pulsar-proxy/src/main/java/org/apache/pulsar/proxy/server/ProxyService.java:262-273` builds its own `TopicListMemoryLimiter` from `ProxyConfiguration`.
- `pulsar-proxy/src/main/java/org/apache/pulsar/proxy/server/LookupProxyHandler.java` (around lines 423–476) acquires heap permits, then updates them to the actual size. It writes the response with `acquireDirectMemoryPermitsAndWriteAndFlush`.

## Configuration
The names are the same in `broker.conf` (`ServiceConfiguration.java:1778-1812`) and `proxy.conf` (`ProxyConfiguration.java:498-528`):

| Setting | Default |
|---|---|
| `maxTopicListInFlightHeapMemSizeMB` | 100 |
| `maxTopicListInFlightDirectMemSizeMB` | 100 |
| `maxTopicListInFlightHeapMemSizePermitsAcquireTimeoutMillis` | 25000 |
| `maxTopicListInFlightHeapMemSizePermitsAcquireQueueSize` | 10000 |
| `maxTopicListInFlightDirectMemSizePermitsAcquireTimeoutMillis` | 25000 |
| `maxTopicListInFlightDirectMemSizePermitsAcquireQueueSize` | 10000 |

The two `MemSizeMB` settings cap the memory in flight. The queue-size and timeout settings cap how many requests can wait for permits and for how long. Requests that exceed them fail rather than pile up.

sent.prompt: I'm adding a small holder object that is created once per read on a hot path in the managed ledger, and I was going to pool it with Netty's Recycler the way OpReadEntry is pooled. Should I? What is the project's position on Recycler in new code, and what is the reasoning behind it?

output.text:
**No. Don't pool it with Recycler.** PIP-443, "Stop using Netty Recycler in new code", sets the project's position. `OpReadEntry` is existing code that predates it, so it isn't a precedent for new code.

**The rule:** new contributions should not use Netty `Recycler`. Existing recyclable classes generally aren't worth removing. Removing one is fine when a recycler bug is hard to diagnose, or when the pooling gets in the way of a refactor.

**The reasoning:**

1. **It's slower than plain allocation.** The PIP cites a benchmark on a GitHub Actions runner:
   - A plain heap-allocated tuple ran at about 468M ops/s.
   - `Recycler` ran at about 36M ops/s, roughly 13x slower.
   - A same-thread `ArrayDeque` pool, which simulates `Recycler`'s best case, ran at about 70M ops/s, roughly 7x slower.
   - `Recycler` is only efficient when `get()` and `recycle()` happen on the same `FastThreadLocalThread`. Otherwise the handle goes through a cross-thread queue.
   - Most of the time, a fresh object gets a no-op handle and is never pooled anyway. Only 1 in 8 gets a real handle.

2. **It's error-prone, like manual `malloc`/`free`.**
   - An exception before `recycle()` skips the recycle (see #13233).
   - If an object is shared across threads, a second `recycle()` throws. That can break the read path, as in #24697.
   - A thread that keeps a reference after another thread recycles it sees either reset fields or an object already reused by another task. The PIP calls the reused-object case the most dangerous, because it raises no exception.
   - Making it safe needs a move-before-publish pattern or a synchronized `recycle()`. The first is easy to forget and the second adds more overhead.

3. **The benefit is doubtful.** No benchmark has shown the GC savings. Recycler dates from before Java 8, mainly to avoid expensive direct `ByteBuf` allocation. Modern collectors, such as Generational ZGC in Java 21+, have much better tail latencies. Any gain is also easy to lose with a small code change.

**What to do instead:** allocate a normal object. If you really need to reduce allocation, use a `FastThreadLocal` that caches a single object or a small queue. That is essentially what `Recycler`'s good case does, and it works better on non-Netty threads. This only works if the holder is used and released on the same thread. If it crosses threads on the read path, plain allocation is the safer choice.

The full text is in `pip/pip-443.md`. The note says that file is missing from the checkout, so I read it through the notes tool.

sent.prompt: Our Rust producer registers a SchemaType.JSON schema whose definition is a JSON Schema document ({"type":"object","properties":{...}}, draft 2020-12). It used to be accepted; after we upgraded the broker, registration is rejected. Why did this change, and is there a way to get the old behaviour back?

output.text:
**Why it changed:** this is PIP-464. For `SchemaType.JSON`, the broker used to try to parse `schema_data` as an Avro schema. If that failed, it fell back to Jackson `JsonSchema` parsing, which accepts any valid JSON. A JSON Schema 2020-12 document like `{"type":"object","properties":{...}}` passed through that fallback.

The fallback hid a problem. Java consumers (`AutoConsumeSchema`, `GenericJsonSchema`) only understand Avro. They failed at read time with `SchemaParseException: Type not supported: object`.

The broker is now strict by default. Your schema isn't a valid Avro schema, so it is rejected at registration. The relevant code is:
- `StructSchemaDataValidator.validate` (`pulsar-broker/.../validator/StructSchemaDataValidator.java:74`) only uses the Jackson fallback when the legacy flag is on.
- `JsonSchemaCompatibilityCheck.checkCompatible` (`JsonSchemaCompatibilityCheck.java:54-89`) rejects any non-Avro schema when the flag is off. The same rule applies to a schema already stored on the topic.

**Getting the old behaviour back:** set this in `broker.conf`:

```
schemaJsonAllowLegacyJacksonFormat=true
```

It is defined in `ServiceConfiguration.java:3971` and defaults to `false`. I haven't checked whether it can be changed without a broker restart. With it on, both the validator and the compatibility check accept the legacy format again. That includes mixed Avro/JSON-Schema cases.

**Recommended fix:** the flag only restores the old behaviour, so any Java consumer using `AutoConsumeSchema` or `GenericJsonSchema` on that topic will still hit the read-time failure. A better fix is to change the Rust producer to send an Avro schema definition as the `SchemaType.JSON` schema data, for example:

```json
{"type":"record","name":"MyRecord","fields":[{"name":"field1","type":"string"}]}
```

Java's `JSONSchema.of()` already does this, and it's what consumers expect. Messages can stay as plain JSON.

I only read the code and PIP-464. I didn't run a broker to confirm the rejection or the flag.

  - `schedulerExecutor`: a single thread named `<name>-scheduler`.
  - `serDesExecutor`: an `OrderedExecutor` named `<name>-worker`, with `.numThreads(numSerDesThreads)`.
- This matches the design in PIP-453, which splits the old single metadata-store thread into event, scheduler and worker threads.

**Which thread runs `MetadataCache` serialization and deserialization**
- The `<name>-worker` threads, i.e. `serDesExecutor`.
- `AbstractMetadataStore` passes `serDesExecutor` and `schedulerExecutor` into each cache it creates (around lines 339, 350 and 361).
- `MetadataCacheImpl` holds that executor in its `executor` field.
- It calls `serde.deserialize(...)` in the cache loader at `pulsar-metadata/src/main/java/org/apache/pulsar/metadata/cache/impl/MetadataCacheImpl.java:165`, running on `executor.chooseThread(path)` (line 173).

**How a thread is picked for a path**
- `OrderedExecutor.chooseThread(path)` hashes the path string to one of the worker threads. The same path always lands on the same thread, which keeps operations on one path in order.
- With one thread, every path on the broker shares it. Loading many topics' metadata after a failover then queues behind that one thread.

- `pulsar-broker/src/main/java/org/apache/pulsar/broker/PulsarService.java` passes it to the store config as `.numSerDesThreads(config.getMetadataStoreSerDesThreads())` at lines 471 and 1467.

- From there it reaches the `AbstractMetadataStore` constructor, via `AbstractBatchedMetadataStore` (line 66) for ZooKeeper and Etcd, or directly for `OxiaMetadataStore`, `LocalMemoryMetadataStore` and `RocksdbMetadataStore`.

The broker refuses to start if brokerDeleteInactiveTopicsEnabled is also true, and also if brokerDeleteInactiveTopicsMode is delete_when_subscriptions_caught_up. Why those two restrictions? output.text:
Both restrictions follow from what "inactive" means and from the goal of never losing data. The code is in `PulsarService.java:960-974` and in `checkGC()` in `PersistentTopic.java:3885`.

## Why the two startup checks

**`brokerDeleteInactiveTopicsEnabled=true` together with close-on-inactive.** The two settings are mutually exclusive because they do opposite things to an inactive topic. Delete removes the topic and its data. Close only unloads it from the broker and leaves the data in place. The garbage-collection scheduler runs when either flag is on (`BrokerService.java:926-929`). If both were allowed, you would have to decide which one wins for each topic. You asked for "release memory without losing data", so the broker refuses to start rather than guess.

**`delete_when_subscriptions_caught_up`.** In that mode a topic counts as inactive as soon as all its subscriptions are caught up, even if consumers are still connected. That is fine for deletion, where `delete()` fails if the topic is busy. For close it would cause trouble:
- Closing such a topic would disconnect its live consumers.
- Those consumers would reconnect immediately and reload the topic.
- The next GC cycle would close it again, so you would get an unload/reload loop.

Only `delete_when_no_subscriptions` is safe, because a topic only counts as inactive when it has no subscriptions and no producers.

## What happens to a namespace with `deleteWhileInactive=true`

Close-on-inactive takes precedence, so the namespace's setting is ignored and the topic is closed, never deleted:
- In `PersistentTopic.checkGC()`, `deleteEnabled = !closeEnabled && isDeleteWhileInactive()` (`:3897`). The delete path is never reached while the broker flag is on.
- `NonPersistentTopic.checkGC()` does the same (`:1094-1095`).
- Your data is safe in this case. The namespace's `maxInactiveDurationSeconds` still applies, as the inactivity threshold before the close.

**A gap in the startup check.** The startup check only looks at the broker-level mode. A namespace or topic policy can set `inactiveTopicDeleteMode` to `delete_when_subscriptions_caught_up` after the broker has started. In that case `PersistentTopic.checkGC()` logs at debug level, "Skipping inactive-topic close", and returns (`:3904-3914`). Those topics are neither closed nor deleted, so they keep their memory. If some of your idle topics aren't being released, check for namespace policies with that mode.

`StructSchemaDataValidator.validate` (`pulsar-broker/.../schema/validator/StructSchemaDataValidator.java:61`) parses the definition with the Avro parser. A JSON Schema document like `{"type":"object","properties":{...}}` isn't a valid Avro schema, because `object` isn't an Avro type and `properties` isn't an Avro keyword. So parsing fails and the broker throws `InvalidSchemaDataException("Invalid schema definition data for JSON schema")`.

Before PIP-464, any Avro parse failure fell through to a lenient Jackson `JsonSchema` parse (the pre-2.1 compatibility path). That is why your document used to be accepted. That fallback is now off by default (`StructSchemaDataValidator.java:74`).

The config comment says the default is deliberately "consistent with what the consumer side requires". Pulsar's own JSON consumers and `GenericJsonSchema` read the definition as Avro. A registered non-Avro definition may therefore be accepted by the broker but still fail on the consumer side.

**Getting the old behaviour back:** set this in `broker.conf` (or your equivalent config) and restart the broker:

```
schemaJsonAllowLegacyJacksonFormat=true
```

It's defined at `pulsar-broker-common/.../ServiceConfiguration.java:3971` and defaults to `false`. With it on, the validator falls back to `JSON_SCHEMA_READER.readValue(data)` for JSON-type schemas that fail Avro parsing.

I haven't run your schema through it. The fallback uses Jackson's `jackson-module-jsonSchema` model, which is based on an older JSON Schema draft. A draft 2020-12 document with newer keywords (`$defs`, `prefixItems`, and so on) could still be rejected. Simple `type`/`properties` documents most likely pass, since that was your old behaviour.

**Longer-term options:**
- **Register the schema as Avro.** Have the Rust producer send an Avro record definition under `SchemaType.JSON`. This is what the Java client does, and it works with consumers and compatibility checks.
- **Use a different schema type.** If the payload is JSON but you want to keep a JSON Schema document, a type that doesn't go through Avro parsing (for example `BYTES` or `NONE`) avoids the validator. The cost is that the broker then does no structural schema enforcement.

output.text:
A scalable topic is a Pulsar topic whose capacity can grow or shrink while it's live, without breaking per-key ordering.

## Why it exists
A partitioned topic routes by `hash(key) % numPartitions`. Changing the partition count therefore remaps keys and breaks ordering. Partitions also can't be reduced, so operators have to guess the right count up front. This motivation is in the "Motivation" section of `pip/pip-460.md`.

## How it works
- **Segments.** The key-hash space is a ring. Each segment owns a contiguous range of it. Splitting or merging segments changes capacity, and the segments form a DAG over time. Because only a range is re-divided, ordering is preserved. Segments are an internal scaling detail, not something applications see.
- **Controller.** Each topic has a leader on the broker, the `ScalableTopicController`. It owns the segment layout and performs splits and merges. It also assigns segments to consumers. Clients learn the layout through a persistent watch session.
- **Auto split/merge.** The controller applies a policy that splits hot segments and merges cold ones, with no operator involved.
- **Consumer types.** These are the three modes:
  - *Stream* gives per-key order and cumulative acks.
  - *Queue* gives parallel delivery with individual acks, and no ordering.
  - *Checkpoint* is unmanaged: the application holds the read position, and it's meant for connectors.
  - Entry-bucketing (key-shared) lets ordered consumption scale beyond one consumer per segment.
- **V5 client.** The new Java client in `pulsar-client-v5` is the reference implementation. It hides segments from applications. It tracks the layout, routes each message to the right segment, and fans reads out across segments.

## Where each one is written down

| Topic | Design (PIP) | Normative spec (`spec/scalable-topics/`) | Code |
|---|---|---|---|
| Overall design and motivation | `pip/pip-460.md` | `README.md`, `terminology.md`, `data-model.md` | `pulsar-common/.../common/scalable/` |
| Controller | `pip/pip-468.md` | `terminology.md` (Controller), `wire-protocol.md` | `pulsar-broker/.../service/scalable/ScalableTopicController.java` |
| Auto split/merge | `pip/pip-483.md` | `data-model.md` | `ScalableTopicController`, covered by `ScalableTopicControllerAutoScaleTest` |
| Consumer types | `pip/pip-460.md` (Consumer Models) | `client-api.md`, `terminology.md` | `ScalableStreamConsumer`, `ScalableQueueConsumer` and `ScalableCheckpointConsumer` in `pulsar-client-v5/.../impl/v5/` |
| Key-shared / entry-bucketing | `pip/pip-486.md` | `key-shared.md` | `ScalableStreamConsumer` and the broker's scalable service code |
| V5 client | `pip/pip-466.md` | `client-api.md`, `wire-protocol.md`, `error-model.md`, `conformance.md` | `pulsar-client-v5/` |

Related PIPs:
- `pip-473`: transactions.
- `pip-475`: migrating regular topics to scalable ones.
- `pip-494`: the spec's change process.
- `pip-496`: Functions and IO.

sent.prompt: You are about to start working on scalable topics in this project. Explain to a newcomer, as briefly as you can, what a scalable topic is and why it exists, and how the controller, automatic split and merge, the consumer types and the V5 client fit together, and say where each one is written down.

output.text:
A scalable topic is a new topic type (called Topics v5 in the code) that can grow and shrink its parallelism while the topic is live, without breaking per-key ordering.

## Why it exists

Partitioned topics route with `hash(key) % numPartitions`. Changing the partition count therefore remaps keys and breaks ordering. Partitions also can never be reduced. Operators have to guess the right count up front, and a wrong guess means waste or hot partitions. A scalable topic splits the hash space into **range segments** instead. A segment can be split or merged, and the key-to-range mapping stays consistent when that happens.

Each segment is still an ordinary managed ledger underneath. Splitting or merging seals the old segments.

## How the pieces fit

- **Controller:** one broker is elected per topic through the metadata store. For Stream and Checkpoint consumers it also hands out segment assignments, and it persists them so a broker failure doesn't force a full rebalance. Clients find it through a push-based watch session, so they get topology updates without polling.
- **Auto split/merge:** the controller watches load and splits hot segments or merges cold ones. This is what removes the need to pick a partition count in advance.
- **Consumer types:** each has its own type-safe interface.
  - **StreamConsumer:** gets exclusive segment assignments from the controller and keeps key order within a segment. Key-Shared-style dispatch inside a segment lets you have more consumers than segments.
  - **QueueConsumer:** subscribes to all segments with shared dispatch. It needs no controller and gives no cross-segment ordering.
  - **CheckpointConsumer:** is assigned segments like the Stream consumer, but tracks positions in a serializable `Checkpoint` instead of subscription cursors. It is meant for Flink and Beam.
- **V5 client:** `pulsar-client-v5` is the Java client for all of this. It tracks the segment layout, routes by key range, and fans out across segments.

## Where each is written down

| Topic | Location |
|---|---|
| Overall design, motivation, consumer models | `pip/pip-460.md` (index at `pip/000-INDEX.md`) |
| Controller | `pip/pip-468.md`; code in `pulsar-broker/.../service/scalable/ScalableTopicController.java` |
| Auto split/merge | `pip/pip-483.md` |
| Key-shared scaling past one consumer per segment | `pip/pip-486.md`, `spec/scalable-topics/key-shared.md` |
| V5 client API | `pip/pip-466.md`; code in `pulsar-client-v5/` |
| Normative client contract | `spec/scalable-topics/`, starting at `README.md`. `client-api.md` and `wire-protocol.md` are the most useful. Terminology is in `terminology.md`. |
| Related PIPs | Transactions in `pip-473`, regular-to-scalable migration in `pip-475`, the spec's change process in `pip-494`, Functions/IO in `pip-496` |

The PIPs record the design rationale. The `spec/` documents are the normative contract. `spec/.../README.md` says every normative change must go through a PIP.

The spec README lists `client-behavior.md` and `java-mapping.md`, but I didn't confirm those two files exist.

**Short answer:** the serialization/deserialization pool is `AbstractMetadataStore.serDesExecutor`. The broker setting that sizes it is `metadataStoreSerDesThreads`, which defaults to 1. With that default, every `MetadataCache` in the store shares one thread, which fits the saturation you're seeing.

**Where the metadata store's threads are created**

All three are created in the `AbstractMetadataStore` constructor, `pulsar-metadata/src/main/java/org/apache/pulsar/metadata/impl/AbstractMetadataStore.java:129-143`:
- `eventExecutor` is a single thread named `<name>-event`, built with `PulsarExecutors.newSingleThreadExecutor`.
- `schedulerExecutor` is a single-thread scheduled executor named `<name>-scheduler`.
- `serDesExecutor` is a BookKeeper `OrderedExecutor` named `<name>-worker`. It is built with `OrderedExecutor.newBuilder().numThreads(numSerDesThreads)`.

**Which thread runs `MetadataCache` serialization and deserialization**

- It is `serDesExecutor`, the `<name>-worker` threads.
- `AbstractMetadataStore` passes it, along with `schedulerExecutor`, into each cache it creates. These are the `MetadataCacheImpl` constructions at lines 339, 350 and 361.
- `MetadataCacheImpl` (`pulsar-metadata/src/main/java/org/apache/pulsar/metadata/cache/impl/MetadataCacheImpl.java`) keeps it in its `executor` field (line 73).
- It runs the work on that executor in the load path (line 173), in the `readModifyUpdate` and `readModifyUpdateOrCreate` paths (lines 218 and 263), and in the `executeOrdered` call at line 295.

**How the thread is picked for a path**

- The cache calls `executor.chooseThread(path)` (lines 173, 218, 263) or `executor.executeOrdered(path, ...)` (line 295).
- Both are methods on BookKeeper's `OrderedExecutor`, which is an external library, so I haven't read its source here. As I recall, it maps the key's hash code onto one of the `numThreads` threads.
- The same path always lands on the same thread, which keeps per-path operations ordered. Different paths can still collide on one thread.
- With 1 thread, everything serializes through that one worker.

**The setting that sizes the pool**

- **Broker config:** `metadataStoreSerDesThreads`, an `int` defaulting to 1 in `pulsar-broker-common/src/main/java/org/apache/pulsar/broker/ServiceConfiguration.java:594`.
- **Config files:** it is also set to `metadataStoreSerDesThreads=1` in `conf/broker.conf:1123` and `conf/standalone.conf:504`.
- **Wiring:** `pulsar-broker/src/main/java/org/apache/pulsar/broker/PulsarService.java` passes it to `MetadataStoreConfig.numSerDesThreads(...)` at line 471 (the configuration metadata store) and line 1467 (the main metadata store).

sent.prompt: We have a few million mostly idle topics and want the broker to release their memory without losing any data, so we turned on brokerCloseInactiveTopicsEnabled. The broker refuses to start if brokerDeleteInactiveTopicsEnabled is also true, and also if brokerDeleteInactiveTopicsMode is delete_when_subscriptions_caught_up. Why those two restrictions? And what happens to a namespace whose inactive-topic policy sets deleteWhileInactive=true while this is on?

output.text:
Both restrictions come from `PulsarService.java:960-974`. The close-mode logic is in `PersistentTopic.checkGC()` (`PersistentTopic.java:3885`). The design is written up in `pip/pip-470.md`.

## Why the two restrictions

**Not together with `brokerDeleteInactiveTopicsEnabled`.** The two flags pick opposite actions for an inactive topic. Delete removes the topic and its data. Close only unloads it from broker memory and keeps the ledgers. Startup rejects the combination so you can't end up with an ambiguous setup. You want data kept, so only close should be on.

**Mode must be `delete_when_no_subscriptions`.** This is about avoiding an unload/reload loop:
- Under `delete_when_subscriptions_caught_up`, `isActive()` only checks for backlog. A topic whose subscriptions are all caught up counts as inactive even while consumers are connected.
- Deleting such a topic is final, so nothing comes back. Closing it disconnects those consumers, and they reconnect straight away. The reconnect reloads the topic, and one inactivity window later GC closes it again.
- That cycle frees no memory and adds reconnect churn for every idle-but-connected consumer.
- Under `delete_when_no_subscriptions`, any subscription keeps the topic active. A connected consumer always implies a subscription, so a topic is only closed once every client has gone.

**Mode overrides at runtime.** Startup validation only checks the broker-level mode. A namespace or topic policy can still set `delete_when_subscriptions_caught_up` on a running broker. In that case `checkGC` logs at debug and skips the close for that topic (`PersistentTopic.java:3904-3913`). That topic is simply never closed, so its memory stays pinned. Nothing is deleted either.

## Namespace with `deleteWhileInactive=true`

Nothing is deleted. The broker-level close switch takes precedence over the policy (`PersistentTopic.java:3893-3897`):

```java
boolean closeEnabled = isCloseWhileInactive();
boolean deleteEnabled = !closeEnabled && isDeleteWhileInactive();
```

While close is on, `deleteEnabled` is always false, so `checkGC` never reaches the delete branch. The topic is closed instead, provided the effective mode is `delete_when_no_subscriptions`. Two other details:
- The `shouldTopicBeRetained()` check is skipped in close mode, since it only guards against data loss.
- `NonPersistentTopic.checkGC` uses the same gate (`NonPersistentTopic.java:1095`).

If you turn close mode off later, that namespace's `deleteWhileInactive=true` takes effect again and topics get deleted. Check namespace and topic policies before you flip the flag off.

`brokerCloseInactiveTopicsEnabled` is dynamic. A runtime change that would leave both flags true is rejected by the same validation path. A runtime change of the mode alone is not rejected, and falls under the per-topic skip above.

sent.prompt: Our Rust producer registers a SchemaType.JSON schema whose definition is a JSON Schema document ({"type":"object","properties":{...}}, draft 2020-12). **Why it changed.** This comes from PIP-464. I only read the design note for it, `pip/pip-464.md`, which is missing from this checkout. I didn't open the broker code, so I haven't confirmed the PIP is fully implemented in your broker version.

For `SchemaType.JSON`, the broker used to accept two definition formats:
- **Avro schema JSON**, such as `{"type":"record","fields":[...]}`. This has been the standard since Pulsar 2.1.
- **Legacy Jackson JSON Schema**, such as `{"type":"object","properties":{...}}`. This is the Pulsar 2.0 format.

`StructSchemaDataValidator` tried Avro first. If that failed, it fell back to Jackson parsing, which accepts any valid JSON. Your JSON Schema 2020-12 document failed Avro parsing and then passed the fallback, so it was registered.

Java consumers (`AutoConsumeSchema`, `GenericJsonSchema`) only understand Avro. They fail on that stored schema with `SchemaParseException: Type not supported: object`. The PIP removed the lenient fallback so the failure shows up when the producer registers, not later when a consumer reads.

The new default makes the validator reject anything that isn't valid Avro. It propagates the Avro `SchemaParseException`. `JsonSchemaCompatibilityCheck` also treats non-Avro schemas as incompatible.

**Getting the old behaviour back.** Set this in the broker's `broker.conf` and restart the broker:

```
schemaJsonAllowLegacyJacksonFormat=true
```

The default is `false`. Setting it to `true` restores the previous lenient fallback exactly. Per the PIP, it is aimed at deployments with genuine legacy-format schemas.

**Caveats**
- **Your consumers may still break.** With the flag on, registration works again, but Java consumers using auto-consume or generic JSON schemas will still fail to read that schema. That was the original problem.
- **Better fix for the Rust producer.** Register an Avro schema definition for the `JSON` type instead, for example `{"type":"record","name":"X","fields":[{"name":"f","type":"string"}]}`. The message payloads can stay plain JSON.
- **Geo-replication.** Keep the flag consistent across clusters. Otherwise one cluster can accept a schema that another rejects.

Topic-list responses are bounded by one shared byte-permit limiter per process. The broker has one and the proxy has its own. In both, the limiter is a `TopicListMemoryLimiter`, built with a heap budget and a direct-memory budget.

## Shared building blocks

- **`pulsar-common/src/main/java/org/apache/pulsar/common/semaphore/`**
  - `AsyncDualMemoryLimiterImpl` is the base class. It holds two `AsyncSemaphore`s, `LimitType.HEAP_MEMORY` and `LimitType.DIRECT_MEMORY`. Each has a byte budget, a bounded wait queue and an acquire timeout.
  - `AsyncDualMemoryLimiterUtil` has two helpers. `withPermitsFuture(...)` runs a function while holding permits and releases them on completion. `acquireDirectMemoryPermitsAndWriteAndFlush(...)` sizes the `BaseCommand` with `getSerializedSize()`, acquires `DIRECT_MEMORY` permits, then serializes and writes. It releases the permits when the socket write completes, or on failure or cancellation.
- **`pulsar-broker-common/src/main/java/org/apache/pulsar/broker/topiclistlimit/TopicListMemoryLimiter.java`** extends `AsyncDualMemoryLimiterImpl`. It adds the Prometheus and OpenTelemetry metrics and the static `estimateTopicListSize(topics)`.
- **`pulsar-broker-common/src/main/java/org/apache/pulsar/broker/topiclistlimit/TopicListSizeResultCache.java`** (with `ResultHolder`) caches the last known size of a namespace's listing. That size is the initial heap reservation, so a request can queue before it lists anything. It is capped at the heap limit.
- **`TopicListing.java`** in the same package identifies what is being listed, for the cache key.

## Broker

The limiter and the size cache are built in the `BrokerService` constructor (`pulsar-broker/src/main/java/org/apache/pulsar/broker/service/BrokerService.java:463-475`). They are exposed as `getMaxTopicListInFlightLimiter()` and `getTopicListSizeResultCache()`.

**GetTopicsOfNamespace**
- `ServerCnx.internalHandleGetTopicsOfNamespace` (`pulsar-broker/src/main/java/org/apache/pulsar/broker/service/ServerCnx.java:3746`) takes the initial size from the `TopicListSizeResultCache` holder.
- It then calls `maxTopicListInFlightLimiter.withAcquiredPermits(initialSize, HEAP_MEMORY, ...)` before it calls `NamespaceService.getListOfUserTopicsByProperties`.
- When the list returns, it computes `TopicListMemoryLimiter.estimateTopicListSize(topics)`, updates the cache, and calls `withUpdatedPermits(...)` to resize the reservation. Filtering, hashing and the response are built while those heap permits are held.
- `PulsarCommandSenderImpl.sendGetTopicsOfNamespaceResponse` (`pulsar-broker/src/main/java/org/apache/pulsar/broker/service/PulsarCommandSenderImpl.java:132-142`) then bounds the serialized response with `DIRECT_MEMORY` permits through `acquireDirectMemoryPermitsAndWriteAndFlush`.
- Before any of this, `ServerCnx` also uses the `lookupRequestSemaphore`, sized by `maxConcurrentLookupRequest`. It rejects with `TooManyRequests`. That limits request count, not bytes.

**Topic-list watches**
- `TopicListService.getTopics(...)` (`pulsar-broker/src/main/java/org/apache/pulsar/broker/service/TopicListService.java:714-757`) does the same heap-permit and size-cache sequence for the initial listing and for re-listings. It lists with `NamespaceService.getListOfUserTopics`. Requests are cancelled if the connection closes or the watcher is removed.
- The outgoing frames go through `PulsarCommandSenderImpl.sendWatchTopicListSuccess` (line 447) and `sendWatchTopicListUpdate` (line 463). Both use `DIRECT_MEMORY` permits.

The admin REST listings use the same limiter and cache. They go through `pulsar-broker/src/main/java/org/apache/pulsar/broker/admin/impl/TopicListResponseMemoryLimiter.java`, which `NamespacesBase`, `PersistentTopicsBase`, `NonPersistentTopics` and `ScalableTopics` call.

**Broker settings** (`ServiceConfiguration.java`, around lines 1782-1812, in `broker.conf`):

| Setting | Default |
|---|---|
| `maxTopicListInFlightHeapMemSizeMB` | 100 |
| `maxTopicListInFlightHeapMemSizePermitsAcquireQueueSize` | 10000 |
| `maxTopicListInFlightHeapMemSizePermitsAcquireTimeoutMillis` | 25000 |
| `maxTopicListInFlightDirectMemSizeMB` | 100 |
| `maxTopicListInFlightDirectMemSizePermitsAcquireQueueSize` | 10000 |
| `maxTopicListInFlightDirectMemSizePermitsAcquireTimeoutMillis` | 25000 |

`maxConcurrentLookupRequest` (default 50000) is the request-count guard mentioned above. `enableBrokerTopicListWatcher` turns watches on or off.

## Proxy

- `ProxyService` builds its own `TopicListMemoryLimiter` and `TopicListSizeResultCache` (`pulsar-proxy/src/main/java/org/apache/pulsar/proxy/server/ProxyService.java:261-274`). The metrics prefix is `pulsar_proxy_`.
- `LookupProxyHandler` (`pulsar-proxy/src/main/java/org/apache/pulsar/proxy/server/LookupProxyHandler.java`) handles `GetTopicsOfNamespace`. Around lines 420-476 it holds `HEAP_MEMORY` permits while the broker's response is held and resized. It then writes the response through `acquireDirectMemoryPermitsAndWriteAndFlush`.
- I found no topic-list watch handling and no limiter use in `ProxyConnection.java`. I did not trace how the proxy forwards watch frames, so I can't say whether they are bounded there.

**Proxy settings** (`ProxyConfiguration.java:498-528`, in `proxy.conf`):
- The names and defaults are the same six `maxTopicListInFlight*` settings as the broker's.
- They are configured separately from the broker's.

- The bound is on estimated bytes in flight, not on topic count. A single namespace whose estimated listing is larger than the heap budget can't be satisfied cleanly, so check that `maxTopicListInFlightHeapMemSizeMB` is sized above your largest namespace listing.

[improve][broker] Lower MAX_COALESCED_BYTES to 16 KiB

Motivation: Consumers behind a TLS-inspecting appliance see any write larger than one 16 KiB TLS record split by the appliance, which adds about 3 ms per extra record. With 64 KiB coalesced writes, the p99 delivery latency for Marlow Exchange's market-data consumers tripled.

Modifications:
- Lower PulsarCommandSenderImpl.MAX_COALESCED_BYTES from 64 KiB to 16 KiB so a coalesced write fits in one TLS record.
- Document the reason next to the constant.
