output.text:
**Short version:** the design takes the "delegator" (the per-shard query coordinator) off StreamingNode and splits it up. Only part of it is built, and none of it serves production queries yet.

## Who does what

The old model puts the delegator on StreamingNode. That would make StreamingNode forward every segment load/release, apply every delete, route every query, reduce every shard's results and relay all QueryNode result traffic. It would be a global bottleneck that is hard to scale. (Source: README §1–2.)

| Component | New role |
|---|---|
| **QueryCoord** | Builds the complete distributed query view and directly manages all sealed-segment load/release. It is the leader of the view state machine. |
| **StreamingNode** | Serves growing data and generates query plans. It only accepts view updates from QueryCoord and no longer loads or releases sealed segments. |
| **QueryNode** | Loads sealed segments. After loading, it subscribes to deletes from StreamingNode and applies them itself. |
| **Proxy** | Runs a two-phase query. Phase 1 gets a shard-level plan from StreamingNode, using the highest Up view at the request's schema version. The plan carries MVCC, optimizations and the view version. Phase 2 sends the plan to StreamingNode and QueryNodes. Proxy does all the distributed reduce. If a node fails or a view is invalidated, the query is cancelled and retried. |

This removes the single-point delegator, so reduce and RPC load scales with Proxy. It also removes idle TimeTick and the strong-consistency tsafe wait.

## Two version numbers

- **DataVersion** is `(streaming_version, compact_version)`. It is a collection-level immutable snapshot of which sealed segments are loadable, each with a manifest version.
  - `streaming_version` goes up only on the flush transaction, which is the growing-to-sealed handoff.
  - `compact_version` goes up for every other membership change: compaction, import, truncate, partition drop and L0 manifest advance.
- **QueryVersion** is `((S,C), Q)` and is per shard and replica. It is the DataVersion plus Q.
  - When the DataVersion increases, Q resets to 1.
  - Q increases for pure redistribution of the same data, such as a balance or a node-crash recovery.

Ordering is lexicographic. An Up view's version can never go backwards.

## State machine

- **Normal flow:** Preparing → Ready → Up → Down → Dropping → Dropped.
- **Error flow:** Preparing → Unrecoverable → Dropping → Dropped.
- **StreamingNode only:** UpRecovering is an extra state used after a crash, while WAL replay catches up. Coord sees it as Up.

How it moves:
- Coord persists Preparing and pushes it to StreamingNode and all QueryNodes through the single `SyncQueryView` RPC.
- When every node reports Ready, Coord pushes Up to StreamingNode. Ready is not persisted.
- When a higher view confirms Up, the old one goes Down. StreamingNode delays its own Down until the serving lease expires and no queries are using the view.
- Dropping is not persisted either.
- QueryNode is stateless and serves as soon as it is Ready. It ignores Up and Down.
- Node responses always carry the latest local state, so Coord can rebuild its picture after a restart.

## How much serves production today

None of it does. The docs say the current code covers StreamingNode execution, the QueryNode extraction and the DataView manager. It does not switch production Proxy routing, and it does not activate the new Coordinator runtime.

- **Implemented:** the StreamingNode plan and execution path (`GetQueryPlan`, `SearchOnView`, `QueryOnView`), the QueryNode resource preparation, and the DataView manager.
- **Not wired:**
  - Proxy has no references to `GetQueryPlan`, `SearchOnView` or `QueryOnView`. I grepped `internal/proxy` and found none, which matches the docs.
  - QueryCoord does not generate QueryViews or publish LoadInfo from the legacy load APIs.
  - The `transform_start_after_timetick` frontier and the remote delete-stream subscription are still TODO.
  - DDL query visibility (truncate and partition drop) is still TODO.
  - WAL-secondary routing is still future work.

## Where it is written down

All paths are under `docs/design-docs/design_docs/qviews/`.

- **Index and architecture:** `README.md`. It covers motivation, the two-phase query, the version examples, the lifecycle, the node interaction tables and `SyncQueryView`.
- **State machine, per node and per state:** `query_view_state_machine.md`.
- **DataView:** `data_view.md` and `data_view_schema.md`.
- **Serving lease:** `query_view_lease.md`.
- **QueryNode side:** `querynode_extraction.md` and `qnview/querynode_queryview_resource_preparation.md`.
- **Query contracts:** the `query/` folder (`query_plan.md`, `query_client.md`, `query_execution.md`, `replica_discovery.md`, `segment_pruning.md`).
- **Also relevant:** `syncer.md`, `balancer_scanning.md`, `collection_load_info.md`, `ddl_visibility.md`, `transform_start_after_timetick.md`, `snview/idf_oracle_runtime.md`, and `../wal/streamingnode_vchannel_wal_view.md`.
- **Wire types:** `pkg/proto/view.proto`.
- **Code:**
  - DataView: `internal/dataview/manager.go`.
  - StreamingNode: `internal/streamingnode/server/{queryplan,viewquery}/`.
  - QueryNode: `internal/views/viewquery/server.go` and `internal/querynodev2/{qnview,qvresource,viewquery}`.

The distributed query view moves the sealed-segment and query work off StreamingNode (SN) and onto QueryCoord (QC), Proxy and QueryNode (QN). It is mostly built but not yet serving production traffic.

## Who does what

The design avoids putting the old delegator on SN. That would route every load and release, every delete apply, every query and every QN result through SN, making it one global bottleneck (`README.md` §1).

| Component | Role |
|---|---|
| **QueryCoord** | Owns all sealed-segment load and release. It builds the complete distributed query view and drives its state machine. It prepares no resources itself. |
| **StreamingNode** | No longer loads or releases sealed segments and no longer forwards searches. It takes view updates from QC, keeps the growing data, and produces query plans. It also runs queries on its own growing data. |
| **QueryNode** | Loads its sealed segments and prepares the resources a view needs. It subscribes to deletes from SN and applies them itself. It can serve once the view is Ready. |
| **Proxy** | Runs the query in two phases. Phase 1 asks SN for a shard-level plan against the highest Up view. Phase 2 sends that plan to SN and the QNs. Proxy does all the distributed reduce, so you scale it by adding Proxies. |

Nodes sync with QC through one RPC, `SyncQueryView`. QC is the leader.

## Versions

- **DataView version** is `(streaming_version, compact_version)`, ordered lexicographically at collection level.
  - `streaming_version` goes up only on the flush transaction, when data moves from growing to sealed.
  - `compact_version` goes up on every other change to which segments are loadable: compaction, import, truncate, partition drop, and L0 manifest advances.
  - Each snapshot is immutable and lists the loadable segments and their manifest versions.
- **QueryView version** is `((S,C), Q)`, per shard and per replica.
  - `(S,C)` is the DataView it was built from.
  - `Q` goes up when segments are only moved between nodes (balance or crash recovery). It resets to 1 when the DataView advances.
  - An Up view's version can only increase.

## State machine

The normal path is `Preparing → Ready → Up → Down → Dropping → Dropped`. The failure path is `Preparing → Unrecoverable → Dropping → Dropped`.

- QC persists Preparing, Up, Down and Unrecoverable to etcd. Ready and Dropping are not persisted and are rebuilt from node responses.
- Ready becomes Up only after SN confirms.
- SN also has an SN-only `UpRecovering` state, used while it replays the WAL after a crash. QC sees it as Up.
- QNs ignore Up and Down. They serve as soon as they are Ready.
- SN delays Up → Down while its serving lease or active queries remain.

## Production status

Mostly not live. The docs say the extracted code does not switch Proxy routing or activate the new coordinator runtime (`README.md` §3; `querynode_extraction.md`). I cross-checked the code and found no match:

- **Proxy:** `internal/proxy` has no calls to `GetQueryPlan`, `SearchOnView` or `QueryOnView`.
- **Coordinator:** the state machine and balancer exist in `internal/views/coord/{coordview,balancer}`. `mix_coord.go` wires only the load-info and segment-metadata RPCs.
- **DataView:** the manager exists in `internal/dataview` and is wired into DataCoord's flush path. Nothing consumes it for query placement yet.
- **SN and QN sides:** SN plan and execution and the QN resource path are implemented. They are exercised through explicit ViewSync and component tests, which the docs say don't prove cluster-wide routing or recovery.
- **Still missing:** the production LoadInfo producer and the base replay cursor. Also missing are remote delete-stream (TransformLog) consumption by QN, DDL query visibility, and the safe `transform_start_after_timetick`.

The documented consistency routing is the primary-WAL owner only.

## Where it's written down

All paths are under `docs/design-docs/design_docs/qviews/` unless noted.

- `README.md` is the index and main design. Start with §2 (architecture), §3 (two-phase query), §5–6 (versions) and §7 (states).
- `data_view.md` and `data_view_schema.md` cover DataView.
- `query_view_state_machine.md` has per-node, per-state detail.
- `query_view_lease.md` covers the SN serving lease.

**What the design says**

The design doc is `docs/design-docs/design_docs/20261019-look-aside-balancer-fix-design.md`. Its fix C section has the intended code at lines 120–149 and the rationale at line 160 ("Seeding"). The seeding rule reads:

- A fresh sample seeds the smoothed value directly only if the previous sample has expired (`nowTs - metrics.ts > b.metricExpireInterval`) or never existed (`ts == 0`).
- In every other case the EWMA is applied.
- The doc says explicitly that `0` cannot be the "unseeded" marker. A smoothed value of 0 is a normal `ServiceTime` for sub-millisecond requests.

The code is at `internal/proxy/shardclient/refined_look_aside_balancer.go:258`:

```go
if math.Float64frombits(metrics.serviceTimeSmooth.Load()) == 0 {
    // seed with the raw sample
```

It seeds whenever the smoothed service time is 0, and it never checks `ts` or `metricExpireInterval` in this method.

**Differences in behaviour**

1. **Outlier after zeros.** Suppose a node has been reporting `ServiceTime` 0 (sub-millisecond), so its smoothed value is 0. One 20ms outlier then sets the smoothed value straight to 20, with no damping. The design chose the `ts`-based rule specifically to prevent this. 2. **Underflow.** The doc names a second case: a long run of zero samples can underflow the float back to 0, which triggers the same re-seeding.

4. **Response time.** The condition tests only `serviceTimeSmooth`, but it also overwrites `responseTimeSmooth`. A node with a smoothed service time of 0 and a non-zero smoothed response time gets its response-time history thrown away.

- The `nil` guard.
- Mirroring the sample to the embedded `LookAsideBalancer.UpdateCostMetrics`.
- Keeping the smoothed values in float64.
- The `ewma` formula.
- The ordering of the stores for `cost` and `ts`.

```go
if nowTs-metrics.ts.Load() > b.metricExpireInterval {
```

Because `ts` starts at 0, a new entry still seeds on its first sample.

sent.prompt: Why is the proxy's MetaCache keyed by collection ID, with collection names and aliases kept only as hints? And how are cache fills kept from racing the invalidations that DDL broadcasts send, so that a describe started before a DDL can't put stale metadata back?

output.text:
The cache is keyed by collection ID because only the ID is stable. Fills and invalidations are ordered by a single read/write lock, `fillMu`. I read the streaming docs (broadcaster, alias and collection message semantics), `internal/proxy/metacache/meta_cache.go`, the proxy's invalidation handler, and the drop-collection callback in rootcoord. I didn't run any tests.

## Why the ID is the key

The primary store is `collections map[UniqueID]*CollectionInfo` (`meta_cache.go:371`). An entry is live if and only if its ID is in that map.

- **IDs are cluster-unique and never reused.** A name or alias is not. A dropped collection's name can be recreated as a different collection. A rename keeps the ID and changes the name. An alias can be re-pointed to another collection. Keyed by name, each of those could make a cached entry silently describe the wrong collection.
- **Names and aliases are hints.** `nameIdx` maps (db, name) to an ID, and `aliasInfo` maps (db, alias) to a real name (`meta_cache.go:380-381`). `getCollection` follows alias to name to ID to primary entry (`meta_cache.go:479-521`). It then checks that the entry still has that exact name and database. After a rename or a same-name recreate, the old hint fails the check and counts as a miss. The cost is one extra describe, never a stale read.
- **Hints are written only together with their entry.** `update()` writes the name hint and the entry's own declared `Aliases` (`meta_cache.go:588-612`). `evictCollectionEntryLocked` (`meta_cache.go:1393`) removes the entry together with its name hint, alias hints and partition list. So every hint can be found from its entry, and no background GC is needed. The reason for this rule is in the code comment. A leftover alias hint would validate again after a same-name recreate and bring back an alias that rootcoord had already dropped.
- **The partition cache is also keyed by ID** (`meta_cache.go:674-680`). A drop and recreate can't alias into old partition lists, and invalidation doesn't need to expand names or aliases.
- **Invalidation is mostly O(1).** `InvalidateCollectionMeta` (`meta_cache.go:1300`) resolves the name, any alias and the forwarded ID to IDs, then evicts those IDs. The broadcasts forward both IDs of an AlterAlias. If a broadcast carries no target ID, `RemoveAliasHolders` scans the cache as a fallback (`meta_cache.go:886`, `impl.go:189-206`).

## How fills are kept from racing invalidations

The mechanism is `fillMu`, a `sync.RWMutex` (`meta_cache.go:420`). It replaced an earlier per-collection version floor.

- **Fills take the read lock.** `updateWithSingleflight` holds `fillMu.RLock` for the whole `sfGlobal.Do` call (`meta_cache.go:698-708`). That covers the describe RPC, the write-back, delivery of the result, and removal of the finished singleflight entry. Fills don't block each other, and cache hits never touch the lock.
- **Invalidations take the write lock.** `InvalidateCollectionMeta`, `RemoveCollection`, `RemoveCollectionsByID`, `RemoveAlias`, `RemoveAliasHolders`, `RemoveDatabase` and `RemoveDatabaseInfo` all take `fillMu.Lock` first, then `m.mu`. This waits for every in-flight fill to finish before evicting.

That leaves two cases for a describe that starts before a DDL:

1. **It started before the eviction.** It finishes, including its write-back, before the eviction can run. The eviction then removes whatever it wrote.
2. **It starts after the eviction.** It reads post-DDL state, because rootcoord commits the DDL in its ack callback before it fans out the expiration. In the drop-collection callback, `c.meta.DropCollection` runs before `ExpireCaches` (`ddl_callbacks_drop_collection.go:131` and `168`).

Details that close the gaps:

- **The lock covers the whole singleflight lifecycle.** The comment at `meta_cache.go:693-697` explains why. If the lock were released inside `update()`, a post-invalidation caller could join the already-finished pre-DDL flight. It would get the stale result directly, without going through the cache maps.
- **The partition fill re-checks the primary entry.** Before writing back, it checks under `m.mu` that the primary entry is still present (`meta_cache.go:1090-1094`). Without that check, a list could be cached with no owner entry, and no later eviction would find it.
- **`RemoveDatabase` drains under the write lock, then releases it.** It detaches the database's hint bucket in O(1) and unlocks, then evicts in batches (`meta_cache.go:1452-1496`). A fill racing that walk can at worst be evicted again, which costs one refetch.
- **Entries with no database aren't cached.** An id-only describe from an old rootcoord returns no database, so it is served uncached (`meta_cache.go:550-560`).

## Costs and one claim I didn't verify

- **Invalidations wait on in-flight fills.** An invalidation waits for the slowest in-flight fill, and new fills queue behind a pending invalidation. Fill RPCs use the caller's context with no MetaCache deadline, so callers must set a sensible one.
- **Deadlock-freedom depends on rootcoord.** The code comment says ack callbacks release the meta lock before the expiration fan-out. That keeps a fill's describe RPC from blocking on the DDL whose invalidation is waiting for that fill. I confirmed the commit-then-expire order in the drop-collection callback, but I didn't trace the lock release itself in rootcoord.

sent.prompt: Why is the proxy's MetaCache keyed by collection ID, with collection names and aliases kept only as hints? And how are cache fills kept from racing the invalidations that DDL broadcasts send, so that a describe started before a DDL can't put stale metadata back?

output.text:
The code matches the design doc (`docs/design-docs/design_docs/20260716-proxy-metacache-id-inverted-index.md`). The implementation is in `internal/proxy/metacache/meta_cache.go`. I read the doc and grepped the `fillMu` sites in that file. I did not read every function body line by line.

## Why the cache is keyed by collection ID

Invalidations arrive by collection id, alias or database. The old primary store was keyed by (db, name), so every eviction had to search for the entry. The doc lists the scans that caused:

- Finding an id's name keys was O(all cached collections).
- The partition sweep was O(all partition entries).
- Alias cleanup was O(the db's aliases).
- Partition-DDL name expansion was O(the db's collections plus aliases).

Each of these ran under the global write lock on every Load, Release, Drop, Rename or Alter broadcast. At around 1M cached collections, every broadcast stalled all queries on the proxy.

The fix is principle P1:

- **Primary store:** `collections` is a map keyed by the cluster-unique id. An entry is live exactly when it is present.
- **Hints:** `nameIdx` (db → name → id) and `aliasInfo` (db → alias → target name) are only hints that resolve to an id. They are written only together with their entry, and the alias hints come only from the entry's declared aliases.
- **Read path:** every read validates the hint against the primary. It checks that the id is live and that the name and db still match. A failed check is a cache miss and costs one extra describe, never a stale read. So a stale name after a rename, or an old id after a drop and recreate, corrects itself on the next read.
- **Eviction:** one routine, `evictCollectionEntryLocked`, removes the entry together with its name hint, its alias hints and its partition list. All of these are reachable from the entry in hand, so invalidation by id is O(1) and no background GC is needed.
- **Partition cache:** it is also keyed by id.

## How fills are kept from racing invalidations

This is principle P2. The old design used per-collection timestamp floors (`collectionCacheVersion`). Those had gaps: alias write-backs were unversioned, there was a bypass when `RequestTime == 0`, and `RemoveDatabase` never raised the floor. The new design uses ordering instead of timestamps, with one global `fillMu sync.RWMutex`:

- **Fills take the read side.** A fill holds `fillMu.RLock` for its whole duration, from the describe RPC through the write-back (`meta_cache.go:698` and `:1051`). Fills don't block each other, and cache hits never touch `fillMu`.
- **Invalidations take the write side.** `fillMu.Lock` waits for all in-flight fills to finish before evicting (`:866`, `:888`, `:1271`).

A describe that started before a DDL therefore has one of two outcomes:

- **It finishes before the invalidation.** Its pre-DDL snapshot is written back, and the eviction that follows then removes it.
- **It starts after the invalidation.** Rootcoord commits the DDL before it broadcasts, so this describe reads post-DDL state.

A pre-DDL snapshot can never land after the eviction. A queued writer also blocks new readers, so a stream of new fills can't starve an invalidation.

Details that keep this safe:

- **Lock order and RPCs:** the lock order is `fillMu` then `m.mu`. `m.mu` is never held across an RPC.
- **Deadlock avoidance:** rootcoord's DDL ack callbacks release the meta lock before the expiration fan-out. A fill's describe is therefore never blocked by the DDL whose invalidation is waiting on that fill. On the proxy, `RemovePartition` does its ensure-describe before it takes the write side.
- **Alter alias:** rootcoord sends both the old and new target ids (`old_collection_id`). The proxy evicts both by id, so a concurrent describe that re-points the alias hint can't hide the old target.
- **Alter database:** this invalidates only `dbInfo`, and it does so under `fillMu`. A pre-alter `DescribeDatabase` can't bring back the old properties.
- **Drop database:** the lock is held only to drain fills and drop the hint buckets. The walk that evicts the db's entries runs afterwards through the same eviction routine.

## Accepted trade-offs

- **Slow fills delay acks:** an invalidation, and so the broadcast ack, waits for the slowest in-flight fill. MetaCache imposes no timeout of its own. A deadline-less RPC that hangs could pin `fillMu` and everything queued behind it. The doc deliberately leaves deadline policy to the API or coordinator-client boundary.
- **Over-invalidation:** duplicate or late broadcasts cost one extra re-describe, because they are not filtered by version.
- **Id-only describe with no db:** if an id-only describe response has no db (an older rootcoord during a rolling upgrade), it is served uncached. No database DDL could find and invalidate such an entry otherwise.

Explain to a newcomer, as briefly as you can, what it changes about who does what between Proxy, QueryCoord, StreamingNode and QueryNode and why, what a DataView version and a QueryView version are, how a query view moves through its states, how much of it serves production traffic today, and where each part is written down.

output.text:
## Distributed query view in brief

### Who does what

The change moves the "delegator" job off a single choke point. Putting it on StreamingNode would force all segment loads, deletes, queries and result traffic through that node. So the roles split like this (`README.md` §1–2):

- **QueryCoord (Coord)** generates the global query view and drives its state machine. It owns sealed-segment load and release, and it no longer manages resource-preparation workflows.
- **StreamingNode (SN)** accepts view updates from Coord and prepares its own resources: growing segments and the WAL-derived input. It also hands out the query plan. It no longer loads or releases sealed segments, forwards searches, or pushes deletes.
- **QueryNode (QN)** loads sealed segments for a view and reports whether they are ready. After a segment loads, the QN subscribes to deletes itself. That delete-stream path is still planned.
- **Proxy** runs a two-phase query. Phase 1 gets a shard-level plan from the SN, which includes the MVCC timestamp, the optimisation and the view version. Phase 2 sends that plan to the SN and QNs and does the final reduce itself. If a node fails or a view is invalidated, the query is cancelled and retried.

The payoffs are that scaling Proxy removes the reduce bottleneck, SN and QN recover independently, and strong-consistency queries skip the 100–200ms tsafe wait.

### Versions

- **DataView version (`DataVersion`)** identifies an immutable collection snapshot of loadable sealed segments. It is a pair `(streaming_version, compact_version)`, ordered lexicographically. `streaming_version` goes up only on the flush transaction. `compact_version` goes up for every other membership change: compaction, import, L0 manifest advance, partition drop and truncate. DataCoord owns it.
- **QueryView version** is `((streaming_version, compact_version), Q)`. `Q` increases for pure redistribution, such as a balance or a node crash, where the data is unchanged. When the DataView part increases, `Q` resets to 1. The version applies per shard per replica. An Up view's version may only increase.

### State machine

The normal path is `Preparing → Ready → Up → Down → Dropping → Dropped`. The error path is `Preparing → Unrecoverable → Dropping → Dropped`.

- In Preparing, Coord persists the state to etcd, then pushes the view to the SN and all QNs.
- When every node reports Ready, Coord pushes Up to the SN. The SN confirms, and Coord persists Up.
- When a higher view confirms Up, or the collection is released, the old view goes Down.
- Down moves to Dropping once the SN confirms Down, and Dropped removes the view.
- Ready is not persisted. After a Coord crash, Coord re-pushes Preparing and catches up from the nodes' responses.
- The SN delays its local Up→Down while its serving lease or active queries still hold the view.
- Coord and nodes talk through one idempotent RPC, `SyncQueryView`. The node's response always carries its latest local state.

### How much serves production traffic today

None of the Coord-side runtime or the Proxy routing does, as far as the docs say. This is an extraction in progress:

- **Built:** the SN query plan and execution path, the QN resource preparation and view-query services, the DataView manager, and an injectable query client.
- **Not switched on:** production Proxy routing, and the Coordinator QueryView runtime that generates views (`README.md` §3). The extraction doesn't publish LoadInfo from the legacy Load APIs, generate QueryViews, or switch Proxy routing (`querynode_extraction.md`).
- **Still planned or TODO:** the remote delete-stream subscription for QNs, WAL-secondary routing, and DDL visibility for truncate and partition drop. The `transform_start_after_timetick` frontier is also a TODO.

I read these claims in the docs and did not cross-check them against the code. `CLAUDE.md` asks for that cross-check before you change anything, so do it before you start.

All paths are under `docs/design-docs/design_docs/`.

| Topic | Location |
|---|---|
| Overview, roles, versions, lifecycle | `qviews/README.md` |
| DataView | `qviews/data_view.md`, `qviews/data_view_schema.md` |
| Per-node state machine | `qviews/query_view_state_machine.md` |
| Serving lease | `qviews/query_view_lease.md` |
| Coord to node sync | `qviews/syncer.md`, `qviews/shard_view_management.md` |
| Balancer | `qviews/balancer_scanning.md` |
| QN extraction and resource preparation | `qviews/querynode_extraction.md`, `qviews/qnview/querynode_queryview_resource_preparation.md` |
| Query path | `qviews/query/` (`query_plan.md`, `query_client.md`, `query_execution.md`, `segment_pruning.md`) |
| SN WAL input | `wal/streamingnode_vchannel_wal_view.md`, `wal/transform_log.md` |

| Wire types and states | `pkg/proto/view.proto` |
| Code | `internal/views/` (including `coord/coordview/state_machine.go`), `internal/dataview/manager.go`, `internal/streamingnode/server/viewquery/`, `internal/querynodev2/{qnview,qvresource,viewquery}` |

sent.prompt: A full (non-partial) upsert into a collection whose primary key has autoID=true now looks the primary keys up before it writes anything. Why? What happens to a row whose key exists, to one whose key is not found, and to one that has no key at all, and why isn't a row that is not found simply inserted under the key the caller sent?

output.text:
**Why the lookup happens first**

The design doc is `docs/design-docs/design_docs/20260803-autoid-upsert-primary-key-preservation.md`.

Before this change, a full upsert on an autoID collection replaced the caller's key for every row. For an existing key `P`, the proxy emitted `Delete(P)` and `Insert(G)`, where `G` was a freshly allocated ID. `P` and `G` can hash to different VChannels, so the two messages can commit in different WAL transactions. A legal snapshot cut can then contain the delete but not the insert, and restoring that snapshot loses the entity. The entity's identity also changed on every upsert.

The new path (`prepareUpsert` in `internal/proxy/dml/task_upsert.go:306-360`) runs a PK-only Query first. It does this to tell an update from a creation before it builds the business key. For an existing row it can then keep `P`, so the delete and insert share one routing key and one VChannel transaction.

**What happens to each row**

| Row | Result |
|-|-|
| Key exists | `Delete(P)` plus `Insert(P)`. The key is preserved and `P` is returned. |
| Key not found | Only `Insert(G)`, where `G` is a newly allocated ID. `G` is returned. |
| No key at all | Rejected. `queryPreExecute` fails with "must assign pk when upsert" (`task_upsert.go:385-389`). The doc says to use Insert to create an entity without a lookup key. |

The key checks run before the query. `checkUpsertPrimaryFieldData` validates the lookup keys at line 339, so deterministic errors and query errors fail before anything is appended to the WAL.

**Why a not-found row isn't inserted under the caller's key**

For a not-found row, `P` is only a lookup key. A "not found" result does not mean the allocator owns `P`. If `P` were inserted directly, it could collide with an ID the allocator has already issued or will issue later. The doc lists "Insert a missing request PK `P`" as a rejected alternative for this reason.

Instead, `allocateMissingAutoIDs` (`task_upsert.go:989-1032`) takes a batch of IDs from the same global allocator that ordinary Insert uses (`common.AllocAutoID`). It writes them over the missing rows' PK values. Allocator ranges don't overlap across proxies, so nothing else can generate the same ID.

The safety invariant is allocator ownership, not `G != P`. If the allocator happens to return a value equal to `P`, that is still safe, because the allocation reserves it. A separate check rejects the case where an allocated ID collides with another key in the same request. The related test is `TestPrepareUpsertFullAutoIDRejectsAllocatedIDCollision`.

**Caveats the doc states**

- `P` is not an idempotency key. Retrying after an ambiguous failure may allocate a new `G` if `P` is still not found. It cannot recover the first `G`.
- Existence follows standard Query semantics. There is no CAS or lock between the lookup and the write.
- Partial upserts keep their existing read, merge and CAS path. They also generate IDs for missing rows, but only when the insert fields are complete.

I read the doc and `task_upsert.go`. I did not read the other sub-documents the project instructions require for streaming-system changes, since this was an explanation and not a code change. I also didn't run any tests.

With the 5s timeout, the unpin was cancelled partway. The leftover pins stayed until the next restart and held segments the garbage collector should have freed. "Well under a second" is true on a single-AZ or local etcd. It isn't true for large snapshots on high-latency etcd, and that case is the one that failed.

**Why 5s is risky.**
- A failed cleanup doesn't fail quickly. It leaks pins silently, because the callers only log a warning and move on (e.g. `snapshot_export_manager.go:196`, `:788`). The leak costs storage that can't be reclaimed.
- The timeout only matters when etcd is slow or stuck. A healthy release finishes early and never waits for it. So a longer value costs nothing in the normal case. In the stuck case it delays a background cleanup, which nothing user-facing waits on.
- Wanting a stuck etcd to fail quickly is better served by other means, such as etcd health checks and alerts. The cleanup deadline is the wrong tool for it.

**What decides the value.** The timeout should be a comfortable multiple of the worst-case healthy release time. That time is roughly (number of etcd round trips for the largest snapshot) × (cross-AZ RTT). The measured worst case is 6–9s, so 20s gives about 2x headroom. Lowering it needs evidence from the slowest supported etcd topology, not the typical one.

**Caveats.**
- The 6–9s figure and the leak come from the commit and comment. I haven't reproduced them, and the commit says it wasn't tested on a live multi-AZ cluster.
- The constant is shared. `snapshotPinCleanupTimeout` is also used for export-job metadata updates, credential clearing and job drops (`snapshot_export_manager.go:192, 635, 722, 767, 784, 797, 818`). The unpin step is the one the evidence covers. At `:784-797` the unpin and the job update each get their own 20s budget.
- If you want fast failure for the non-pin paths such as `DropJob`, split the constant. Give those paths their own shorter timeout and leave the unpin at 20s.
- A better fix for the underlying slowness would be to batch the unpin writes, so release time stops scaling with snapshot size × RTT. That would be a separate change.

The splitting happens in the WAL adaptor's append path, and the reassembly happens in the WAL adaptor's catch-up scanner.

## Configuration switch
- **`streaming.splitChunkSN`** turns the splitting on. It is declared as `StreamingCfg.SplitChunkSN` in `pkg/util/paramtable/component_param.go` (key at ~line 9435) and documented in `configs/milvus.yaml` (~line 1748). It defaults to `false` and supports live refresh.
- `proxy.splitChunk` (`SplitChunkProxy`, default `true`) is the paired rollout switch on the proxy side. It keeps the old row-based size packing. The docs say to enable `streaming.splitChunkSN` on every StreamingNode first, then disable `proxy.splitChunk`.

## Splitting (append side)
- **`internal/streamingnode/server/wal/adaptor/wal_adaptor.go`**
  - `walAdaptorImpl.appendWithOptionalChunking` (~line 298) checks `SplitChunkSN`. It splits only if the payload is larger than the per-record budget. It then appends each chunk with `appendOneWithRetry` and returns the first chunk's message ID as the logical ID. It is called from the append loop at ~line 230.
  - `chunkPayloadSize` and `computeChunkPayloadSize` (~lines 349–370) give the per-record budget. That is the backend's max message size minus the reserve, using `pulsar.maxMessageSize`, `pulsar.messageReserveSize`, and similar. A budget of 0 (RocksMQ or an unknown WAL) means no chunking. The result is cached for 1 second (`chunkPayloadSizeRefresh`).
- **`pkg/streaming/util/message/chunk.go`**
  - `SplitIntoChunks` slices the payload and writes the `messageChunkIndex` and `messageChunkTotal` properties on each chunk. The chunk keeps the original message type and properties.

## Reassembly (read side)
- **`pkg/streaming/util/message/chunk.go`**
  - `ChunkAssembler.Push` buffers chunks, keyed by the original message's time tick. It returns the assembled message once the last chunk arrives, and it swallows duplicate redeliveries.
  - `AssembleChunks` concatenates the payloads, strips the chunk markers, and keeps the first chunk's message ID.
  - `AdvanceTimeTick` and `discardRunsAtOrBefore` drop orphaned runs.
  - `ErrCorruptedChunk` is returned for bad markers or inconsistent runs.
- **`internal/streamingnode/server/wal/adaptor/scanner_switchable.go`**
  - `catchupScanner` holds a `chunkAssembler message.ChunkAssembler` field (~line 119).
  - `consumeWithScanner` (~line 159) calls `Push` on each message before any other processing, so later stages only see complete messages.
  - It also calls `AdvanceTimeTick` for raw v0 TimeTick messages (~line 197).
  - `Do` (~line 134) stops retrying and fails the scanner when it gets `ErrCorruptedChunk`.

## Related guard
`ProduceServer.validateMessage` in `internal/streamingnode/server/service/handler/producer/produce_server.go` (~line 228) rejects client messages that already carry the reserved chunk markers (`IsChunkedPayload`). Such a message would otherwise be read back as a corrupted chunk run and take the pchannel down.

sent.prompt: What does Import V3 change about how bulk import works compared with Import V2, and why was it needed? Is it what runs by default now?

output.text:
Import V3 is not the default. It's off unless an operator turns on `dataCoord.import.enableImportV3`. I checked the design doc, the config default and the version-selection code, and they agree.

## What changes from V2 to V3

The source for this is `docs/design-docs/design_docs/20260921-import-v3-reshard-design.md`.

**V2 reads every source file twice and writes straight into segments:**
1. `PreImportTask` parses the whole file, keeps only statistics, and hashes rows.
2. `ImportTaskV2` reads the file again, hashes rows per file-group, and writes into pre-allocated segments.

**V3 reads each source once and reorganizes in the pipeline:**
1. **`preimport` (count-only):** It only computes exact per-file row counts and sizes. It doesn't hash rows. For Parquet and NumPy it reads the count from file metadata. Backup imports only size the object list.
2. **`reshard`:** It reads each source once, normalizes the rows, routes them to a `(vchannel, partition)` bucket, sorts them, and writes immutable sorted fragments plus a manifest. Overflow spills to local disk.
3. **Planning:** It packs fragments into per-segment plans for each bucket, across all source tasks.
4. **`import` (`ImportTaskV3`):** It does a k-way merge over one plan's fragments and writes exactly one formal segment, using the existing Storage V2/V3 writers.

The job state machine also changes. V3 adds `Resharding` and `Planning` states and has no `Sorting` stage.

## Why it was needed

- **Segment shape:** In V2, every file-group task splits the same bucket, which produces many small segments. In V3 the pipeline decides segment shape, not the file-group boundary.
- **Metadata size:** V2's `hashed_stats` table grows with vchannels × partitions and can exceed etcd's default 1.5 MiB request limit. V3 has no such table, so a 1024-partition table can import natively.
- **No post-import sort:** V3 output is already sorted, so the `Sorting` compaction is skipped.
- **Schema changes mid-import:** V2 can hang in `IndexBuilding` if the collection is altered during an import. V3 compares an import-relevant schema projection at planning, at each result acceptance, and before index building. If it differs, the job fails with `ErrImportSysFailed` (2101).
- **Reuse of the first read:** V2's preimport leaves no reusable output. V3's first read produces the fragments.

## Is it the default?

- **Config default:** `dataCoord.import.enableImportV3` defaults to `false`. This is set in `configs/milvus.yaml:1049` and `pkg/util/paramtable/component_param.go:8004`. The design doc's status line also says "default `false`".
- **Version selection:** In `internal/datacoord/services.go:2085-2092`, an unversioned request becomes V2. It becomes V3 only if the gate is on and the job is neither L0 nor a snapshot source.
- **Explicit versions:** A request that names V2 or V3 explicitly keeps that version.
- **Rollout constraints:**
  - The gate is one-way. Turning it off after activation is unsupported.
  - Enable it only once all DataNodes and all possibly-active DataCoords support V3.
  - The version is persisted in the WAL and the job, so a V3 job always finishes as V3.
  - Rolling back to a binary without V3 support is forbidden while any V3 job or task is still active.

L0 imports stay on V2 even with the gate on.

I read the design doc and the version-selection code, but not the DataNode or planner implementation. The doc's behavior claims are therefore its own, not confirmed against that code.

sent.prompt: Why is the proxy's MetaCache keyed by collection ID, with collection names and aliases kept only as hints? And how are cache fills kept from racing the invalidations that DDL broadcasts send, so that a describe started before a DDL can't put stale metadata back?

output.text:
The MetaCache is keyed by collection ID because IDs are the only stable identity. Fills are kept from racing invalidations by a single RWMutex, `fillMu`. I read `internal/proxy/metacache/meta_cache.go`, the streaming-system overview, `broadcaster.md` and `message-semantic-collection.md`. The code and docs didn't contradict each other on this. I didn't run tests or read the proxy-side code that receives the invalidation calls.

## Why ID is the key and names and aliases are hints

- **Names and aliases are mutable.** A collection can be renamed, moved to another database by `RenameCollection` (which keeps the ID), dropped and recreated under the same name, or have an alias repointed.
- **IDs are cluster-unique and never reused.** A same-name recreate gets a new ID, so it can't land on an old entry. The same goes for the partition cache, which is keyed by `fmt.Sprint(collectionID)` (`meta_cache.go:674`).
- **The primary store is `collections map[UniqueID]*CollectionInfo`** (`meta_cache.go:371`). An entry is live if and only if its ID is in that map.
- **`nameIdx` and `aliasInfo` are validated on every read.** `getCollection` (`:479`) follows alias → real name → ID → primary entry. It then checks that the entry's schema name and database still match. If they don't, the lookup is a miss and costs one extra describe. A stale hint can never produce a stale read.
- **Hints are written only together with their entry.** `update()` writes the name hint and only the aliases the entry itself declares (`:607`).
- **One routine evicts them.** `evictCollectionEntryLocked` (`:1393`) removes the entry, its alias hints, its name hint and its partition list together. No hint can be left without an owner, so there is no background GC.
- **The alias rule matters after a drop.** If an alias hint outlived its collection, it would validate again after a same-name recreate and bring back a deleted alias.

## How fills are kept from racing invalidations

`fillMu` (`:420`) replaced an earlier per-collection version floor.

- **Fills take the read side.** `updateWithSingleflight` (`:698`) and `GetPartitionInfos` (`:1051`) hold `fillMu.RLock` for the whole singleflight lifecycle. That covers the describe RPC, the write-back, delivery of the result, and singleflight removing the finished flight.
- **Invalidations take the write side.** `RemoveCollection`, `InvalidateCollectionMeta`, `RemoveCollectionsByID` and `RemoveDatabase` take `fillMu.Lock` before `m.mu`. They wait for every in-flight fill to finish.
- **So a fill is either before or after the DDL, never straddling it.** A describe started before the DDL has already written back and returned before the eviction runs, and the eviction deletes what it wrote. A fill that starts after the eviction reads post-DDL state, because rootcoord commits before it broadcasts.
- **The lock covers the singleflight cleanup, not only the callback.** If it were released inside the callback, an invalidation could finish while a new caller still joined the completed old flight. That caller would get the pre-DDL result straight from singleflight, bypassing the maps (comment at `:693`).
- **Partition fills check the primary entry before caching.** At `:1090` the write-back happens only if the collection's primary entry is still present, checked under `m.mu`. This covers an invalidation that lands between resolving the ID and taking the lock. It also covers `RemoveDatabase`'s walk, which runs after it releases `fillMu`.
- **`RemoveDatabase` is the one exception to a full drain.** It holds `fillMu` only for the drain and the O(1) detach, then releases it before the O(N) walk. A fill that races the walk gets evicted with its hints, so the cost is one refetch.

## Costs and limits

- **Invalidations wait for the slowest in-flight fill.** The fill RPC uses the caller's context with no extra MetaCache deadline, so callers must set one.
- **Fills issued while an invalidation is pending block behind it.** Cache hits never touch `fillMu`, and fills don't block each other.
- **It doesn't deadlock against the DDL.** The comment at `:416` says rootcoord's ack callbacks release the meta lock before the expiration fan-out. A fill's describe RPC is therefore never blocked by the DDL whose invalidation is waiting on that fill. I took this from the comment and didn't trace it in rootcoord.
- **The broadcaster guarantees the ordering.** In `broadcaster.md`, ack callbacks run only after all VChannels have acked. Callbacks for tasks with conflicting resource keys run in CChannel TimeTick order, and they retry until they succeed. That is what makes "rootcoord commits, then broadcasts" reliable.

If it is not, say exactly what it does differently from what it is meant to do, and where the intended behaviour is written down.

output.text:
No, `UpdateCostMetrics` has drifted from its design in one place: it decides when to seed the smoothed values differently.

**What the design says**

The design doc is `docs/design-docs/design_docs/20261019-look-aside-balancer-fix-design.md`, in the "C: EWMA smoothing of cost metrics" section. It says to re-seed the smoothed values with the raw sample when the previous sample has expired or never existed:

```go
if nowTs-metrics.ts.Load() > b.metricExpireInterval {
    // seed with the fresh sample
} else {
    // apply the EWMA
}
```

Its comment says: "0 cannot mark 'unseeded' because it is ServiceTime's normal value."

**What the code does**

`internal/proxy/shardclient/refined_look_aside_balancer.go:258` seeds when the smoothed service time equals 0:

```go
if math.Float64frombits(metrics.serviceTimeSmooth.Load()) == 0 {
```

This is the sentinel the design rejects. It differs in two ways:

1. **Sub-millisecond workloads lose the response-time smoothing.**
   - When the node reports `ServiceTime` of 0, `serviceTimeSmooth` stays at 0.
   - Every update then takes the seed branch, and `responseTimeSmooth` is overwritten with the raw `ResponseTime` sample.
   - So on the exact workload fix C targets, response time is never smoothed.
   - The service time hits the same trap only until a non-zero sample arrives. After that it is smoothed normally.

2. **Stale smoothed values are never re-seeded.**
   - The code never checks `metricExpireInterval` here.
   - After a node has been idle past the expiry window, a new sample is blended into the old smoothed value instead of replacing it.
   - The design wants the fresh sample to replace it.

**What I didn't check**

I didn't run the tests. I also didn't check whether the tests in `refined_look_aside_balancer_test.go` cover either case.

The fix is to replace the condition on line 258 with `nowTs-metrics.ts.Load() > b.metricExpireInterval`. `nowTs` is already computed on line 255, just before the check. A new entry has `ts == 0`, so it still gets seeded on the first sample.

I haven't made the change. Do you want me to apply it and add tests for the two cases above?

## What changes

The design doc is `docs/design-docs/design_docs/20260921-import-v3-reshard-design.md`.

**Import V2**
- Every source file is read twice. `PreImportTask` parses the whole file and keeps only statistics. `ImportTaskV2` then reads it again, hashes rows per file-group, and writes straight into pre-allocated segments.
- Each file-group task splits the same `(vchannel, partition)` bucket on its own. That produces many small segments.

**Import V3**
- The source is parsed once. A `ReshardTask` reads each file, normalizes it, routes rows to their bucket, sorts them, and writes immutable sorted fragments.
- A planning stage then packs fragments into per-segment plans. Each plan stays within one bucket and can span source tasks.
- Each `ImportTaskV3` does a k-way merge over one plan and writes exactly one formal segment, using the existing Storage V2/V3 writers.
- Preimport becomes count-only. It gives exact per-file row counts, so ordinary imports can get deterministic PK/RowID ranges. Backup imports run a size-only variant.
- The pipeline decides segment shape, not the file-group boundary.
- The job moves through new states: `Resharding`, `Planning`, and `AssigningIDRange` for ordinary imports.

## Why it was needed

- **No reusable first read:** V2's preimport output can't be reused.
- **Cross-file planning:** Bucket ownership has to exist before task boundaries. Otherwise segments can't be planned across files.
- **etcd limit:** `hashed_stats` can exceed etcd's default 1.5 MiB request size. V3 removes it, so tables with 1024 partitions import natively.
- **No post-import sort:** The output is already sorted, so the post-import `Sorting` compaction is skipped.
- **Schema change mid-import:** V2 can hang in `IndexBuilding` if the collection is altered during an import. V3 compares an import-relevant schema projection and fails explicitly.

- **Version choice:** DataCoord resolves the version before broadcast. It picks V2 unless the gate is on and the job is not L0. L0 import always stays on V2.
- **One-way gate:** Turn it on only after every DataNode and every DataCoord that could become active supports V3. The gate only affects new requests. Persisted jobs resume with the version they were stored with. Turning it off again after activation is unsupported.

**Why the response is tagged instead of the request filtered**

The reasoning is in the comment on `ShardLeadersList.resource_groups` (`pkg/proto/query_coord.proto:369-400`). The tag is filled in `internal/querycoordv2/utils/util.go:216`. It is `replica.GetResourceGroup()`, appended in the same branch as the node ID, address and serviceable flag, so all four arrays stay index-aligned.

- **Tag on the response, not a field in the request:** the proto comment gives two reasons.
  - A request filter breaks against an old coordinator. It would ignore the unknown field and return unfiltered leaders in a response shape the caller can't tell from a filtered one.
  - A tag degrades safely. An old coordinator leaves `resource_groups` empty while still filling the other three arrays, and the caller reads empty as "unknown". The proxy also neutralizes the tags if the arrays ever arrive misaligned.
- **Why the proxy can't derive it from node membership:** the tag is the replica's resource group, not the node's.
  - A replica can borrow nodes from another group. Querycoord models this as `num_outgoing_node` and `num_incoming_node`, so a node being in group X does not mean the replica it serves belongs to X.
  - These two diverge during rebalance windows, which is when a caller asking this question most needs the right answer.

  - Replicas that aren't query-visible yet are filtered out in `GetShardLeaders` (`services.go:841`). A group that is still coming up therefore doesn't appear at all.

- **Unknown group:** an unknown group name is rejected up front with `ErrResourceGroupNotFound` (`services.go:76`). This stops a client polling a misspelled group from waiting on -1 forever.
- **Loaded collection, group set:** `utils.LoadPercentageByResourceGroup` (`services.go:154`) computes the figure. The implementation is in `utils/resource_group_load_percentage.go`.

  - It takes the minimum across those replicas.
  - It reads the targets once, with `NextTargetFirst`. This avoids a 100/0 flap when a promotion briefly clears the next target.

sent.prompt: Why is the proxy's MetaCache keyed by collection ID, with collection names and aliases kept only as hints? And how are cache fills kept from racing the invalidations that DDL broadcasts send, so that a describe started before a DDL can't put stale metadata back?

output.text:
I've read the MetaCache, the proxy's invalidation handler, the rootcoord expiry path and the broadcaster doc. That's enough to answer.

## Why the cache is keyed by collection ID

`MetaCache.collections` is the only store, and an entry is live exactly when its ID is present (`internal/proxy/metacache/meta_cache.go:365`). IDs are cluster-unique and never reused. That gives three properties:

- **Drop and recreate can't alias.** A recreated collection has a new ID, so it can't pick up the old collection's schema or partition list. The partition cache is also keyed by ID (`buildPartitionCacheKey`, line 678).
- **Rename is safe.** A rename keeps the ID and changes the name. The old name hint still points at the live ID, but `getCollection` checks that the entry still carries that name and database (lines 498-504), so it misses.
- **One entry per collection, however it's addressed.** A collection looked up by name, by alias or by ID resolves to the same entry. Invalidating that one entry covers every way of addressing it.

`nameIdx` (db → name → id) and `aliasInfo` (db → alias → real name) are only hints. Every read goes alias → real name → ID → primary entry, then re-checks that the entry's name and database match. A stale hint costs one extra describe and never a stale read.

Hints are written only together with their entry, in `update()` (lines 588-612). Aliases come only from the entry's own declared `Aliases`. Because of that, `evictCollectionEntryLocked` (line 1393) can find and delete every hint an entry owns, along with its partition list. Nothing can dangle, so there's no background GC.

Cleaning up the alias hints matters for correctness. A leftover alias hint would validate again after a same-name recreate and bring back a dropped alias.

## How fills are kept from racing invalidations

The mechanism is `fillMu`, an `RWMutex` that replaced an older per-collection version floor (comment at line 399).

- **Fills take the read side for their whole lifecycle.** That covers the describe RPC, the write-back, delivering the result and removing the finished singleflight entry (`updateWithSingleflight`, lines 698-699). `GetPartitionInfos` and `GetDatabaseInfo` do the same. Fills don't block each other, and cache hits never touch this lock.
- **Invalidations take the write side before they evict.** `InvalidateCollectionMeta`, `RemoveCollection`, `RemovePartition`, `RemoveAlias`, `RemoveDatabase` and `RemoveDatabaseInfo` all do this. The write lock waits for every in-flight fill to finish, so a describe that began before the DDL has written back and delivered its result before the eviction runs. The eviction then deletes that write-back.
- **Fills that start after the eviction see post-DDL state.** This relies on rootcoord committing the change before it broadcasts the invalidation. I confirmed this for DropCollection. Its ack callback persists `meta.DropCollection` and only then calls `ExpireCaches` (`ddl_callbacks_drop_collection.go:131` and `:168`). I did not check the other DDL callbacks one by one.
- **The read lock is held past the singleflight callback.** The comment at line 693 explains why. A completed flight stays in the singleflight map until its own cleanup. If the lock were released earlier, an invalidation could finish while a new caller still joined the old flight and received pre-DDL data directly, bypassing the cache.
- **Partition fills only write back if the primary entry is still live** (lines 1090-1094). The check and the write share `m.mu`. Without it, a partition list could end up with no owning entry, and a later eviction would never remove it. `stalePartitionCacheLocked` also calls `Forget` on the singleflight key so later fills start fresh.
- **`RemoveDatabase` holds the write lock only briefly.** It detaches the database's hint bucket and drops it, then releases `fillMu` before walking the primary entries in batches. A fill that races the walk may get over-evicted, which costs one refetch and leaves no dangling hint.

Costs the code accepts:

- An invalidation waits for the slowest in-flight fill, so callers must set sensible deadlines on their contexts.
- Fills issued while an invalidation is pending briefly block behind it.

**Deadlock risk.** The comment at line 416 says rootcoord ack callbacks release the meta lock before fanning out expirations. That means a fill's describe RPC is never blocked by the DDL whose invalidation is waiting on that fill. I only read this in the comment and did not trace the rootcoord side to confirm it.

**The guard** is in `internal/core/src/storage/minio/GuardedS3EndpointProvider.h`:

sent.prompt: snapshotPinCleanupTimeout in internal/datacoord/snapshot_manager.go is 20 seconds. Someone points out that releasing pins normally finishes in well under a second and wants 5 seconds again so a stuck etcd fails quickly. Is that safe? Recommend, and explain what decides the value.

output.text:
**Recommendation: keep 20s. Reverting to 5s isn't safe.**

**What decides the value:** the slowest legitimate release you need to complete, not the typical one. The "well under a second" figure holds for a single-AZ or low-latency etcd. The commit that raised the timeout (0add447) records a case where it doesn't hold. On a deployment with etcd spread over three availability zones about 40 ms apart, releasing the pins of a large snapshot took 6–9 seconds. That time is mostly sequential etcd round trips, so it grows with latency and with the number of pins. A 5s deadline cancelled the release partway. The pins then stayed until the next restart and held segments that GC should have freed.

**Why the trade-off favors the longer value:**
- A timeout that is too short fails silently and leaks. A partial release leaves pins that block GC, and nothing retries them until a restart.
- A timeout that is too long only delays an already-failing cleanup by up to 15s. This is a background cleanup path, so nobody waits on it interactively.
- "Fail quickly on stuck etcd" has little value here. A stuck etcd also fails the other etcd calls, and the callers only log a warning and move on.

**Caveats:**
- **Shared constant:** `snapshotPinCleanupTimeout` is also used in `snapshot_export_manager.go`. That includes the unpin after a failed `CreateJob` (line 192), the failed-job update (722), terminal job cleanup (767, 784, 797) and job drop (818). All of these get the longer bound. They are the same kind of etcd-bound cleanup, so I think that's fine, but it is a side effect.
- **Unverified:** the commit says no tests were run and the fix wasn't tried on the Ostrava deployment. 20s is about 2x the worst observed 9s, which is a judgment call, not a measured limit.
- **Possible improvements:**
  - If the fast-fail concern is real, make the value configurable through paramtable instead of a constant. Single-AZ deployments could then pick a lower one.
  - Alternatively, make release resumable or batched so it doesn't depend on one deadline.
  - If larger snapshots or higher latency push release time toward 20s, the constant will need to grow, or the release will need to be made incremental.

Why was it done that way, and why can't the proxy just work out each leader's group from which nodes are in which resource group? While you're at it, how is one resource group's load progress reported?

output.text:
I read the proto comments and the code that builds and consumes the tag. This all comes from the comments and code. I didn't run any tests.

## Why GetShardLeaders tags each leader and doesn't take a resource group in the request

`ShardLeadersList` now carries `resource_groups`. It is parallel to `node_ids`, `node_addrs` and `serviceable` (`pkg/proto/query_coord.proto:369-400`). Querycoord fills it in `internal/querycoordv2/utils/util.go:216` with `replica.GetResourceGroup()`. The proto comment gives these reasons:

- **Mixed-version safety.** An old coordinator ignores a filter in the request and answers unfiltered, in a response shape the caller can't tell apart from a filtered one. With a response tag, an old coordinator leaves the field empty. The proxy reads an empty list as "unknown group", not as "no group".
- **One cached answer.** The proxy caches one leader list per collection. A response tag lets that single list serve every resource group, and the proxy filters it locally (`FilterByResourceGroup`). A request filter would need a call and a cache entry per group.
- **Rolling upgrades.** The proxy handles a missing or mismatched tag array without panicking (`internal/proxy/shardclient/manager.go:242-273`). An empty array gives "unknown group". A non-empty array of the wrong length is thrown away entirely, because a misaligned tag could route traffic into the wrong group. An unknown entry never matches a named group.

## Why the proxy can't derive each leader's group from node membership

- **The tag is the replica's group, not the node's.** A replica can borrow nodes from another resource group. Querycoord models this as `num_outgoing_node` and `num_incoming_node`. Node-set membership therefore isn't replica membership. The two disagree during rebalances, which is when a caller most needs the answer.
- **The mapping is gone by the time the proxy sees the response.** The response flattens every replica into one list per channel. Only querycoord still has the replica in hand when it builds the list (`util.go:196-199`). The proxy can't recover the mapping afterwards, so it has to be on the wire.

The tag also does not say whether a group can serve. Replicas that aren't query-visible yet are dropped before the list is built. A group that is still coming up therefore doesn't appear at all, and absence doesn't mean the group holds no replica. For that question there is a separate call, `GetShardLeaderReadinessByResourceGroup` (`internal/querycoordv2/shard_leader_readiness.go`). It distinguishes "shards without a leader" from "no replica in this group".

## How one resource group's load progress is reported

- **Client entry point.** `ShowCollectionsRequest` has a `resource_group` field. `ShowLoadCollections` (`internal/querycoordv2/services.go:60`) calls `utils.LoadPercentageByResourceGroup` when it is set. The result goes into `inMemory_percentages`.
- **Availability flag.** `query_service_available` follows the same scope, through `checkAnyReplicaAvailableInResourceGroup`.
- **Unknown group.** The request is refused with `ErrResourceGroupNotFound` (300), before any collection is looked at.
- **What the number is.** It is the fraction of the current work set that the group's replicas carry right now. The work set is the channel targets plus sealed-segment targets, measured against `NextTargetFirst`. The per-replica walk is in `internal/querycoordv2/utils/resource_group_load_percentage.go:436`. If a group has several replicas, the figure is the minimum across them, so the group counts as ready only when its slowest replica is.

| Value | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `-1` | The group has no replica of the collection. A collection that isn't loaded at all also gives `-1` for a scoped request, instead of `CollectionNotLoaded`. |
| `0` | A replica exists but has picked up none of the targets. This also happens briefly after an ungraceful restart, before the targets are rebuilt. |
| `1`–`99` | Partial progress. Any progress rounds up to at least 1. |
| `100` | Every current target is carried. |

- **Errors.** `ErrServiceNotReady` (retriable) means the coordinator isn't wired up yet. `ErrCollectionNotLoaded` (non-retriable) means the load failed. The failed-load error is normalized so a retriable cause isn't retried for 24 hours.
- **A figure of 100 is not a "can serve" verdict.** The percentage counts query-invisible replicas, but readiness and routing don't. A group can read 100 while readiness says `Ready=false`. The 100 can also drop back below 100 when a flush or compaction output lands in the next target. The code says not to gate a switchover on `== 100` in addition to `Ready`. Use the percentage for progress and `GetShardLeaderReadinessByResourceGroup` for "may I route to it".

## Why `GetShardLeaders` tags leaders instead of taking a resource group

The tag lives in `ShardLeadersList.resource_groups` (`pkg/proto/query_coord.proto:369-399`). It is parallel to `node_ids`, `node_addrs` and `serviceable`. It is filled in `GetShardLeadersWithChannelsAndReplicaFilter` (`internal/querycoordv2/utils/util.go:216`) with `replica.GetResourceGroup()`.

The proto comment gives these reasons:

- **The coordinator is the only place that knows which replica a leader belongs to.** The response flattens every replica into a single list per channel. Once the response is built, the leader-to-replica mapping is gone. The tag has to be attached while the replica is still in hand, in the loop at `util.go:201`.
- **Old coordinators fail visibly.** An old coordinator ignores an unknown request field and returns an unfiltered answer that looks like a filtered one. With a response tag, an old coordinator leaves the list empty. The caller treats an empty list as "unknown", not "no resource group". Proto3 gives no other way to tell the two apart.
- **One response serves every group.** The proxy can cache a single shard-leader table and read out whichever group it needs. That matches the `TestGetShardLeadersReadsWholeTableOnce` test in `internal/proxy/shardclient/manager_test.go`. I inferred this from the test name and did not read the proxy code.

## Why the proxy can't infer a leader's group from node membership

The tag is the replica's resource group, not the node's. A replica can borrow nodes from another resource group. Querycoord models this as `num_outgoing_node` and `num_incoming_node`. So a node sitting in group A's node set can be leading a replica that belongs to group B.

The two views also diverge most during rebalance. That is when a caller asking this question needs the right answer. The proxy would have to rebuild the replica-to-node mapping itself, and only querycoord holds that mapping.

The tag has limits:

- **It does not say whether a group can serve.** Replicas that aren't query-visible yet are filtered out before the list is built (`services.go:841`). A group that is still coming up simply doesn't appear. Absence therefore doesn't mean the group has no replica.
- **Readiness has to come from a separate call.** `GetShardLeaderReadinessByResourceGroup` (`internal/querycoordv2/shard_leader_readiness.go:38`) tells the cases apart. `ShardLeadersReasonShardsWithoutLeader` means the group holds a replica and is still loading. `ShardLeadersReasonNoReplicaInResourceGroup` means it holds nothing. `shard_leader_rg_tag_test.go` pins this.
- **The arrays stay aligned.** Every append happens inside the same `info != nil` branch (`util.go:212-217`). The proxy also neutralizes the tags if a response ever arrives misaligned.

## How one resource group's load progress is reported

`ShowCollectionsRequest` has an optional `resource_group` field (`query_coord.proto:225`). The handler is `ShowLoadCollections` in `services.go:60`.

- **Unknown group:** the call returns `ResourceGroupNotFound` before looking at any collection (`services.go:76`).
- **Scoped percentage:** `inMemory_percentages` comes from `utils.LoadPercentageByResourceGroup` (`services.go:154`, implementation in `internal/querycoordv2/utils/resource_group_load_percentage.go`). For each replica in that group, `replicaLoadPercentage` computes the fraction of target channels and sealed segments carried by the replica's own nodes. I read the comment at `services.go:151` and the per-replica code. I did not read the aggregation across replicas, so I can't confirm it takes the minimum, though the comments near `resource_group_load_percentage.go:360` describe the result as a min.
- **Query-invisible replicas are counted.** These are the ones the load-config path is waiting on. As a result, 100% here doesn't by itself mean the group can serve. Readiness is the real gate.
- **Target snapshot:** it reads `NextTargetFirst`, so a promotion doesn't make the figure flap between 100 and 0.
- **No replica in the group:** the value is `-1`. This also applies to a collection that isn't loaded at all, unless a load failure is recorded, in which case the call returns `CollectionNotLoaded`. In the unloaded case the other fields come back as `query_service_available=false`, `refresh_progress=0` and empty `load_fields`.
- **`query_service_available`** follows the same scope. It comes from `checkAnyReplicaAvailableInResourceGroup`, so another group serving doesn't make this one look healthy.
- **Without `resource_group`:** you get the collection-wide figure, as before.

sent.prompt: What does Import V3 change about how bulk import works compared with Import V2, and why was it needed? Is it what runs by default now?

output.text:
**No. Import V2 is still the default.** V3 is opt-in behind `dataCoord.import.enableImportV3`, which defaults to `false` (`pkg/util/paramtable/component_param.go:8004`, `configs/milvus.yaml:1049`).

I read the design doc (`docs/design-docs/design_docs/20260921-import-v3-reshard-design.md`) and the version-selection code. I did not read the V3 pipeline code itself, so what follows about its behavior comes from the doc.

## What changes

**V2:**
- Every source file is read twice. `PreImportTask` parses the whole file and keeps only statistics. `ImportTaskV2` then re-reads it, hashes rows per file-group, and writes straight into pre-allocated segments.
- Every file-group task splits the same `(vchannel, partition)` bucket. That produces many small segments.
- A `hashed_stats` table grows with vchannels × partitions.
- A sort compaction (`Sorting`) runs after the import.

**V3 (sort-based re-shard):**
1. **Count-only preimport.** It gets exact per-file row counts and sizes without hashing. Parquet and NumPy counts come from file metadata. JSON and CSV are scanned. Backup imports only size their object list.
2. **Reshard, the only real read.** Each source is parsed once. Rows are normalized, routed to a `(vchannel, partition)` bucket, sorted, and written as immutable Parquet fragments plus a manifest. Memory is bounded by a slot budget, and overflow spills to local Arrow IPC files.
3. **Planning.** Fragments are packed per bucket into one plan per segment, across all source tasks.
4. **Import.** Each `ImportTaskV3` does a k-way merge over one plan and writes exactly one sorted segment through the existing Storage V2/V3 writers. Segment shape is decided by the pipeline, not by file-group boundaries.

The job state machine also changes. V3 adds `Resharding` and `Planning` states and drops `Sorting`, because its output is already sorted. Progress weights differ accordingly.

## Why it was needed

- Bucket ownership has to be settled before task boundaries for cross-file segment planning to work. V2 routes rows inside per-file tasks, so it can't do that.
- `hashed_stats` can exceed etcd's default 1.5 MiB request limit. V3 has no such table, so tables with 1024 partitions can import natively.
- V2 reads each file twice, and its first read leaves nothing reusable.
- V2 can hang in `IndexBuilding` if the collection schema is altered mid-import. V3 compares an import-relevant schema projection at several points and fails with `ErrImportSysFailed` instead.
- Output is fewer, larger, already-sorted segments, with no post-import sort compaction.

## When V3 actually runs

The gate is in `internal/datacoord/services.go:2085-2092`. A request with no explicit version resolves to V2. It becomes V3 only if `enableImportV3` is true and the import is not L0 and not a snapshot source. The resolved version is written into the WAL message and the job.

The doc calls the gate one-way:
- Turn it on only after all DataNodes and all DataCoords that could become active support V3.
- A V3 job always finishes as V3.
- Turning the flag off again, or rolling back to a binary that doesn't know V3, is unsupported while V3 jobs or temporary prefixes exist.

The code also excludes snapshot-source imports from V3. The design doc only mentions L0.

sent.prompt: Where does the StreamingNode split an oversized WAL record into chunks before appending it, and where are the chunks put back together when the WAL is read? Name the files and the functions or types involved, with paths relative to the repository root, and the configuration switch that turns the splitting on.

output.text:
**Splitting (append side)**

- `internal/streamingnode/server/wal/adaptor/wal_adaptor.go`
  - `walAdaptorImpl.appendWithOptionalChunking` (line 298) is called from the append path at line 230. It returns the message unsplit when the switch is off. It also leaves the message whole when the payload is no larger than the per-record budget, or when the budget is 0.
  - Otherwise it calls `message.SplitIntoChunks(msg, chunkPayloadSize)`. It then appends each chunk with `appendOneWithRetry`.
  - `walAdaptorImpl.chunkPayloadSize` and `computeChunkPayloadSize` (lines 349 and 361) work out the per-record payload budget. It comes from the active backend's enforced limit, or from Woodpecker's configured chunk threshold. The value is cached and refreshed at most once per second (`chunkPayloadSizeRefresh`). A backend with no limit gets 0, which disables chunking.
- `pkg/streaming/util/message/chunk.go` holds the split logic: `SplitIntoChunks` (line 27). The helpers `IsChunkedPayload`, `ChunkIndex` and `ChunkTotal` read the chunk metadata.

**Reassembly (read side)**

- `internal/streamingnode/server/wal/adaptor/scanner_switchable.go`
  - The scanner holds a `chunkAssembler message.ChunkAssembler` field (line 119).
  - It calls `s.chunkAssembler.Push(msg)` (line 159) so that later stages see one complete message. On a time-tick message it calls `AdvanceTimeTick` (line 197) to discard incomplete runs. It treats `message.ErrCorruptedChunk` as a special error (line 134).
- `pkg/streaming/util/message/chunk.go` holds the reassembly logic:
  - `ChunkAssembler` is the type, and `Push` (line 145) is its main method.
  - `AssembleChunks` (line 86) merges the chunks into one message.
  - `parseChunkMetadata`, `discardRunsAtOrBefore`, `AdvanceTimeTick` and `sameChunkBytes` are internal helpers.

**Configuration switch**

The switch is `streaming.splitChunkSN`. It is defined in `pkg/util/paramtable/component_param.go` (line 9435) as `StreamingCfg.SplitChunkSN`. It defaults to `false` and is documented in `configs/milvus.yaml` (line 1748). It can be changed while the node is running.

`proxy.splitChunk` (`ProxyCfg.SplitChunkProxy`, default `true`) is a different mechanism. It splits at the proxy, for example in `internal/proxy/dml/task_delete.go`. The docs say to enable `streaming.splitChunkSN` on every StreamingNode first, then disable `proxy.splitChunk`.

I read `streaming-system.md` and searched the code. I did not open the `wal/` or `message/` sub-docs that CLAUDE.md asks for. I also did not read the bodies of these functions in full, or cross-check the docs against them. The locations and behavior above come from grep output and the code comments around the matches.

sent.prompt: snapshotPinCleanupTimeout in internal/datacoord/snapshot_manager.go is 20 seconds. Someone points out that releasing pins normally finishes in well under a second and wants 5 seconds again so a stuck etcd fails quickly. Is that safe? Recommend, and explain what decides the value.

output.text:
**Recommendation: keep 20 seconds. Reverting to 5 seconds isn't safe.**

**What decides the value.** The timeout has to exceed the worst-case time to release pins on the slowest etcd deployment you support. It shouldn't be set from the typical case. The comment on the constant (`snapshot_manager.go:88-98`) and commit `b5e4b18` record why:
- On the Ostrava deployment, etcd spans three availability zones about 40 ms apart.
- Releasing the pins of a large snapshot takes 6 to 9 seconds there.
- With the 5 second timeout, the cleanup was cancelled midway.
- The pins then stayed until the next restart and held segments that garbage collection should have freed.

"Well under a second" is probably true on a local or single-AZ etcd. It doesn't hold on the high-latency one, and that's the deployment the value was raised for. A 5 second timeout would bring the leak back there.

**Why "fail fast" doesn't help here.** A tight timeout makes sense when a fast failure leads to a retry or a visible error. This cleanup runs on a context built with `context.WithoutCancel`, and some paths use `m.ctx` (`snapshot_export_manager.go:192`, `:635`, `:722`, `:767`, `:784`, `:797`, `:818`). When it times out, it only logs a warning. Cancelling it midway leaves a partial release. It doesn't free the caller to do anything useful sooner. A stuck etcd would still be noticed at 20 seconds, and the warning logs would still show it.

**Side effect to be aware of.** The constant is shared by every cleanup call site listed above, including the export manager's. So the 20 seconds applies to all of them, not only the pin release. The commit says this too. Those are background cleanups, so the longer limit costs little.

**If the goal is still to detect a stuck etcd sooner**, leave the timeout alone and do one of these:
- Alert on the "failed to release … pin" warnings or on the `setSnapshotActivePinsGauge` gauge not dropping.
- Log or measure the cleanup duration, so you can pick the value from real latency data.
- Split the constant into per-path values, if one path really needs to be tighter.

I didn't change any code, and I haven't verified the 6–9 second figure myself. It comes from the commit message and the comment. The commit also says "Not tested". If you want a lower value, first measure release time on a high-latency etcd with a large snapshot.
