Why does the precompiled managed code go into a section of its own rather than the usual text section? The R2R format is full of RVAs: how are they expressed in a Mach-O object, and why is that the right thing to measure them from? Why does the runtime ask the host for the composite image instead of opening the dylib itself? And what is `--rtr-header-symbol-name` for?

output.text:
Your questions are answered by the design doc, `docs/design/coreclr/botr/readytorun-platform-native-envelope.md`. I read that and the crossgen2 option plumbing. I did not read the Mach-O object writer, so I haven't checked that it matches what the doc describes.

**Why managed code gets its own section (`__TEXT,__managedcode`)**
The doc gives two reasons: the Apple linker treats `__TEXT,__text` specially, and `__managedcode` matches what NativeAOT already does. The doc doesn't say what the special treatment is. The point is that R2R code isn't ordinary native code the linker should optimize or rearrange. Section placement for the rest:
- Read-only data goes to `__TEXT,__const`. That covers jump tables, CLR metadata, Win32 resources, unwind and GC info, and the R2R headers.
- Fixup tables stay in `__DATA,__data`.
- Import thunks stay in `__TEXT,__text`, as in the PE layout.

**How RVAs are expressed**
R2R, like PE, stores offsets from an image base. COFF has a native "RVA from image base" relocation, but Mach-O doesn't. The doc's answer is:
- The base symbol is `__mh_dylib_header`, which the Apple linker provides.
- Each RVA is emitted as a Mach-O subtractor relocation meaning "symbol address − `__mh_dylib_header` address".

This base is the right one for three reasons:
- It sits at the Mach header, which is the address `dlinfo` and `dladdr` return as the image base. The runtime can therefore add an RVA to the base it already has.
- The Mach header describes the image's extent, so the runtime can use it to bound reads of R2R data.
- The linker resolves the subtraction at link time, so the values stay correct wherever the dylib is loaded.

A related choice is that symbol ranges are a start symbol plus "end − start + end size" using a subtractor. The reason is that Apple linkers have trouble when several symbols are defined at the same address.

**Why the runtime asks the host instead of opening the dylib**
The runtime now calls a new `get_native_code_data` callback on `host_runtime_contract`. The doc's stated rationale is that the host does the actual load. It might call `dlopen`, or use something statically linked into the host. The host also owns any caching. The runtime passes the component assembly path and the owner composite name, and gets back the R2R header pointer, image size and image base. If the callback fails, the runtime falls back to IL and the JIT. The doc doesn't spell out further reasons. The design does let hosts that statically link the image work without a file to open, and it keeps the loading policy out of the runtime.

sent.prompt: We're moving an interface from [ComImport] to [GeneratedComInterface] and want to declare C# properties on it rather than hand-written get_X/set_X methods. In what order do the generated slots for a property with both accessors come, and why that order? Why does the generator not distinguish propput from propputref, and why can't I declare an init accessor? Why does it reject so many property shapes outright instead of doing something reasonable with them? And if I want a property that wraps two methods that are not next to each other in the interface, how do I do that?

output.text:
These answers come from the design docs in `docs/design/libraries/ComInterfaceGenerator/`, mainly `Properties.md` and `DefaultImplementedMembers.md`. I haven't read the generator source or tested any of this.

**Slot order.** A `{ get; set; }` property gets two consecutive slots, getter first and setter second. They sit right after the slots of whatever members precede the property in source order. The getter is `HRESULT get_Foo(out T value)` and the setter is `HRESULT set_Foo(T value)`. The doc gives one reason for the order: it matches the layout the built-in CLR produces for a `[ComVisible(true)]` managed interface with the same property. That keeps source-generated and `[ComImport]` interfaces wire-compatible, which matters for your migration. Get-only and set-only properties each get a single slot. Indexers follow the same rule, with the index parameters placed before the value parameter.

**No propput/propputref distinction.** The doc lists this as a non-goal. `propputref` exists in TLB metadata and in `IDispatch::Invoke`, but not in a plain `IUnknown` vtable. Every setter maps to one slot. The doc also says dispid and `IDispatch` integration are out of scope.

**No `init` accessor.** `init` versus `set` is a distinction at the C# call site only, and the vtable can't represent it. The generator rejects `init` with `SYSLIB1091`, even if the accessor has a body. If the accessor should be in the vtable, use `set`. Otherwise, the doc suggests a default-implemented `init`-style helper through a separate managed-only abstraction.

**Why so many shapes are rejected.** The doc says the supported surface is "intentionally narrow". Anything outside it gets `SYSLIB1091` so that supported semantics can be widened later without breaking existing users. Accepting a shape now and changing its meaning later would be a breaking change. Several of the rejections have more specific reasons:
- **Mixed bodied and bodiless accessors:** these are rejected because all accessors must agree (`PropertyAccessorsMustBeAllOrNothing`). The C# compiler also rejects some of them first, with CS0525.
- **`[MarshalAs]` on a property:** C# rejects it itself with CS0592, because the attribute can't target properties. Put it on the accessor return or parameter instead. `[MarshalUsing]` is allowed on a property and applies to both accessors.
- **`extern`, `required`, `sealed`, `virtual` and `abstract`:** these modifiers aren't supported on properties. `abstract` is the interface default anyway.
- **Accessor-level accessibility** such as `{ get; private set; }`: C# rejects it with CS0442 on abstract accessors.

**A property over two non-adjacent methods.** Use a default-implemented member (DIM). Declare the two real COM methods as ordinary methods, then add a property with bodies on both accessors. Accessors with bodies get no vtable slot.

```csharp
[GeneratedComInterface, Guid("…")]
public partial interface IFoo
{
    double ReadValue();            // ABI slot
    // …other methods in between…
    void WriteValue(double value); // ABI slot
    double Value { get => ReadValue(); set => WriteValue(value); }  // no slot
}
```

- **Naming:** don't name the methods `get_Value` and `set_Value`. C# reserves those names once a property `Value` exists, so it fails with CS0082. Pick other names, as above.
- **All-or-nothing:** both accessors need bodies.
- **Marshalling attributes:** putting `[MarshalUsing]` or `[MarshalAs]` on the DIM only produces a warning. Put them on the real methods instead.
- **Inheritance:** a derived interface can't declare a DIM property that shadows an inherited `get_X`/`set_X` method pair, for the same naming reason.

sent.prompt: I'm about to start working on the cDAC (the data contract reader). Explain to a newcomer, as briefly as you can: what the data contracts are and what problems they solve compared with the classic DAC and DBI; what the runtime publishes so a reader can find them; how contracts are versioned, when a change needs a new version and when an existing one may be amended, and what is fixed for a release; what the reader version is and how it differs from a contract version; and where each part is written down.

output.text:
# cDAC in brief

## What data contracts are, and what they fix
A data contract is the runtime's promise to outside tools. It says that if you read process memory (live or from a dump) and interpret it the documented way, you get a specific piece of runtime state. A contract has two parts:
- **Physical layout:** type sizes, field offsets and global values.
- **Algorithm:** how to turn that data into an answer. The docs usually write this as C#-like pseudocode.

The classic debugger design needs a DAC and a DBI that exactly match the runtime build. Contracts remove that requirement. The cDAC is a reader that works from the descriptor instead. The design doc lists four problems this addresses:
- **Security:** the matching DAC/DBI may be untrusted, for example for a custom or third-party runtime build.
- **Servicing:** a debugger-only fix currently needs a new runtime build.
- **Acquisition:** it can be hard to find the DAC/DBI for an exact runtime version.
- **Cross-architecture:** the host/target binaries may not exist.

## What the runtime publishes
- The runtime exports a symbol named `DotNetRuntimeContractDescriptor`. Its `magic` value ("DNCCDAC\0") also tells you the endianness.
- The descriptor holds flags (pointer size), a JSON string, and a table of pointer slots that the JSON refers to.
- The JSON has these parts:
  - **`types`:** field offsets and sizes.
  - **`globals`:** integers, pointers or strings.
  - **`sub-descriptors`:** pointers to descriptors owned by external components.
  - **`contracts`:** a map of contract name to version string, such as `{"Thread":"c1"}`. A runtime may not list two versions of the same contract.
- If several runtimes are loaded in one process, look for the symbol in each module.

## Contract versioning
- Version identifiers are just distinct labels. A "higher" one isn't necessarily newer. Each must be unique and documented in `main`.
- **A new version is needed** when the runtime changes data structures or algorithms in a way that is incompatible with the previous version.
- **An existing version may be amended** only for compatible changes, in two cases:
  - fixing a documentation bug, or
  - adding optional globals, types, fields or algorithms. For example, a new API that returns a default or an error on older runtimes, or an existing API that returns richer information.
  
  A tool that implements the original definition must still understand a runtime that advertises the amended one. The docs say there is "subjective leeway" in judging this.
- **What is fixed for a release:** for a given major release, the set of supported contract versions stays fixed from the first release candidate through the last servicing build. Before RC you can change it, but carefully, because it breaks tools. The design doc suggests feature branches or opt-in switches.
- Contracts refer to each other by name without a version.
- Fields missing on a given runtime produce an error when read.

## Reader version vs. contract version
- **Contract version:** a per-contract label. It says how the runtime lays out and interprets one subsystem.
- **Reader version:** a single advisory number for the reader as a whole. The runtime publishes the `RecommendedReaderVersion` global. The reader reports what it understands through `IRuntimeInfo.GetCurrentReaderVersion()`. If the runtime's value is greater, the tool can suggest updating. An older reader isn't blocked from inspecting the runtime.
- Version 2 is an example. It added an optional interpreter JIT manager global. Readers on version 1 ignore it, and version 2 readers tolerate it being absent.
- Version 3 is another. It added `StackWalk` `c2`, so an older reader can't silently use a stale algorithm.

## Where it's written down
All of this is under `docs/design/datacontracts/`:
- `datacontracts_design.md`: the motivation, versioning rules, and the format for contract docs.
- `contract-descriptor.md`: the physical descriptor, the symbol, and the `contracts` JSON.
- `data_descriptor.md`: the types and globals JSON.
- `<ContractName>.md`: one file per contract, such as `Thread.md` or `StackWalk.md`. Every version of a contract lives in its own file.
- `reader-version-history.md`: what each reader version added.
- `contract_csharp_api_design.cs`: the `Target` API used by the pseudocode.

I haven't read `data_descriptor.md` yet, so check it for the field details.

**Recommendation: don't revert to 8 KB just because the buffer is small by convention. Keep the larger default, or pick a middle value such as 16–32 KB. Whichever you choose, update the tests, which currently fail.**

**What decides the value**

The buffer is a per-watcher cost, and it only applies on Windows. At `FileSystemWatcher.Windows.cs:54` it is allocated with `NativeMemory.Alloc(_internalBufferSize)` for each watcher while it is running. On Windows, `ReadDirectoryChangesW` also charges the buffer against the kernel's non-paged pool, so the reviewer is right about that cost. The size you want depends on two things:

- **Event rate versus drain rate.** Each event takes roughly 16 bytes of header plus the UTF-16 file name, so about 60–100 bytes for typical paths. 8 KB holds roughly 80–130 events. A burst of 2,000–3,000 renames produces two events per rename (old name and new name), which is about 4,000–6,000 events and several hundred KB if every one of them is buffered. That figure is my estimate, not something I measured.
- **How many watchers a process creates.** The non-paged cost is multiplied by the number of watchers. 64 KB × 1,000 watchers is 64 MB. At 8 KB it is 8 MB.

**Is reverting safe?**

It is safe in the sense that it only restores the old behavior. It also brings back the bug in the commit message: bursts overflow, `Error` is raised, and events are lost. Callers who hit that today can set `InternalBufferSize` themselves, but they only find out after losing events. That is the reviewer's argument for keeping the default small.

**Problems with the current change**

- `tests/FileSystemWatcher.unit.cs:26` and `:264` still assert `8192`. They will fail with the 64 KB default, and I haven't run them.
- A larger default isn't a fix for overflow. The commit's own numbers suggest 64 KB is borderline for a 3,000-rename burst. A watcher that needs reliability should set `InternalBufferSize` explicitly and handle `Error` by rescanning the directory.
- The buffer size is a public default that applications depend on. Raising it silently changes memory use for every Windows app that creates many watchers.

**My suggestion**

Keep the original default of 8 KB, which is the conservative choice for a shared runtime, and document the burst case in the `InternalBufferSize` docs. Alternatively, compromise at 32 KB. If you keep 64 KB, get measurements of non-paged pool use with many watchers first. In every case, fix the two test assertions to match whatever you decide.

sent.prompt: We're moving an interface from [ComImport] to [GeneratedComInterface] and want to declare C# properties on it rather than hand-written get_X/set_X methods. In what order do the generated slots for a property with both accessors come, and why that order? Why does the generator not distinguish propput from propputref, and why can't I declare an init accessor? Why does it reject so many property shapes outright instead of doing something reasonable with them? And if I want a property that wraps two methods that are not next to each other in the interface, how do I do that?

output.text:
**Short version:** the generator emits the getter slot first, then the setter slot. It leaves out distinctions that a plain `IUnknown` vtable can't express. It rejects shapes it can't map faithfully, so the supported set can grow later without breaking anyone. For a property over two non-adjacent methods, declare the methods as ordinary members and add a property with bodies that calls them. I read `docs/design/libraries/ComInterfaceGenerator/Properties.md`, `DefaultImplementedMembers.md` and `ComMethodInfo.cs`. I didn't compile or run anything.

**1. Slot order**

`T Foo { get; set; }` gets two consecutive slots, getter first and then setter. Those slots come right after the slots of the members declared before it, in source order. A `{ get; }` or `{ set; }` property gets a single slot. The getter is `HRESULT get_Foo(out T value)` and the setter is `HRESULT set_Foo(T value)`.

The reason for the order is that it matches the vtable the built-in CLR produces for a `[ComVisible(true)]` managed interface with the same property (`Properties.md:27`). The point is that source-generated and built-in COM stay wire-compatible. `AddPropertyAccessorInfos` hard-codes this: it adds `GetMethod` and then `SetMethod` (`ComMethodInfo.cs:314-315`). Indexers follow the same rule.

**2. No propput vs propputref**

This is a stated non-goal (`Properties.md:14`). The propput/propputref split exists in type-library metadata and in `IDispatch::Invoke`. A bare `IUnknown` vtable has nothing to encode it, so every setter maps to one slot. The doc also says properties here are `IUnknown`-only, with no dispid integration.

**3. No `init` accessor**

`init` and `set` differ only at the C# call site, where `init` is restricted to object initialisers. In the vtable both are the same `HRESULT set_Foo(T)`. The generator therefore has no faithful way to treat `init` differently. It rejects `init` outright with `SYSLIB1091`, even when the accessor has a body (`ComMethodInfo.cs:441-456`). Quietly turning it into a plain `set` would change what the interface means. The doc's advice is to use `set` if the accessor should be in the vtable. Otherwise, put an `init`-style helper in a separate managed-only layer.

**4. Why it rejects so many shapes**

`Properties.md:37` says it directly: the supported surface is "intentionally narrow", so supported semantics can be expanded later without breaking existing users. Rejecting is the cheap way to leave room to add behaviour later.

Each rejection also has its own reason:
- **`extern`, `required`, `static` and other modifiers:** these have no vtable meaning, and the code falls through to a diagnostic for any modifier it doesn't recognise (`ComMethodInfo.cs:410-433`).
- **Mixed bodied and abstract accessors:** this would put the getter in the vtable but not the setter, or the reverse. That would silently change marshalling per accessor, so you must commit to one shape (`:473-496`).
- **`ref` and `ref readonly` returns:** a COM vtable has no representation for them (`:504-514`).
- **A `[MarshalUsing]` with no marshaller type on an accessor:** it could partly conflict with a property-level `[MarshalUsing]` and silently shadow it when the two are merged (`:516-528`).
- **`[MarshalAs]` on a property:** the C# compiler already rejects it (CS0592), so it never reaches the generator.
- **`virtual` and `sealed` modifiers:** the doc says these aren't currently supported on properties (`Properties.md:82`).

**5. Property over non-adjacent methods**

Use a default-implemented member (DIM). A property whose accessors all have bodies gets no vtable slot. It is managed-only sugar over ordinary ABI methods, which can sit anywhere in the interface:

```csharp
[GeneratedComInterface, Guid("…")]
public partial interface IFoo
{
    double ReadValue();               // ABI slot
    // ...any other members...
    void WriteValue(double value);    // ABI slot, anywhere else

    double Value                      // zero slots
    {
        get => ReadValue();
        set => WriteValue(value);
    }
}
```

Two pitfalls:
- **Don't name the ABI methods `get_Value` and `set_Value`.** C# reserves those names once a property `Value` exists, so you get CS0082. Pick other names, as above. The same restriction applies when a derived interface tries to shadow them.
- **Every accessor needs a body.** Mixing a bodied accessor with a bodiless one is `SYSLIB1091` `PropertyAccessorsMustBeAllOrNothing`.
- **Marshal attributes on a DIM only warn.** They do nothing, because a DIM never goes through marshalling. Put `[MarshalUsing]` on the underlying ABI methods instead.

## Data contracts, briefly

**What they are.** A data contract is a written promise from the runtime to tools. If a tool reads a .NET process's memory (live or from a dump) and interprets it as the contract says, it can work out specific facts about runtime state. A contract covers two things: the physical layout of the data (types, field offsets, sizes, globals) and the algorithm for turning that data into answers. Algorithms are written as C#-like pseudocode against the `Target` API. The cDAC is the reader that implements these contracts.

**Problems they solve compared with the classic DAC and DBI.** The classic design needs DAC and DBI binaries that exactly match the runtime being debugged. That causes four problems:
- **Security:** the matching binaries may come from an untrusted custom or third-party runtime build.
- **Servicing:** a debugger-only fix can't ship without a new runtime build.
- **Acquisition:** it's hard to find the matching binaries.
- **Cross-architecture:** the host and target binaries may not exist.

Contracts remove the need for matching binaries. The reader lives with the tool and learns what to do from data the runtime publishes.

**What the runtime publishes.**
- The module hosting the runtime exports a symbol, `DotNetRuntimeContractDescriptor`. A tool looks for it in each loaded module, which finds every runtime in the process.
- The struct holds a magic number (`"DNCCDAC\0"`, which also reveals endianness), flags (pointer size), a pointer to a UTF-8 JSON descriptor, and a pointer-data array that the JSON indexes into.
- The JSON has the data descriptor and the compatible contracts:
  - The data descriptor lists type layouts and globals, plus optional sub-descriptors for data owned by external components.
  - The compatible contracts are a `"contracts"` map from contract name to version string, for example `{"Thread":"c1"}`. Listing two versions of one contract is an error.

**Contract versioning.**
- Version identifiers are just distinct strings. A "higher" one isn't necessarily newer. They must be unique, and documented on `main`.
- **A new version is required** when the runtime changes its data structures or algorithms in a way that is incompatible with the previous version.
- **An existing version may be amended** only to fix a documentation bug or to add optional globals, types, fields or algorithms. The amendment must stay compatible. A runtime advertising version X must work with a tool that implements the original X and with one that implements any amended X. Typical additions are new APIs that return a default value or error on older runtimes, or an existing API that returns richer data.
- **What is fixed for a release:** the set of supported contract versions stays fixed for a major release, from the first release candidate through the last servicing build. Before the first RC it can change, but carefully, because that breaks tools. Ideally such changes stay behind feature branches or opt-in switches until tools support them.
- Contracts refer to other contracts by name only, without a version.

**Reader version versus contract version.**
- A contract version describes one contract's layout and algorithm. The runtime picks it and publishes it per contract.
- The reader version is a single advisory number for the whole reader. It says when updating a tool's reader is recommended. It doesn't mean older readers can't inspect the runtime.
- The runtime publishes its recommended version in the `RecommendedReaderVersion` global. The reader reports what it understands through `IRuntimeInfo.GetCurrentReaderVersion()`. A tool suggests an update when the runtime's value is greater than the reader's.
- Reader version 2, for example, added support for the interpreter JIT manager. Reader version 3 added support for cached ReadyToRun argument maps, and its changes go with `StackWalk` version `c2`.

**Where each part is written down** (all under `docs/design/datacontracts/`):

| Topic | File |
|---|---|
| Overview, motivation, versioning rules, contract doc format | `datacontracts_design.md` |
| Descriptor struct, magic, flags, exported symbol, `"contracts"` JSON | `contract-descriptor.md` |
| Types and globals JSON format | `data_descriptor.md` |
| Each contract, with all its versions in one file | `<ContractName>.md` (for example `Thread.md`, `StackWalk.md`) |
| Reader version history | `reader-version-history.md` |
| `RecommendedReaderVersion` and `GetCurrentReaderVersion` | `RuntimeInfo.md` |

# cDAC in brief

## What data contracts are, and why

A data contract is a versioned, documented promise from the runtime to outside tools. It has two parts:
- **Physical layout:** type sizes, field offsets, and global values.
- **Algorithms:** how to turn those bytes into useful answers, such as the methods on a `MethodTable` or how to walk a stack.

A tool reads target memory (live process or dump) and interprets it using the contract. The cDAC is the managed reader that does this.

The classic DAC and DBI must match the exact runtime build, which causes four problems. The contracts address each one:
- **Security:** a matching DAC/DBI for a custom or third-party runtime may be untrusted. A reader that ships with the tool doesn't depend on it.
- **Servicing:** a debugger-only fix needs no new runtime build.
- **Acquisition:** there's no need to find the matching DAC/DBI.
- **Cross-architecture:** a host or target DAC/DBI that isn't available no longer blocks you.

## What the runtime publishes

- **Export:** the module hosting the runtime exports a `DotNetRuntimeContractDescriptor` symbol. If a process holds several runtimes, look in every loaded module.
- **Header:** the struct starts with a magic value (`"DNCCDAC\0"`, which also reveals endianness), flags (pointer size), a pointer to a JSON blob, and a pointer-data array. Indirect values in the JSON index into that array.
- **JSON blob:** it holds four things:
  - `types`: layouts, with field offsets and optional sizes.
  - `globals`: ints, pointers, or strings.
  - `sub-descriptors`: pointers to descriptors owned by other components.
  - `contracts`: a map of contract name to a single version string, for example `{"Thread":"c1"}`. Listing several versions of one contract is an error.

## Versioning of contracts

- **Version identifiers:** a contract version is just a string (`c1`, `c2`, …). It is not ordered, so a "higher" one isn't necessarily newer. Each must be unique and documented on `main`.
- **New version needed:** whenever the runtime changes data structures or algorithms in a way that isn't compatible with the previous version.
- **Amending an existing version:** this is allowed only to fix a doc bug or to add optional globals, types, fields, or algorithms. The amendment must stay compatible, so a tool written against the original definition still works. Typical examples are a new API that returns a default or error on older runtimes, or an existing API that returns richer information. There is some subjective leeway in judging this.
- **Fixed per release:** for a major release, the set of supported contract versions stays fixed from the first RC through the last servicing build. Before RC you may change it, but carefully, because that breaks tools. Ideally you do it on a feature branch or behind an opt-in switch, after tools already support the new version.
- **Cross-references:** contracts refer to each other by name, without a version.
- **Missing fields:** reading a field the target doesn't define produces an error.

## Reader version

The reader version is an advisory number that says "you should update your reader." It is independent of contract versions and doesn't mean an older reader can't inspect the runtime.
- The runtime publishes the `RecommendedReaderVersion` global.
- The reader reports what it understands through `IRuntimeInfo.GetCurrentReaderVersion()`.
- A tool suggests an update when the recommended version is greater than the reader's.

Contract versions are a compatibility mechanism: they say which layouts and algorithms the runtime uses. The reader version is a hint only. Version 3, for example, suggests updating because older readers can't correctly handle a target that publishes `StackWalk` `c2`.

All of these are under `docs/design/datacontracts/` unless noted:
- `datacontracts_design.md`: motivation, versioning rules, and the format of contract docs.
- `contract-descriptor.md`: the physical descriptor struct, the JSON `contracts` key, and the export symbol.
- `data_descriptor.md`: the JSON layout of types and globals.
- `<ContractName>.md` (for example `Thread.md`): one file per contract, with the API and every version's algorithm.
- `reader-version-history.md`: what each reader version added.
- `RuntimeInfo.md`: related to the reader-version API.
- `src/native/managed/cdac/README.md`: the reader implementation.
- `src/coreclr/debug/datadescriptor-shared/README.md` and `src/coreclr/tools/cdac-build-tool/README.md`: the runtime side that produces the descriptor.

- **When an existing version may be amended:** only for compatible changes.
  - Fixing a documentation bug.
  - Adding optional globals, types, fields or algorithms.
  - Adding APIs that return a default value or error on older runtimes.

- **What is fixed for a release:**

- **Cross-references:** contracts refer to other contracts by name without a version.

- **Contract version:** per contract, set by the runtime, and describes how the runtime's data and algorithm work. It is a compatibility requirement.
- **Reader version:**

  - The runtime publishes its recommendation in the `RecommendedReaderVersion` global.

| Reader version history | `reader-version-history.md` |
| Reader version APIs and global | `RuntimeInfo.md` |
| Reader implementation | `src/native/managed/cdac/` (start with its `README.md`) |

All three are documented design decisions in this repo, not bugs. The first two are known limitations and the third is a deliberate narrow allowlist. The relevant sources are `docs/design/tools/illink/task-cache.md` and `src/tools/illink/src/ILLink.Tasks/LinkTask.cs`.

## 1. A runtime upgrade on the agents still gives cache hits

**Intended: yes, by design.** The cache key covers these inputs:
- the task assembly
- the `dotnet` host executable
- the whole linker assembly
- your input assemblies and their sidecars

It does not cover the runtime or CoreLib that runs the child linker process. The design doc (`task-cache.md:42-46`) gives the reasons:
- MSBuild's own runtime identity doesn't tell you which runtime the child process resolves.
- runtimeconfig roll-forward settings don't identify the resolved CoreLib either.
- Resolving it would need extra host information or another process.

It lists "resolved child-runtime identity" as a follow-up. The usage doc says to "clear or isolate the cache when that distinction is required."

Your cache may also be wrong in a related way. Cecil and the linker's deployment config files aren't fingerprinted either (`task-cache.md:38`). They only invalidate entries if the linker binary itself changes.

**What to do:**
- Fold a runtime or agent-image version into `ILLINK_EXPERIMENTAL_CACHE_PATH`, for example `.../illink-$(dotnet --version)`. Alternatively, clear the cache whenever the agent image changes. A versioned path is the more reliable option.
- If you use a restored CI snapshot, put the same version in its cache key (the repo's `setup-illink-cache.yml` is a model).
- Do the same for SDK or ILLink package bumps that change Cecil or config but not `illink.dll`.
- Clear the cache once now, since the existing entries were produced under the old runtime.

## 2. The warnings-as-errors gate misses trimming warnings

**Intended: yes, a documented limitation.** A cache hit restores the output directory and never runs the linker. Linker warnings are therefore not replayed to the console or binlog (`task-cache.md:89-92`). Any gate that depends on them, such as `TreatWarningsAsErrors` or `WarningsAsErrors=IL2026;...`, only sees warnings on cache misses. Diagnostic replay is the other listed follow-up.

The cached entry is only stored after a successful link. If the link failed, nothing is cached, so the build fails every time. An entry that exists is from a build whose warnings did not fail it at the time. A later hit then passes silently, even if you have since tightened the warning policy. The warning policy is not part of the cache key.

**What to do:**
- Run the gate on a build that does not use the cache. For example, a CI job (or a nightly or PR-gate job) with `ILLINK_EXPERIMENTAL_CACHE` unset, or with a fresh cache path. Keep the cache for the fast build jobs.
- Don't rely on a cached build as your only trim-warning check.
- If you change which warnings are errors, also clear the cache or change its path.

## 3. Projects with `ExtraArgs` never hit the cache

**Intended: yes, an allowlist.** Arbitrary `ExtraArgs` bypass the cache because they could add inputs, outputs or side effects that aren't tracked. `TryAddCacheableExtraArgsInputs` (`LinkTask.cs:399`) accepts only this exact shape:

```
--ignore-link-attributes true [ (--link-attributes FILE | --substitutions FILE | -d DIR)* ]
```

This is the shape the runtime libraries build uses. Anything else returns false and the task logs a low-importance message: `ILLink cache bypassed: extra arguments are not supported.`

- Arguments must be in that order. The first option must be `--ignore-link-attributes true`.
- Any other flag bypasses the cache.
- Unbalanced or mixed quoting bypasses it.
- A missing or unreadable XML file bypasses it.

The same bypass applies to `CustomSteps`, `CustomData`, `DumpDependencies`, `DependenciesFileFormat`, and any task-level `EnvironmentVariables` (`LinkTask.cs:298`). Check whether you set any of these too.

**What to do:**
- Run with detailed or diagnostic verbosity and look for `ILLink cache bypassed:` to see which reason applies to each project.
- Where you can, move the extra arguments to first-class task properties or MSBuild properties. Only the allowlisted shape is cacheable, so the other options are to drop the extra flags or accept uncached links for those projects.
- Don't try to work around the allowlist by editing `LinkTask.cs` to widen it unless you also hash the new inputs. The bypass exists to prevent stale or incorrect hits.

- The feature is labeled experimental and "may change or be removed without notice."
- The environment variables are read from the process environment. Set them before MSBuild starts, because reused MSBuild node processes keep the environment they started with.

sent.prompt: I'm about to start working on the cDAC (the data contract reader). Explain to a newcomer, as briefly as you can: what the data contracts are and what problems they solve compared with the classic DAC and DBI; what the runtime publishes so a reader can find them; how contracts are versioned, when a change needs a new version and when an existing one may be amended, and what is fixed for a release; what the reader version is and how it differs from a contract version; and where each part is written down.

output.text:
## cDAC in brief

**What contracts are, and what they fix.** A data contract is a documented promise from the runtime to outside tools. It gives the memory layout of a subset of runtime structures (field offsets, sizes, globals). It also gives the algorithms for turning those structures into useful answers, usually as C#-style pseudocode. The reader (the cDAC) is a managed library that reads target memory and follows those rules.

The classic DAC and DBI must match the exact runtime build, which causes four problems. These are all listed in `datacontracts_design.md`:
- **Security:** the matching DAC and DBI may be untrusted (custom or third-party runtime builds).
- **Servicing:** a debugger-only fix needs a new runtime build.
- **Acquisition:** you have to find the matching DAC and DBI binaries.
- **Cross-architecture:** the host/target DAC and DBI may not exist.

Contracts remove the exact-match requirement.

**What the runtime publishes.**
- The runtime exports a `DotNetRuntimeContractDescriptor` symbol. Its magic value is "DNCCDAC\0", and it also records pointer size and endianness.
- It points to a JSON blob plus a pointer-data array.
- The JSON holds the type layouts (`types`) and the `globals`. It can also hold `sub-descriptors` for externally described data.
- It holds a `contracts` map of contract name to version string, for example `{"Thread":"c1"}`.
- A descriptor must not list two versions of the same contract.
- Readers look in each loaded module to find every runtime in a process.

**Contract versioning.**
- Version strings are opaque identifiers. A "higher" one isn't necessarily newer, only different.
- Every version must be documented on `main` with a non-conflicting ID.
- **New version:** required when the runtime changes data structures or algorithms in a way that is incompatible with the previous version.
- **Amend in place:** allowed only for compatible changes. These are documentation bug fixes, or additive changes such as optional globals, types, fields, or APIs. New APIs must return a default or an error on older runtimes. A tool implementing the original definition must still work.
- **Fixed per release:** for a major release, the set of supported contract versions must not change from the first release candidate through the last servicing build. Changing it before RC1 is allowed but risky. Do it in feature branches or behind opt-ins, after tools support the new version.
- **Cross-contract references:** contracts refer to each other by name without a version.
- **Missing fields:** reading a field the target doesn't define is an error.

**Reader version vs contract version.**
- A contract version belongs to one contract. It says which layout and algorithm the target runtime uses.
- The reader version is a single advisory number for the whole reader. It says when updating the reader is recommended. It does not say an older reader can no longer inspect the runtime.
- The runtime publishes `RecommendedReaderVersion` as a global. The reader reports what it understands through `IRuntimeInfo.GetCurrentReaderVersion()`. A tool suggests an update when the runtime's number is greater than the reader's.
- Example: reader version 3 was prompted by `StackWalk` `c2`. A reader that only knows `c1` can't safely handle such targets, but a version 3 reader handles both.

**Where it's written down** (all under `docs/design/datacontracts/`):
- `datacontracts_design.md`: the motivation, versioning rules, and the contract doc format.
- `contract-descriptor.md`: the physical descriptor, the magic value, the JSON `contracts` key, and the exported symbol.
- `data_descriptor.md`: the types and globals JSON format.
- `<ContractName>.md`: one file per contract, such as `RuntimeTypeSystem.md` and `Thread.md`. Each file holds all versions of that contract.
- `reader-version-history.md`: what each reader version added.
- `RuntimeInfo.md`: the contract that exposes runtime info, including the reader version.

The code is in `src/native/managed/cdac/`. The native hook is `src/coreclr/debug/daccess/cdac.h`.

sent.prompt: The JIT can now inline runtime-async methods that really await into their async callers. Why couldn't such a call simply be inlined like any other call: what observable behaviour disappears when both the call site and the callee's body are removed? When an inlined callee suspends, is resumed and then logically returns to its caller, what does the JIT have to emit at that point, and why does part of it need help from the async infrastructure rather than being done in JIT'ed code? Why is the inlining expected to pay off anyway? And which awaits does it still refuse to inline?

output.text:
Source: `docs/design/coreclr/jit/runtime-async-inlining.md`. I also grepped the JIT to confirm the refusal cases. The doc's "Special cases" section still says only never-suspending inlinees are supported. That text looks stale, because `fginline.cpp:2531` and `fginline.cpp:2747` now emit the `RestoreInlinedFrameContexts` call.

**Why it isn't an ordinary inline**

Inlining removes both the call site and the callee, and runtime-async attaches observable behaviour to each.

- **Call site:** every suspending await saves the `ExecutionContext`, which is what carries `AsyncLocal` values. Task and ValueTask awaits also capture a continuation context: the `SynchronizationContext`, the `TaskScheduler`, or the thread pool for `ConfigureAwait(false)`. The continuation is resumed there.
- **Callee:** every async body is wrapped in a capture and restore of the thread's execution and synchronization contexts. The restore is skipped if the method finished after resuming.

If both disappear, `AsyncLocal` values and the continuation context are no longer preserved across suspension.

**What the JIT emits when the inlinee resumes and logically returns**

On resumption, async infrastructure restores the saved `ExecutionContext` and puts the continuation in the right context, as normal. When the inlinee then logically returns to its caller, no real frame returns, so the JIT has to do what the infrastructure would have done. This is the "post-inline IR", and it runs only if `resumed_callee` is true:

1. Restore the `ExecutionContext` that was captured for the caller, using `continuation.ExecutionContextForB`.
2. Check whether the code is on the caller's captured continuation context. If it isn't, suspend, switch and resume there with `await AsyncHelpers.SwitchContext(...)`.
3. Set `resumed_caller = true`. If the inlinee threw after resuming, it must also rethrow the exception, and the caller's own context restore must be skipped.

The suspension side matters too. A suspension inside an inlinee has to capture the contexts for every logically elided frame, in `…ForB` and `…ForA` fields of one reused continuation. It does this conditionally on the `resumed_*` flags.

**Why the infrastructure has to help**

The JIT can't make a thread run on a given `SynchronizationContext`, `TaskScheduler` or the thread pool. The only way to get there is to post a callback, which means suspending, switching and resuming. So the JIT expands only the `resumed_C` check inline. Everything after that is a single `AsyncHelpers.RestoreInlinedFrameContexts` call. It restores the `ExecutionContext`, runs `IsOnRightContext`, and does the suspend-and-switch itself.

**Why it still pays off**

- The synchronous path is the common one. The JIT only needs to know `resumed_C` is false, and constant propagation can then remove the post-inline work.
- When the check is reached after a resume, at least one suspension and resumption has already happened, so the extra cost is small by comparison.
- `IsOnRightContext` is almost always true, because the synchronization context is rarely changed mid-async-method. The doc says that if this were common, inlining probably wouldn't be profitable.
- Inlinees that can't suspend lose the capture, restore and flag overhead. The suspension sequences can share tails.

**What is still refused**

Awaits inside try regions. `inline.def` has two fatal observations for this:

- `CALLEE_AWAIT_IN_TRY`: the callee has an await inside a try.
- `CALLSITE_AWAIT_IN_TRY_REGION`: the call site is inside a try region and the callee has an await.

The doc says correct handling would need catch-and-rethrow in the post-inline IR, so it skips this case "initially".

sent.prompt: FileSystemWatcher's default InternalBufferSize in FileSystemWatcher.cs is now 64 KB instead of 8 KB. A reviewer notes that on Windows the buffer comes from non-paged memory, that the guidance has long been to keep it small, and that an application that needs more can set InternalBufferSize itself; they ask to put the default back to 8 KB. Is that safe? Recommend, and explain what decides the value.

output.text:
**Recommendation: don't revert to 8 KB. Keep the 64 KB default, but I'd tighten the change as described below. The reviewer's concern is real, but it's smaller than it sounds.**

**What decides the value**

The right default depends on two costs.

- **Cost of a larger default.** Only Windows uses the buffer. In `FileSystemWatcher.Windows.cs:146` it is a native allocation (`NativeMemory.Alloc(_internalBufferSize)`) handed to `ReadDirectoryChangesW`. The reviewer is right that the kernel locks it into non-paged memory. Linux and macOS ignore the setting (`FileSystemWatcher.Linux.cs:100-102` says the implementation doesn't use it). The cost is therefore 56 KB more per watcher instance on Windows. It matters only for processes that create hundreds or thousands of watchers. One watcher per folder in a large tree is the usual case.
- **Cost of a smaller default.** Overflow loses events silently. The watcher raises `Error` with `InternalBufferOverflowException`, and every change in the burst is dropped. The commit message describes exactly this failure: 2,000–3,000 renames in about a second overflowed 8 KB. Each rename event takes roughly 12 bytes plus the filename in UTF-16 (old and new names, so about 100 bytes for typical names). 8 KB holds about 80 events and 64 KB about 600.

**Where the reviewer has a point**

- "The app can set `InternalBufferSize` itself" is a weak argument. The app only knows to do that after it has already lost events. Because the failure is silent, many apps never find out. A default shouldn't make people hit a data-loss path first.
- "Keep it small" is long-standing guidance, but it comes from a time when non-paged pool was scarce. It is a resource-pressure argument, not a correctness one.

sent.prompt: We're moving an interface from [ComImport] to [GeneratedComInterface] and want to declare C# properties on it rather than hand-written get_X/set_X methods. In what order do the generated slots for a property with both accessors come, and why that order? Why does the generator not distinguish propput from propputref, and why can't I declare an init accessor? Why does it reject so many property shapes outright instead of doing something reasonable with them? And if I want a property that wraps two methods that are not next to each other in the interface, how do I do that?

output.text:
Everything below comes from the generator source (`ComMethodInfo.cs`) and the design docs under `docs/design/libraries/ComInterfaceGenerator/`. I haven't compiled or run anything.

## Slot order for `{ get; set; }`

A property with both accessors gets two consecutive vtable slots. The getter comes first, then the setter, immediately after the slots of whatever was declared before it. A read-only or write-only property gets a single slot. The signatures are `HRESULT get_Foo(out T value)` and `HRESULT set_Foo(T value)`.

The code emits the getter then the setter (`ComMethodInfo.cs:312-315`). The comment there gives the reason: it matches the CCW vtable layout the built-in CLR produces for a `[ComVisible(true)]` managed interface. Keeping that order means a `[ComImport]` interface moved to `[GeneratedComInterface]` keeps the same ABI, so existing native peers still line up.

## No propput vs. propputref

The generator doesn't distinguish them because the distinction doesn't exist in an `IUnknown` vtable. `Properties.md:14` lists it as a non-goal. `propputref` lives in TLB metadata and in `IDispatch::Invoke`. Properties on a generated interface are exposed through the `IUnknown` vtable only, with no dispid integration. Every setter maps to one slot.

## No `init` accessor

`init` versus `set` is a distinction at the C# call site, and the vtable has no way to express it. The check runs before the default-implementation check (`ComMethodInfo.cs:441-456`), so `init` is rejected even if the accessor has a body. The diagnostic is `SYSLIB1091`. Use `set`. If you need init-only semantics, put them in a separate managed-only abstraction.

## Why so many shapes are rejected

`Properties.md:37` says the supported surface is intentionally narrow. Rejecting a shape now lets semantics be added later without breaking anyone who relied on the old behavior. A silent guess would become a compatibility commitment. Specific cases:

- **`extern`, `required`, `static`, `virtual`, `sealed`, `partial`:** these hit the "unsupported modifier" default case (`ComMethodInfo.cs:421-431`).
- **`init`:** covered above.
- **Mixed bodied and abstract accessors:** this gets `PropertyAccessorsMustBeAllOrNothing` (`ComMethodInfo.cs:490`). A property whose getter is in the vtable and whose setter isn't would change marshalling semantics per accessor without any visible sign.
- **`ref` and `ref readonly` returns:** a COM vtable has no representation for them. Methods are rejected the same way.
- **`[MarshalUsing]` on an accessor without a marshaller type:** a count-only attribute could partly conflict with a property-level `[MarshalUsing]` and silently shadow it in the merge. You can put the marshaller type and count together on one accessor attribute, or put the count-only attribute on the property.
- **`[MarshalAs]` on the property:** C# itself rejects this with CS0592, so the generator never sees it.

## A property wrapping two non-adjacent methods

Declare the two ABI methods as ordinary abstract methods wherever their vtable slots need to be. Then add a property with bodied accessors that calls them. A property whose accessors all have bodies is a default-implemented member and gets no vtable slot (`DefaultImplementedMembers.md`).

```csharp
[GeneratedComInterface, Guid("…")]
public partial interface IFoo
{
    double ReadValue();                       // slot n
    void Other();                             // slot n+1
    void WriteValue(double value);            // slot n+2
    double Value { get => ReadValue(); set => WriteValue(value); }   // no slot
}
```

The ABI methods can't be named `get_Value` and `set_Value`. Once the interface declares a property `Value`, C# reserves those names, and you get CS0082 (`DefaultImplementedMembers.md:39-67`). Give them different names such as `ReadValue` and `WriteValue`. The names are only managed-side identifiers, so they don't affect the wire ABI. The same applies to derived interfaces.

Marshalling attributes on the bodied property or accessors have no ABI effect and produce a `SYSLIB1091` warning. Put `[MarshalUsing]` and `[MarshalAs]` on the ABI methods.

sent.prompt: We turned on ILLINK_EXPERIMENTAL_CACHE for our library builds and hit three surprises. After we upgraded the .NET runtime installed on the build agents, the trimmed output still came straight from the cache. Our warnings-as-errors gate stopped catching trimming warnings on some builds. And projects that pass extra linker arguments through ExtraArgs never hit the cache at all. Is each of these intended, and why? What should we do about each one?

output.text:
All three behaviors are intended and documented. They're the experimental feature's stated trade-offs, not bugs. The sources are `docs/design/tools/illink/task-cache.md` and `src/tools/illink/src/ILLink.Tasks/LinkTask.cs`.

## 1. A runtime upgrade didn't invalidate the cache

**Why:** The cache key covers the task assembly, the dotnet host executable (`pathToTool`) and the linker assembly (`illink.dll`). It does not cover the runtime or CoreLib that runs the child linker process (design doc, "Input discovery and eligibility"). The design says this is deliberate. MSBuild's runtime identity doesn't identify the child's runtime. Roll-forward settings don't tell you which CoreLib gets resolved. Resolving it would need extra host information or another process. So a runtime installation change alone "need not invalidate entries". The doc lists resolved child-runtime identity as a follow-up.

The key does include the host executable. If the upgrade replaced the `dotnet` binary that `DotNetPath` points to, that would change the key. The side-by-side install case, where `dotnet` stays the same and a new shared runtime appears, is the one that slips through.

**What to do:** Treat a runtime change as a manual cache-invalidation event.
- Point `ILLINK_EXPERIMENTAL_CACHE_PATH` at a directory that includes the runtime version, for example `.../illink-8.0.x`. Bump it as part of the agent image update.
- Or purge or clear the cache directory when you upgrade agents.
- The CI recipe in `docs/tools/illink/illink-tasks.md` uses a job-private directory, so the same approach works with a versioned cache key.

The same applies to Cecil and other bundled linker dependencies. They aren't fingerprinted unless the linker binary also changes.

## 2. The warnings-as-errors gate stopped catching trimming warnings

**Why:** Cache hits don't run ILLink, so they don't replay warnings. The doc says: "Hits do not replay linker warnings or other diagnostics. This can omit console/binlog warnings and affect external warning-as-error policies." On a hit, `ExecuteNormally` is never called, so no `IL2xxx` or `IL3xxx` output reaches MSBuild. Your gate only sees warnings from builds that missed the cache. Diagnostic replay is the other listed follow-up.

**What to do:** Don't rely on a cached build for the gate.
- Run the gate job with `ILLINK_EXPERIMENTAL_CACHE` unset. That job is the one that must see every warning.
- Or keep caching for dev and PR builds, and run a periodic or release build uncached as the authoritative check.
- Don't enable it on any job whose job is to report linker diagnostics. The doc says callers who need diagnostics must disable caching.

Also note that a green build from a cache hit proves nothing about warnings. It only shows the same inputs once linked without failing.

## 3. Projects with `ExtraArgs` never hit the cache

**Why:** `DescribeInvocation` returns `null`, which bypasses the cache, whenever `ExtraArgs` isn't in one narrow supported shape (`LinkTask.cs:399-476`). The only accepted form is:

```
--ignore-link-attributes true [--link-attributes FILE | --substitutions FILE | -d DIR]...
```

That is the policy the runtime library builds use. Anything else bypasses, because arbitrary arguments can add undeclared inputs, outputs or side effects, and the cache couldn't tell what to hash. The same applies to custom steps or data, dependency dumps, and `ToolTask.EnvironmentVariables` overrides (`LinkTask.cs:298-303`). A malformed or unreadable path in those arguments also bypasses.

The bypass is logged at low importance: "ILLink cache bypassed: extra arguments are not supported." Run with `-v:diag` or check the binlog to confirm which projects hit it.

**What to do:**
- If your extra arguments are really that runtime-library shape, make them match it exactly. The first option must be `--ignore-link-attributes true`, followed only by the supported pairs. Quoting must be well-formed.
- If you pass other options, look for a first-class task property instead. `ExtraArgs` is the one escape hatch the cache can't see through.
- If you need the extra arguments, accept that those projects won't be cached. Don't try to work around it. The bypass is protecting you from stale outputs.

## Summary

| Surprise | Intended? | Action |
|---|---|---|
| Stale hit after runtime upgrade | Yes, runtime identity isn't hashed | Version or clear the cache on agent upgrades |
| Missing trim warnings on hits | Yes, no diagnostic replay | Run the warning gate uncached |
| `ExtraArgs` never caches | Yes, only a narrow shape is allowed | Conform to that shape or accept no caching |

Since the feature is labeled experimental and "may change or be removed without notice", I'd keep it off the jobs that produce your shipping or gating artifacts.

**No, it has drifted from its spec.** The resolver order is reversed.

**What the code does**

`AddComponent` (`ComponentLoadContext.cs:51-65`) builds the new resolver array as `[resolver, .. _resolvers]`. That puts the newest component's resolver at the front. A code comment (lines 57-58) says this is deliberate: "The most recently loaded component is consulted first, so a component loaded later can supply a newer version of a dependency it shares with earlier ones."

`Load` (line 69) and `LoadUnmanagedDll` (line 83) walk the array from index 0 and return the first hit. So the **last-loaded component wins** for both managed and native lookups.

**What it is meant to do**

The spec is `docs/design/features/native-hosting-load-context.md`, in two places:
- Line 39: "That ALC will resolve dependencies using the `.deps.json` from the components, in precedence order corresponding to the order in which the components were loaded into it."
- Line 68: "Resolvers are queried in the component load order — the first one wins."

Under the spec, the **first-loaded component wins**. The code does the opposite for every context that has two or more components.

**Where it is not wrong**
- The first resolver is created in the constructor (lines 31-43), so the first component starts at the front. The ordering only breaks once a second component is added.
- The caller, `ComponentLoadContextManager.Get` (`ComponentLoadContextManager.cs:91-104`), matches the spec. It creates the ALC with the first component and calls `AddComponent` for later ones.
- Isolated contexts hold one component, so they are unaffected.

**Fix**

Append instead of prepend: `[.. _resolvers, resolver]`. The comment at lines 57-58 should then be removed or reworded. If last-wins is the behaviour you actually want, the spec at lines 39 and 68 needs to change instead.

sent.prompt: crossgen2 can now emit a composite ReadyToRun image as a Mach-O object for macOS (`--obj-format macho`). Why does the precompiled managed code go into a section of its own rather than the usual text section? The R2R format is full of RVAs: how are they expressed in a Mach-O object, and why is that the right thing to measure them from? Why does the runtime ask the host for the composite image instead of opening the dylib itself? And what is `--rtr-header-symbol-name` for?

output.text:
These answers come from the design doc `docs/design/coreclr/botr/readytorun-platform-native-envelope.md`, plus the crossgen2 option definitions. I didn't read the object-writer code, so the doc describes the design and I haven't checked it against the implementation.

**Why code goes in `__TEXT,__managedcode` and not `__TEXT,__text`**

The doc gives two reasons. The linker treats `__TEXT,__text` specially, and `__managedcode` matches what NativeAOT already does. Precompiled managed code is not ordinary native code, so keeping it out of `__text` stops the linker from applying its text-section handling to it. The image's other native pieces stay put: import thunks remain in `__text`, and read/write data such as fixup tables stays in `__DATA,__data`. Read-only data (jump tables, metadata, unwind and GC info, the R2R headers) goes to `__TEXT,__const`.

**How RVAs are expressed, and why measure from there**

- The R2R format, like PE, stores RVAs relative to the image base. COFF objects can express this natively, but Mach-O objects can't.
- The Apple linker does provide a base symbol, `__mh_<output>_header`. For a dylib that is `__mh_dylib_header`.
- The object writer uses `__mh_dylib_header` as the base symbol. It emits each RVA as a subtractor relocation, "symbol location − `__mh_dylib_header` location". Mach-O supports subtractor relocations natively, and the linker resolves them to a fixed offset.
- That symbol is the right base for two reasons:
  - It sits at the address `dlinfo` and `dladdr` return as the image base. The runtime can therefore add an RVA to the base it gets from the loader and land on the right byte.
  - It points at the Mach header. The runtime can read that header to find the image size and bound its reads of R2R data.

A related design choice is how symbol ranges are represented. Apple linkers have trouble when several symbols are defined at the same location. So a range's start is just the start symbol, and its size is "end symbol location − start symbol location + end symbol size", again using subtractor relocations.

**Why the runtime asks the host for the composite image**

- The runtime doesn't open the dylib itself. For a component assembly with `READYTORUN_FLAG_PLATFORM_NATIVE_IMAGE`, it reads `OwnerCompositeExecutable` and calls a new `get_native_code_data` callback in `host_runtime_contract`.
- The host returns the `READYTORUN_HEADER` pointer, the image size and the load base.
- The doc says this leaves "the actual load" to the host. The host might `dlopen` a shared library or use something statically linked into itself. It also handles any caching.
- If the callback fails, the runtime falls back to IL and the JIT.

**What `--rtr-header-symbol-name` is for**

- It overrides the exported symbol name for the `READYTORUN_HEADER`. The default is `RTR_HEADER`.
- It is meant for custom hosts that link several R2R images directly, instead of loading them dynamically with `dlopen`. Each image then needs a distinct export name, or the symbols collide.
- The host must look up the header with the matching custom name. The SDK or build link step must also keep that export in the final dylib.
- It requires `--composite` and must not be empty or whitespace. `Resources.resx` defines both errors.

sent.prompt: We turned on ILLINK_EXPERIMENTAL_CACHE for our library builds and hit three surprises. After we upgraded the .NET runtime installed on the build agents, the trimmed output still came straight from the cache. Our warnings-as-errors gate stopped catching trimming warnings on some builds. And projects that pass extra linker arguments through ExtraArgs never hit the cache at all. Is each of these intended, and why? What should we do about each one?

output.text:
All three are documented, intended behaviors of this experimental cache. They come from the design doc (`docs/design/tools/illink/task-cache.md`) and the usage doc (`docs/tools/illink/illink-tasks.md`). I read those two docs and didn't run a build or read the task source (`LinkTask.cs`), so I haven't reproduced any of this on your setup.

## 1. Runtime upgrade on the build agents, but output still came from the cache

**Intended, but only as a known limitation.** The cache key covers these inputs:
- arguments
- input files and their sidecars
- the task assembly
- the selected dotnet host executable
- the whole linker assembly

It deliberately does not identify the runtime that executes the child linker process. The design doc gives two reasons. MSBuild's own runtime identity doesn't establish the child's. Runtimeconfig roll-forward settings also don't tell you which CoreLib actually gets resolved. Identifying it would take extra host information or another process. The doc lists "resolved child-runtime identity" as a follow-up. The usage doc says runtime installation changes "are not guaranteed to invalidate entries."

**What to do:**
- Treat a runtime upgrade on the agents as a cache-invalidation event. Clear the cache or point `ILLINK_EXPERIMENTAL_CACHE_PATH` at a new directory when the agent image changes.
- A simple way to do that is to put the runtime version in the cache path or CI cache key, for example `.illink-cache-<runtime-version>`.
- If the trimmed output could differ across runtime versions in your case, you can disable caching on the agents that need it.
- The same applies to the bundled linker dependencies (Cecil, deployment config). They aren't fingerprinted either, unless the linker binary itself changes.

## 2. Warnings-as-errors gate missed trimming warnings on some builds

**Intended.** The design doc says "Hits do not replay linker warnings or other diagnostics." It also says this "can omit console/binlog warnings and affect external warning-as-error policies." On a hit, ILLink never runs. The cached output directory is restored, and no `ILxxxx` warnings are emitted. Your gate only sees warnings on cache misses, so the "some builds" are almost certainly the hits.

**What to do:**
- Don't rely on the cached build to enforce the gate. The doc says callers who need diagnostics must disable caching.
- One option is to run the trim-warning gate in a job or configuration with `ILLINK_EXPERIMENTAL_CACHE` unset. The cached build then only produces artifacts.
- The other option is to disable the cache for any build that enforces the gate.
- Don't treat a green gate on a cached build as proof that the code is warning-free.
- Trim and AOT analyzer warnings (`IL2xxx`/`IL3xxx` from the Roslyn analyzers with `EnableTrimAnalyzer`) come from the compiler, not the linker. Those still fire on cached builds. Only warnings that ILLink itself produces are lost.

## 3. Projects passing `ExtraArgs` never hit the cache

**Intended.** The design doc says arbitrary `ExtraArgs` bypass caching, with a diagnostic. The reason is that arbitrary arguments can introduce undeclared inputs, outputs, or side effects the key can't see. The same bypass applies to:
- custom steps/data
- dependency-dump options
- explicit `ToolTask.EnvironmentVariables` overrides

Only the runtime-repo library-build forms are supported: `--ignore-link-attributes true`, followed by zero or more `--link-attributes FILE`, `--substitutions FILE`, or `-d DIRECTORY` pairs. The XML files and everything in the search directories get content-hashed.

**What to do:**
- Look at the bypass diagnostic in the build log. It should name the unsupported argument.
- If the arguments are really link-attributes, substitutions, or `-d` directories, move to the supported form. The form is strict: `--ignore-link-attributes true` must come first, and the XML files must be readable.
- For anything else, use the SDK-level equivalents where they exist, such as `TrimmerRootDescriptor` or `TrimMode`. The SDK computes those into task parameters.
- Otherwise accept that those projects go uncached. The cache is a poor fit for them, and widening it isn't something you can configure.

## Cross-cutting advice

- Because of the first two points, I'd limit the cache to builds where stale-runtime reuse and lost diagnostics are acceptable. Everything else should run uncached.
- The feature is labeled experimental, and neither the configuration nor the on-disk format is a supported compatibility surface. Pin your expectations accordingly.

sent.prompt: DefaultExpect100ContinueTimeout in HttpHandlerDefaults now waits 3 seconds for a 100 Continue before sending the request body. A reviewer points out that 1 second was the default for years, that servers which ignore Expect: 100-continue now delay every such request by 3 seconds, and asks to put it back to 1. Is that safe? Recommend, and explain what decides the value.

output.text:
**I recommend putting it back to 1 second** and having clients of the Quillmere gateway set `Expect100ContinueTimeout` themselves. I haven't run any tests or checked what else depends on the old value. This is based on the commit and the constant's definition.

**What the timeout costs.** It's a ceiling on the wait, not a fixed delay. It only applies to requests that opt in with `Expect: 100-continue`.
- A server that answers with 100 or a final status, such as a 401, ends the wait immediately, so the timeout value doesn't matter for it.
- A server that ignores the header makes the client wait the full timeout on every such request. The reviewer is right that this goes from 1s to 3s.
- A server that answers slowly but eventually answers is where a longer timeout helps. The client doesn't give up and send a body the server was about to reject.

**What decides the value.** It's a trade-off between two costs:
- The first is added latency on every request to a server that never answers. Everyone pays this, and it's small per request.
- The second is a wasted body upload when a slow but compliant server hasn't answered in time. Few people pay it, but it's large for multi-gigabyte uploads.

A library-wide default should protect the common case. The common case is servers that either answer quickly or ignore the header, and 1s has worked for them for years. The 1.4–2.2s figure comes from one gateway. That makes it a property of that deployment, not a general network characteristic. Raising the global default makes every ignoring server slower to fix one slow validator.

**Why I'd revert.**
- The commit's own message says the per-handler override already exists on both `HttpClientHandler` and `SocketsHttpHandler`. That fixes the Quillmere case with no cost to anyone else.
- Raising the default is a behavior change for all callers. A 3s stall on non-compliant servers is hard to diagnose and is the sort of regression people hit after upgrading.
- Even 3s is only a margin over the observed 2.2s. A slow token check will still sometimes exceed it, so the default can't fully solve the problem anyway.

**When I'd keep 3s.** Keep it only if there's evidence that many servers validate credentials before answering. Measure how common those servers are against how many ignore the header. Without that data, I'd go with the reviewer.

**Suggested follow-up.** Revert the constant to `TimeSpan.FromSeconds(1)`. Keep the comment, but reword it to point Quillmere users at `Expect100ContinueTimeout`. I can make that change and grep for tests or docs that mention the old value if you'd like.

**Is the revert safe?** Not for the case that prompted the change. The commit message (13419661) and the comment on the field (`FileSystemWatcher.cs:41-47`) record the failure. A render-farm folder saw 2,000–3,000 `.partial` → final-name renames within about a second. At 8 KB the watcher overflowed and raised `Error`, the final names were missed, and finished jobs were never delivered. Reverting brings that bug back for anyone who hits the same pattern and doesn't know to set `InternalBufferSize`. The failure is silent apart from the `Error` event, which most apps don't handle.

**Where the reviewer is right**
- On Windows the buffer is real, per-watcher memory. The managed side allocates it with `NativeMemory.Alloc(_internalBufferSize)` (`FileSystemWatcher.Windows.cs:54`). The same size is handed to `ReadDirectoryChangesW`, which uses it for the kernel's buffer. I'm relying on the reviewer's claim that this comes from non-paged memory, and I haven't checked that. The unit test comment (`FileSystemWatcher.InternalBufferSize.cs:33-38`) says the OS uses `InternalBufferSize` for its internal buffer.
- The cost is per watcher. Apps with hundreds or thousands of watchers would pay 8× more by default (for example, 1,000 watchers would be 64 MB instead of 8 MB).
- Setting `InternalBufferSize` is a valid escape hatch, and it has always been the documented one.

**What decides the value**
1. **Per-event cost.** Each Windows event takes about `12 + 2 × (filename length + 1)` bytes, as `FileSystemWatcher.InternalBufferSize.cs:37` notes. A rename produces two events, old name and new name. With roughly 40-character names, one rename costs about 2 × 94 ≈ 190 bytes.
   - At 8 KB, that is about 43 renames before overflow.
   - At 64 KB, it is about 340 renames.
   - A burst of 2,000–3,000 renames needs about 400–600 KB at that name length. So 64 KB doesn't hold it either, and the commit's claim that "64 KB holds a burst of that size" looks wrong unless the names are very short. Please check that number before defending the change.
2. **Burst size against how fast the handler drains.** Overflow depends on how many events arrive before the next `ReadDirectoryChangesW` is re-issued. A slow handler makes it worse.
3. **Number of watchers.** This sets the cost of a larger default. It is the reviewer's real argument.
4. **Platform.** Linux ignores the value (`FileSystemWatcher.Linux.cs:100-102`), so the default only matters on Windows. macOS has its own restart path.

**Practical options**
- **Keep 64 KB** if you accept the memory cost and re-check the claim above. The default would then change observable behaviour for every consumer.
- **Revert to 8 KB** and fix the render-farm app by setting `InternalBufferSize` and handling `Error` (rescan the directory when it fires). This is the conservative, compatible choice. It matches long-standing guidance and what the reviewer asked for.
- **Pick a middle value** only if you can justify it from the arithmetic in point 1.

My lean is the revert plus a fix in the affected app. A runtime default shouldn't be tuned to one workload, and the 64 KB figure doesn't cover that workload anyway.

**If you keep 64 KB, the tests need updating.** `FileSystemWatcher.unit.cs:26` and `:264` still assert `Assert.Equal(8192, watcher.InternalBufferSize)` and will fail. The public docs also state the 8 KB default. I haven't changed any files.

- The doc gives two reasons. The linker gives `__TEXT,__text` special treatment, and `__managedcode` matches what NativeAOT already does.
- Read-only R2R data goes to `__TEXT,__const`. That covers jump tables, CLR metadata, Win32 resources, managed unwind info, GC info and the R2R headers.
- Import thunks stay in `__TEXT,__text`. Fixup tables stay in `__DATA,__data`, as they do in the PE layout.
- The doc doesn't say what the special treatment is, so I won't guess.

**How RVAs are expressed in Mach-O**
- Mach-O has no equivalent of the PE image base. COFF objects can express "offset from image base" directly.
- The doc uses the linker-provided symbol `__mh_dylib_header` as the base symbol. It's `__mh_<output>_header`, and it is the dylib version because the final image is a dylib.
- Each RVA is emitted as a Mach-O subtractor relocation meaning "symbol address − `__mh_dylib_header` address". The linker resolves it, and the runtime adds the result to the image base.
- Range sizes use the same mechanism: "end symbol − start symbol + end symbol size". A range starts at its start symbol. This avoids defining several symbols at one address, which the Apple linkers handle badly.

**Why `__mh_dylib_header` is the right base**
- It sits at the address that `dlinfo` and `dladdr` return as the image base. The runtime can therefore turn the RVAs into pointers using only what the loader already reports.
- It points at the Mach header. That lets the runtime work out the image size and bound its reads of R2R data.

**Why the runtime asks the host for the image**
- The runtime calls a new `get_native_code_data` callback in `host_runtime_contract`. It passes the component assembly path and the owner composite name.
- It gets back the R2R header pointer, the image size and the image base. If the call fails, the runtime falls back to IL and the JIT.

- That fits because the image is now an ordinary platform shared library rather than a PE file the runtime maps itself. The host decides how that library is found and loaded.

**What `--rtr-header-symbol-name` is for**
- By default the object exports the `READYTORUN_HEADER` as `RTR_HEADER`. This option renames that export.
- It's for custom hosts that link several R2R images directly instead of loading them with `dlopen`. In that case the exports would collide, so each image needs a distinct name. The host must then look up the header by the matching custom name.

output.text:
These answers come from `docs/design/coreclr/botr/readytorun-platform-native-envelope.md`. I spot-checked them against the code, and the code matches.

## Why managed code gets its own section (`__TEXT,__managedcode`)

The doc gives two reasons:

- **The linker treats `__TEXT,__text` specially.** Precompiled managed code isn't ordinary native code, and the linker shouldn't process it the way it processes `__text`.
- **It matches NativeAOT.** `ObjectNodeSection.ManagedCodeUnixContentSection` is `"__managedcode"` (`src/coreclr/tools/Common/Compiler/DependencyAnalysis/ObjectNodeSection.cs:49`). NativeAOT's bootstrap uses `section$start$__TEXT$__managedcode` and `section$end$__TEXT$__managedcode` to bracket the managed code range (`src/coreclr/nativeaot/Bootstrap/main.cpp:89`). A dedicated section gives the linker start and end symbols for that range.

The other R2R data is split up too:
- Read-only data goes to `__TEXT,__const`. That covers jump tables, metadata, unwind and GC info, and the R2R headers.
- Fixup tables stay in `__DATA,__data`.
- Import thunks stay in `__TEXT,__text`.

## How RVAs are expressed, and why measure from there

Mach-O has no image-base-relative address like COFF/PE does. The doc's answer has two parts:

- **Base symbol.** The object writer is constructed with `baseSymbolName: "__mh_dylib_header"` (`ReadyToRunObjectWriter.cs:335`). This is the Apple linker's symbol for the start of a dylib.
- **Encoding.** Each RVA is a Mach-O *subtractor* relocation, meaning `symbol − __mh_dylib_header`. The linker resolves it to a constant, so the RVA is fixed at link time and needs no runtime fixup.

Why this base is the right one:
- `__mh_dylib_header` sits at the address `dlinfo` and `dladdr` return as the image base. The runtime can therefore add an RVA to the `dlopen` base and get the same address the linker computed.
- It points at the Mach header. The runtime can parse that header to get the image size and bound its reads of R2R data.

The same subtractor mechanism represents range sizes, as `end − start + end size`. Apple linkers have trouble with several symbols defined at one location, so each range is identified by its start symbol only.

## Why the runtime asks the host instead of calling `dlopen`

For a component assembly with `READYTORUN_FLAG_PLATFORM_NATIVE_IMAGE`, the runtime reads `OwnerCompositeExecutable`. It then calls the host's `get_native_code_data` callback (`vm/hostinformation.cpp:139`) with the assembly path and the owner composite name. The host returns the R2R header pointer, the image size and the image base. If the callback fails, the runtime falls back to IL/JIT.

The doc says this "leaves it to the host to do the actual load". Examples are `dlopen` of a shared library, or something statically linked into the host itself. The host also owns any caching. The runtime can't assume the composite image is a loadable file at a known path. In an Apple app bundle, for example, it may be linked into the executable. The callback also means the runtime never has to implement a platform loader for Mach-O. It only needs the header pointer, the size and the base.

## What `--rtr-header-symbol-name` is for

By default `crossgen2` exports the `READYTORUN_HEADER` as `RTR_HEADER`. The option overrides that name. It is meant for custom hosts that **link several R2R images directly** instead of loading them dynamically through `dlopen`. In that case the images would all export `RTR_HEADER` and collide, so each needs a distinct name. The host then has to look the header up under the matching custom name. The SDK or build step that links the object into the final dylib must preserve that export under whichever name was used.
